pulls.title: RF03: don't unqualify correlated references in APPLY / LATERAL subqueries
pulls.body: ### Brief summary of the change made Fixes #8626. With `single_table_references = unqualified`, RF03 treated a subquery in the FROM clause as a single table select, even when it referenced tables of the outer query. T-SQL `CROSS APPLY` / `OUTER APPLY` and `LATERAL` joins allow that. The fix then removed those qualifiers, so `a.patientid = s.patientid` became `patientid = patientid`, which is always true. AL05 and ST05 could then make the result worse (see the issue). RF03 already counts the parent query's tables as visible for subqueries in the SELECT / WHERE clauses. This PR does the same for FROM clause subqueries, but only when one of their references uses an outer table. In valid SQL, only correlated subqueries (APPLY / LATERAL) do that. When the outer tables count as visible, the select has more than one table, so RF03 no longer offers unsafe fixes. Details: - Inner aliases shadow outer aliases with the same name. Those references point at the inner table and don't count as outer references. - CTEs are skipped. A CTE can't see the FROM clause of the main query, so CTE behaviour doesn't change. - Uncorrelated APPLY subqueries and plain derived tables are still single table selects and are still fixed as before. ### Are there any other side effects of this change that we should be aware of? - In `unqualified` mode, RF03 no longer reports qualified references inside a correlated APPLY / LATERAL subquery, not even references to the subquery's own table (`a.patientid` in the issue example). This is the same as the existing behaviour for correlated `WHERE EXISTS (...)` subqueries. - An uncorrelated APPLY subquery is still reported and fixed, while an uncorrelated `WHERE EXISTS` subquery is not. Both outcomes are safe. This PR doesn't change it. - For CTEs, behaviour is unchanged. RF03 still flags and fixes a qualifier in a CTE that names an alias of the main query (which is invalid SQL). A test now pins that existing behaviour. ### Pull Request checklist - [x] Please confirm you have completed any of the necessary steps below. - Included test cases to demonstrate any code changes, which may be one or more of the following: - `.yml` rule test cases in `test/fixtures/rules/std_rule_cases`: new cases in `RF03.yml` for T-SQL OUTER/CROSS APPLY, Postgres LATERAL, `qualified` mode, uncorrelated APPLY, a plain derived table and a CTE. - Added appropriate documentation for the change: not needed, no config or user-facing docs change. - Created GitHub issues for any relevant followup/future enhancements if appropriate: none yet. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) --- ## Summary by cubic Fixes #8626. With `single_table_references = unqualified`, RF03 treated FROM clause subqueries as single-table selects even when they referenced the outer query's tables, which `CROSS`/`OUTER APPLY` and `LATERAL` joins allow. The fix stripped those qualifiers, turning `a.patientid = s.patientid` into `patientid = patientid`, which is always true. RF03 now counts the tables of every enclosing query (walking the full ancestor chain, normalized to the dialect's casing) as visible for a subquery in the FROM clause, and for WHERE/SELECT subqueries whose direct parent has no tables, when any reference uses them. With more than one visible table the rule no longer offers the unsafe fix. Schema-qualified names are matched in full, so an inner `other.orders` no longer shadows an outer `public.orders`; longer qualifiers win over prefix matches. **Notes** - Inner aliases shadow outer aliases with the same name; those references don't count as outer. - A reference can name an unaliased T-SQL table variable in brackets (e.g. `[@orders].id`); such references keep the subquery correlated in `unqualified` mode. - CTEs can see the queries enclosing their `WITH` statement, so a CTE inside a LATERAL subquery keeps its qualifiers; a main-query CTE still can't see its FROM clause. - Uncorrelated APPLY subqueries and plain derived tables are still treated as single-table selects and fixed as before. - In `unqualified` mode, RF03 no longer reports qualified references inside correlated APPLY/LATERAL subqueries, even to the subquery's own table, matching the existing `WHERE EXISTS` behavior. - In `qualified`/`consistent` mode, RF03 still reports unqualified references in correlated APPLY/LATERAL subqueries but no longer fixes them, since the reference could point at an outer table. Unaliased T-SQL table variables count as visible outer tables only here, since only adding qualifiers can be unsafe. - In `qualified` mode, RF03 no longer qualifies references in a plain derived table nested in a LATERAL/APPLY subquery, since such a table can still see the enclosing queries' columns. Written for commit 7d2eccac0ad3844b05f3c27f8ebf6a11e8a5d9ab. Summary will update on new commits.

pulls.title: Don't move templated comments in LT05's long line fix
pulls.body: Fixes #8616. ### Problem `sqlfluff fix` **corrupts files** when LT05 moves a long trailing comment which contains a Jinja tag. The moved copy is built from the comment's `raw`, i.e. the *rendered* text, so the tags are dropped from the copy. The original comment is then only partly deleted, because `_iter_templated_patches` splits the deletion at the tag placeholders and `generate_source_patches` skips the parts which contain a tag: ```sql -- comment more text here that goes on and on and on select a, b, c from tbl {% if true %} more{% endif %} text here that goes on and on and on ``` The text left on the code line is then parsed as SQL, so `sqlfluff lint` reports `PRS` and spurious aliasing rules (`AL01`, `AL05`) on the fragments. For `{% set %}` and `{{ ... }}` tags the deletion is skipped as a whole instead, so the comment ends up duplicated — once more on every fix run — and the line is still too long. The normal break path of LT05 already guards against this with `_is_templated_safe_break` (#7640), but `_fix_long_line_with_comment` had no equivalent check. ### Fix Don't move a comment which isn't literal in the source. If it spans a templated section it contains tags, and those tags cannot survive being moved, so the line is reported as unfixable instead: ```python if comment_seg.pos_marker and not comment_seg.pos_marker.is_literal(): reflow_logger.debug(" Unfixable because comment is not literal.") return elements, [] ``` This follows the two existing unfixable guards in the same function (`noqa`, and "comment too long anyway"), and leaves comments which merely *follow* templated code untouched — only a comment which itself spans a templated section is now left alone. ### Behaviour after this change `sqlfluff fix` reports `3 unfixable linting violations found` for the three examples in the issue, exits 0, and the files are left byte-for-byte unchanged. Plain long comments are still moved as before. ### Tests Three cases added to `test/fixtures/rules/std_rule_cases/LT05.yml`, one per tag type from the issue (`{% if %}`, `{% set %}`, `{# #}`). Each asserts the violation is reported and that **no** fix is applied. All three fail without the guard and pass with it. - `pytest test/rules/yaml_test_cases_test.py -k LT05` → 60 passed - `pytest test/utils/ test/rules/ test/core/rules/` → 2972 passed, 104 skipped - `ruff format --check` / `ruff check` clean ### AI assistance disclosure Per CONTRIBUTING.md ("AI-Assisted Contributions"): this change was drafted with AI assistance. I validated it manually by reproducing the corruption from the issue on `main` (2e22757), confirming the three corrupted outputs, then confirming byte-identical files and an "unfixable" report with the fix applied; I verified plain comments are still moved, checked the guard against the existing `pos_marker` idiom in this module (`Optional[PositionMarker]`, so the `None` case is excluded), confirmed all existing LT05 cases still pass, and checked that removing the guard makes exactly the three new tests fail. I'm happy to walk through the reflow flow if useful. --- ## Summary by cubic Fixes #8616. LT05's long line fix corrupted files when it moved a trailing comment containing a Jinja tag: the moved copy is built from the comment's rendered text, so tags were dropped and leftover tag text was parsed as SQL. Comments that span a templated section are now left in place and the line is reported as unfixable instead. - Adds a guard that skips moving any comment whose position isn't literal in the source, matching the existing unfixable cases in the same function. - Adds three LT05 test cases covering `{% if %}`, `{% set %}`, and `{# #}` tags inside comments, each asserting the violation is reported with no fix applied. Written for commit 155d83b53f63fdaf76b5d5bb45ed195625a32d8e. Summary will update on new commits.

pulls.title: BigQuery: parse WITH expressions
pulls.body: ### Brief summary of the change made fixes #8608 BigQuery has a `WITH` expression. It assigns one or more variables and returns its last argument, for example `WITH(a AS 1, b AS a + 1, a + b)`. The bigquery dialect has no grammar for it. Most of these statements are unparsable, and `WITH(a AS (SELECT 1), a)` parses as a call to a function named `WITH`. This change adds `WithExpressionSegment`, with the type `with_expression`. The grammar is `WITH ( variable_name AS expression [, ...], result_expression )`, from the [BigQuery operators page](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/reference/standard-sql/operators#with_expression). The segment goes into `Expression_D_Potential_Select_Statement_Without_Brackets`, which sits in the inner `OneOf` of `Expression_D_Grammar`. A `WITH` expression can therefore stand where any other expression can, and it takes array subscripts and struct fields after it. `BaseExpressionElementGrammar` tries `FunctionSegment` before `ExpressionSegment`. The function grammar therefore took `WITH(...)` first when the arguments also fit a function call. This change adds `WITH` to the `anti_template` of `FunctionNameIdentifierSegment`, next to `STRUCT` and `ARRAY`. The variables of a `WITH` expression are declared in place. `get_select_statement_info` in `utils/analysis/select.py` now finds the references to each variable and drops them from the reference buffer by id. A reference counts only when it is in a later expression of the same `WITH` expression. That expression can hold a subquery or a nested `WITH` expression. For a subquery, the analysis finds the enclosing `WITH` expressions through the parents of the select. This applies to every clause, join conditions and `UNNEST` included. A backtick-quoted variable or reference matches the same name without backticks. RF01, RF02 and RF03 therefore do not report these references. A column with the same name as a variable still gets RF02. This holds in the select clause, in the other clauses, in the assignment of that variable and in an outer select. It also holds in a subquery inside the assignment of that variable. The BigQuery page writes `WITH(` with no space, as it does for `ARRAY(` and `STRUCT(`. A new `[sqlfluff:layout:type:with_expression]` section in `default_config.cfg` sets `spacing_within = touch:inline`, the same as `struct_type`. LT01 accepts `WITH(` and fixes `WITH (` to `WITH(`. Measured with `Linter.parse_string`, one statement at a time: | statement | `main` at `44751a642` | this branch | |---|---|---| | `SELECT WITH(a AS '123', b AS CONCAT(a, '456'), c AS '789', CONCAT(b, c)) AS result;` | unparsable | `with_expression` | | `SELECT WITH(a AS RAND(), a - a);` | unparsable | `with_expression` | | `SELECT WITH(s AS SUM(input), c AS COUNT(input), s/c) FROM UNNEST([1.0, 2.0, 3.0]) AS input;` | unparsable | `with_expression` | | `WITH my_table AS (SELECT 1 AS x, 2 AS y) SELECT WITH(a AS SUM(x), b AS COUNT(x), a/b) AS avg_x FROM my_table;` | unparsable | `with_expression` | | `SELECT WITH(a AS 1, a) + 1;` | unparsable | `with_expression` | | `SELECT CONCAT(WITH(a AS 'x', a), 'y');` | unparsable | `with_expression` | | `SELECT WITH(a AS WITH(b AS 1, b + 1), a * 2);` | unparsable | `with_expression` | | `SELECT x FROM t WHERE WITH(a AS x * 2, a) > 10;` | unparsable | `with_expression` | | `SELECT WITH(a AS [1, 2], a)[OFFSET(0)];` | unparsable | `with_expression`, `array_accessor` | | `SELECT WITH(a AS STRUCT(1 AS x), a).x;` | unparsable | `with_expression`, `semi_structured_expression` | | `SELECT WITH(a AS (SELECT 1), a);` | function named `WITH` | `with_expression` | | `SELECT WITH(1);` | function named `WITH` | unparsable | | `SELECT WITH(a AS 1);` | unparsable | unparsable | The first four statements come from the BigQuery page. The last two do not match the documented grammar, which needs at least one variable and a result expression. The Python parser and the Rust parser built from this branch give the same result for all 13 statements. A `WITH` clause still parses as before. I checked a `WITH` clause in a scalar subquery, after `IN` and after `FROM`, on `main` and on this branch. An example is `SELECT (WITH c AS (SELECT 1 AS x) SELECT x FROM c) AS y;`. A quoted function name, as in `` SELECT `with`(1); ``, also still parses. ### Are there any other side effects of this change that we should be aware of? - The `select.py` change applies only to a select that contains a `with_expression` or sits inside one. Only the bigquery dialect makes that segment. - AL05 now reads `t.x` in `WITH(t AS STRUCT(1 AS x), t.x)` as the variable, not as a table alias `t`. A table alias `t` with no other use therefore gets AL05. The BigQuery page does not say if a variable hides a table alias with the same name. - `SELECT WITH(1);` parsed as a function call on `main` and is unparsable on this branch. - No other dialect inherits from bigquery. ### Pull Request checklist - [x] Please confirm you have completed any of the necessary steps below. - Included test cases to demonstrate any code changes, which may be one or more of the following: - [x] `.yml` rule test cases in `test/fixtures/rules/std_rule_cases`: 5 cases in `RF01.yml`, 7 in `RF02.yml`, 1 in `RF03.yml` and 2 in `LT01-functions.yml`. 6 of them put a variable in a subquery inside a `WITH` expression. Each change below makes some of the 15 cases fail: - The filter removed from `select.py`: 7 fail. - The filter only in the select clause: 1 fails. - A variable in scope before its own assignment: 3 fail. - The backticks kept in the variable name or in the reference name: 1 fails. - The variables excluded by name for the whole select: 1 fails. - No variables from the enclosing `WITH` expressions: 4 fail. - The variables from the innermost enclosing `WITH` expression only: 1 fails. - All variables of an enclosing `WITH` expression in scope, in any order: 2 fail. - The layout section reverted: 2 fail. - [x] `.sql`/`.yml` parser test cases in `test/fixtures/dialects` (note YML files can be auto generated with `tox -e generate-fixture-yml`): `test/fixtures/dialects/bigquery/with_expression.sql` and its `.yml` from `python test/generate_parse_fixture_yml.py -d bigquery -f 'with_expression*'`. The fixture holds the four examples from the BigQuery page and both accessor statements. It also has `WITH` expressions in an arithmetic expression, a function argument, another `WITH` expression and a `WHERE` clause. With the segment back in `Expression_C_Grammar`, 3 dialect tests fail on this fixture. - Full autofix test cases in `test/fixtures/linter/autofix`. - [x] Other: `test/dialects/bigquery_test.py` requires a parse error for `WITH(1)` and `WITH(a AS 1)`, with and without a space before the bracket. - [x] Added appropriate documentation for the change. The new segment carries the link to the BigQuery page. - [ ] Created GitHub issues for any relevant followup/future enhancements if appropriate. None needed: this PR fixes the RF01, RF02, RF03 and LT01 cases. Test results: ``` Python parser Rust parser test/rules/yaml_test_cases_test.py 2542 passed 2542 passed test/dialects/bigquery_test.py test/dialects/dialects_test.py -k bigquery 459 passed 459 passed pytest test (full suite) 11409 passed, 8 failed utils/build_parsers.py bigquery --table-driven exit 0 utils/build_lexers.py bigquery exit 0 ruff format --check . 480 files already formatted ruff check . All checks passed! pre-commit run --files all hooks passed ``` The 8 failures in the full suite are plugin tests. The same 8 fail on `main` in my environment, because the example plugin is not installed. I built the Rust parser with Rust 1.98.1, not the pinned 1.96. AI usage: I used Claude Code CLI with Opus 5.5 and Codex. --- ## Summary by cubic Adds parsing for BigQuery `WITH` expressions, which assign variables and return their last argument (`WITH(a AS 1, a + 1)`). These previously failed to parse or were misparsed as a call to a function named `WITH`. Fixes #8608. - New `WithExpressionSegment` (type `with_expression`) sits in `Expression_D_Potential_Select_Statement_Without_Brackets` so it takes array and struct accessors after it, and `WITH` joins `STRUCT` and `ARRAY` in the function name anti-template. - Select analysis drops references to declared `WITH` variables (backtick-quoted and bare names match) so RF01, RF02, and RF03 don't flag them; subqueries inside the expression can use the variables of enclosing expressions. - Parser fixtures cover the BigQuery documented examples plus nested, embedded, WHERE-clause, and accessor cases; rule cases keep subqueries valid BigQuery by selecting one column. **Behavior changes** - `SELECT WITH(1);` parsed as a function call on `main` and is now unparsable, since the documented grammar requires at least one variable and a result expression. - LT01 now flags the space between `WITH` and `(` in `WITH(...)`; `sqlfluff fix` rewrites it to `WITH (`. Written for commit 1f953318020fd5a6b26233241e1f013606289faa. Summary will update on new commits.

pulls.title: LT05: Do not move a trailing comment that contains a template tag
pulls.body: ### Brief summary of the change made makes progress on #8616 LT05 moves a long trailing comment before or after its line. When the source of the comment contains a Jinja tag, both moves corrupt the file: - With `trailing_comments = before` (the default), LT05 builds the moved comment from the rendered text, so the tags are lost. The delete of the original is split at the tag placeholders, and `generate_source_patches` skips the parts that contain a tag. - With `trailing_comments = after`, LT05 inserts a break before the tag placeholders. The tags, and any text between them, are copied onto the code line. `_fix_long_line_with_comment` now reports the line as unfixable when `comment_seg.pos_marker.is_literal()` is false. The check runs before both moves. The normal break path has a similar check in `_is_templated_safe_break` (#7640). Measured with `sqlfluff fix --dialect ansi --rules LT05` on the three files from #8616: | file | `main` at `2e2275713`, `before` | `main`, `after` | this branch, both modes | |---|---|---|---| | q1, `{% if %}` | the text from the first tag on stays on the code line as SQL | ` {% if true %} more{% endif %}` is copied onto the code line | file unchanged | | q2, `{% set %}` | the comment is in the file twice | `{% set q = 1 %}` is copied onto the code line | file unchanged | | q3, `{# #}` | the text from the tag on stays on the code line as SQL | `{# x #}` is copied onto the code line | file unchanged | On `main`, the command exits with 0 in both modes and reports 3 fixable violations. On this branch, it reports 3 unfixable violations, prints no "Skipping edit patch" warning and exits with 1. ### Are there any other side effects of this change that we should be aware of? In `after` mode, `main` moves `select a, b, c from tbl -- comment{{ 'x' }} more text here that goes on and on and on` correctly. This branch reports that line as unfixable. A `{{ '' }}` tag in the same place gets the corrupt result on `main`, so I kept one check for all tags. This PR does not fix the double count in #8616. LT05 still counts each tag in the comment twice, so q3 (77 characters) is reported as `84 > 80`. The count comes from `_source_char_len`. My open PR #8605 also changes that function, so I left the count for a separate PR. ### Pull Request checklist - [x] Please confirm you have completed any of the necessary steps below. - Included test cases to demonstrate any code changes, which may be one or more of the following: - [x] `.yml` rule test cases in `test/fixtures/rules/std_rule_cases`: three new LT05 cases, for `{% if %}` and `{% set %}` in `before` mode and for `{% if %}` in `after` mode. All three fail on `main`. With this branch, `test/utils/reflow`, `test/rules` and `test/core/linter` give 2982 passed and 101 skipped. `ruff format --check .`, `ruff check .` and `mypy -p sqlfluff` are clean. - [x] Added appropriate documentation for the change. None needed. - [x] Created GitHub issues for any relevant followup/future enhancements if appropriate. The double count stays open in #8616. AI usage: I used Claude Code CLI with Opus 5.5 and Codex. --- ## Summary by cubic Prevents LT05 from moving a trailing comment that contains a template tag, since both move directions corrupt the file. Moving the comment before the line rebuilds it from rendered text and loses the tags; moving it after copies the tags and interleaved text onto the code line. - Comments whose source is not literal are reported as unfixable in both `trailing_comments` modes. - Uses the same position marker check as `_is_templated_safe_break` so a comment without a marker does not crash. - Adds test cases for `{% if %}` and `{% set %}` blocks and for `after` mode. - Makes progress on #8616; the double count of tag characters remains unfixed. Written for commit 79e315d7f6ed69ea8fd6b4a6a0cdd265c4ea17b9. Summary will update on new commits.

pulls.title: Keep the token text before a Jinja tag inside the token
pulls.body: ### Brief summary of the change made fixes #8611 A token can span a Jinja tag, as in `b{% if true %}c{% endif %}`. The lexer then yields the placeholder for the tag, and its indent or dedent, before the token. Their templated position is after the start of the token. `BaseSegment._position_segments` and `_iter_templated_patches` used that position as a boundary. A fix next to the token then deleted the text before the tag. The change has three parts: - A new helper, `inside_next_segment_flags` in `parser/helpers.py`, flags each zero-length segment that sits inside a later sibling. It makes one backward pass over the siblings. - `_position_segments` and `_iter_templated_patches` skip such a segment, as they already skip the empty template placeholder from #6261. When the previous sibling is such a segment, a new segment starts at its end point. - With the correct position, `_iter_templated_patches` dropped a gap in the templated file after an insertion, so a moved token kept its old text. The patch now covers that gap. LT02 plus LT09 on `select\nb{# note #}c` needs this part. Measured with `Linter.lint_string(sql, fix=True)` and the `ansi` dialect: | rules | input | `main` at `2e2275713` | this branch | |---|---|---|---| | LT02 | `select\nb{% if true %}c{% endif %}` | `select\n {% if true %}c{% endif %}` | `select\n b{% if true %}c{% endif %}` | | LT01 | `select a , b{% if true %}c{% endif %}` | `select a, {% if true %}c{% endif %}` | `select a, b{% if true %}c{% endif %}` | | LT01 | `select b{% if true %}c{% endif %}, a , x` | `select {% if true %}c{% endif %}, a, x` | `select b{% if true %}c{% endif %}, a, x` | | LT05 | the trailing comment example from the issue | `-- trailing comment here` is deleted | the comment moves to its own line | | LT05 | `{% if false %}select <65 a>{% endif %}select 1` | the 65 `a` are deleted | the 65 `a` are kept | | default | `select a, b{% if true %}c{% endif %}` | `a,{% if true %}` then `b{% if true %}c{% endif %}`, the tag is duplicated | `a,` then `b{% if true %}c{% endif %}` | ### Are there any other side effects of this change that we should be aware of? I ran 508 inputs through `main` and this branch. They cover `{% if %}`, `{% for %}`, `{# #}`, `{{ '' }}`, whitespace control, several rules together, and a few dialects. The fix loses text on 209 inputs on `main` and on 22 inputs on this branch. All 22 are intended rule edits, for example CV02 `ifnull` to `COALESCE` and CV05 `= null` to `is null`. No input loses or duplicates more text on this branch than on `main`. Two things I did not change: - With the default rules, LT02 indents a token that spans an `{% if %}` block one level more than its siblings. The indent for the tag sits before the token. On `main` the same input duplicates the tag. - LT05 still deletes text when it moves a `--` comment that itself contains an `{% if %}` or `{# #}` tag. `main` gives the same output. LT05 builds the moved comment from the rendered text, so that is a separate problem. I filed it as #8616. The change is in Python only, in code that runs after the lexer. ### Pull Request checklist - [x] Please confirm you have completed any of the necessary steps below. - Included test cases to demonstrate any code changes, which may be one or more of the following: - [x] Other: `test__fix__token_spanning_jinja_tag` in `test/core/linter/fix_test.py`, with 6 cases for LT01, LT02, LT05, LT09 and LT02 plus LT09. When I revert the `base.py` change, the skip in `patch.py` or the gap part in `patch.py`, at least one case fails. The full `test/` suite has 11393 passed and 2629 skipped. The 8 failures are the example plugin and diff-quality plugin tests, which fail the same way on `main` in my environment. `mypy -p sqlfluff.core --strict`, `ruff format --check .` and `ruff check .` are clean. - [x] Added appropriate documentation for the change. None needed. - [x] Created GitHub issues for any relevant followup/future enhancements if appropriate. The LT05 comment case above is #8616. AI usage: Claude Code CLI with Opus 5.5. I checked the fix with the before and after runs above and the test run. --- ## Summary by cubic Fixes #8611 so lint auto-fixes no longer delete the text before a Jinja tag when a token spans the tag, as in `b{% if true %}c{% endif %}`. **Bug Fixes** - Treats a zero-length segment positioned inside a later sibling (a tag placeholder or its indent) like the existing empty template placeholder from #6261: it is skipped when looking for segment end points and when generating patches. - When the previous sibling is such a segment, a new segment now starts at the end point instead, so fixes keep the text before the tag. - Patches now cover a templated-file gap after an insertion so a moved token retains its old text. - Computes the inside-next-segment flags in a single backward pass per sibling list, avoiding quadratic patch generation on long runs of zero-length segments (a 3200-block stress case went from 13s to 3.3s). - Adds regression tests covering LT01, LT02, LT05, and LT09, including a comment-move case that loses text on the old behavior. Written for commit 282bb2f6955c12ccb84a967cf40a81434ed4aa54. Summary will update on new commits.

pulls.title: dbt templater: check for dbt-core at runtime instead of depending on it
pulls.body: ### Brief summary of the change made fixes #8505 `sqlfluff-templater-dbt` declares `dbt-core>=1.4.1`. In a `dbt-oss` 2.x environment, that makes pip install dbt-core alongside it. Both distributions ship the `dbt` import package, so dbt-core overwrites dbt-oss's files without any warning. `pip check` passes, but `dbt` is now dbt-core. The issue has the full reproduction. In the issue, @rubytobi suggested a runtime check in the templater. This PR adds that check. It also drops the declared dependency, because a check alone runs only after the install has already overwritten dbt-oss. - **`pyproject.toml`:** the `dbt-core>=1.4.1` requirement is removed. A comment records why. - **`templater.py`:** `DbtTemplater.__init__` calls a new `check_dbt_installation()` before importing anything from dbt. sqlfluff only creates the templater when `templater = dbt` is selected, so other templaters are unaffected. The check raises `SQLFluffUserError`, which the CLI reports as `Error loading config: …` with a non-zero exit. It refuses in three cases: - **dbt-oss is installed**, alone or next to dbt-core. It can't be supported: the templater captures the Jinja environment by patching `jinja2.Environment.from_string` while dbt compiles, and dbt-oss renders Jinja in Rust. dbt-oss's Python surface is only `dbtRunner.invoke()` plus the artifact dataclasses. - **dbt-core is missing.** The message says to install it with an adapter. - **dbt-core is older than 1.4.1**, the same minimum as before. Only `X.Y.Z` is compared, so pre-releases like `1.10.0b1` pass. - **Docs:** a note in `configuration/templating/dbt.rst` saying the templater needs dbt-core but doesn't install it, and that dbt-oss isn't supported. - **Tests:** `test__templater_dbt_missing` is replaced. It only ran when `dbt` wasn't importable, which never happens in the dbt tox envs. It also expected a `pip install sqlfluff[dbt]` message that nothing in the code produces. The new tests fake the installed packages, so they run in every dbt env. ### Are there any other side effects of this change that we should be aware of? - **Installing only `sqlfluff-templater-dbt` no longer installs dbt-core.** Most setups won't notice: the templater has always needed an adapter, and adapters depend on dbt-core (checked for `dbt-postgres` 1.11, `dbt-spark` 1.10 and `dbt-databricks` 1.12). If an adapter doesn't, the new error says what to install. CONTRIBUTING.md sends backwards-incompatible changes through the major-release process, so I'll follow the maintainers' call on whether this waits for one. - **`pip check` no longer flags a dbt-core older than 1.4.1.** The runtime check covers it. - **CI keeps working:** the dbt tox envs already install `dbt-core` explicitly from `constraints/dbt*.txt`. ### Pull Request checklist - [x] Please confirm you have completed any of the necessary steps below. - Included test cases to demonstrate any code changes, which may be one or more of the following: - Other: `test__templater_dbt_installation_errors` and `test__templater_dbt_installation_ok` in `plugins/sqlfluff-templater-dbt/test/templater_test.py`. - Added appropriate documentation for the change. - Created GitHub issues for any relevant followup/future enhancements if appropriate. (None needed.) ### Testing and AI disclosure This change was drafted with Claude Code: the root-cause analysis, the code, the tests and this description. I reviewed the diff and checked it as follows: - **Unit tests, dbt-core 1.10, Python 3.12:** the new tests plus the templater tests that don't need a database all pass. I didn't run the Postgres-backed tests locally, so I'm relying on CI for those. - **Linting:** `ruff check` and `ruff format --check` are clean on the plugin. - **End to end:** in a fresh venv I ran `pip install dbt-oss==2.0.4`, then installed this branch's plugin. `dbt --version` still reports `dbt-oss 2.0.4`, and no dbt-core was installed. `sqlfluff lint --templater dbt` exits 2 with the dbt-oss message, and `sqlfluff lint --templater jinja` in the same env still works. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) --- ## Summary by cubic Fixes #8505 by removing the `dbt-core>=1.4.1` dependency from `sqlfluff-templater-dbt` and checking the dbt installation at runtime instead. The old dependency made pip install dbt-core into a `dbt-oss` environment, where it silently overwrote the `dbt` package dbt-oss ships. - The templater now refuses to start (with a clear error) when dbt-oss is installed, when dbt-core is missing, or when dbt-core is older than 1.4.1. - Installing only `sqlfluff-templater-dbt` no longer installs dbt-core; most adapters already depend on it. Written for commit 7778f5c4e7883f43eb8b383b9fe7f2dbbeb75ae0. Summary will update on new commits.

pulls.title: fix(AL05): keep ClickHouse table function aliases in joins, comma lists
pulls.body: ### Brief summary of the change made Makes progress on #4743 (the table function alias point). ClickHouse requires an alias on a table function when its FROM clause has more than one table source: either side of a join, CROSS JOIN included, or a comma list. The error is `ALIAS_REQUIRED` (code 206), controlled by `joined_subquery_requires_alias`, which is on by default. AL05 flagged those aliases and `sqlfluff fix` removed them, producing SQL that ClickHouse refuses: ```sql SELECT count() FROM numbers(3) INNER JOIN numbers(2) AS b ON 1 = 1 -- Code: 206 SELECT count() FROM numbers(3), numbers(2) AS b -- Code: 206 SELECT count() FROM numbers(3) -- ok, no alias needed ``` For ClickHouse only, AL05 now counts the table sources of each SELECT's own FROM clause, and keeps the alias of any table function in a FROM clause with more than one source. A lone table function, with or without ARRAY JOIN, is still flagged. The count stops at nested SELECTs, so a UNION branch, a CTE or the query inside `view()` keeps its own count. ### Are there any other side effects of this change that we should be aware of? Other dialects are unchanged (an ANSI case covers this). The rule assumes the ClickHouse default for `joined_subquery_requires_alias`, since it cannot see server settings. ### Pull Request checklist - [x] Please confirm you have completed any of the necessary steps below. - Included test cases: `.yml` rule test cases in `test/fixtures/rules/std_rule_cases/AL05.yml` (left and right side of a join, comma list, CROSS JOIN, a lone table function, ARRAY JOIN, UNION and CTE scoping, a nested `view()`, and an ANSI control). AI assistance: the code and tests were drafted with an AI assistant. I checked the behaviour against ClickHouse 26.9.6.6 (`clickhouse-local`, default settings) for the join, comma list, CROSS JOIN, lone table function, ARRAY JOIN and `view()` cases, confirmed the new pass cases fail without the change, and reviewed the diff. --- ## Summary by cubic Fixes the AL05 autofix producing invalid SQL for ClickHouse by keeping table function aliases in FROM clauses with more than one table source. ClickHouse requires an alias on any table function on either side of a join or in a comma list, while `sqlfluff fix` previously stripped those aliases, yielding SQL that ClickHouse rejects with `ALIAS_REQUIRED` (code 206). Sources are counted per SELECT, so UNION branches, CTEs, and queries inside `view()` keep their own count; a lone table function, with or without ARRAY JOIN, is still flagged. Only the table function's alias is kept—unused aliases on plain tables in the same join are still removed. Other dialects are unchanged, and the rule assumes ClickHouse's default `joined_subquery_requires_alias` setting since it can't read server settings. Written for commit bc962f7043d17b0ab5ad024e422290ad2ee1aa57. Summary will update on new commits.

pulls.title: fix(mysql): stop silent misparses from the catch-all typed-literal rule
pulls.body:
### Brief summary of the change made I'm sorry this is so large but it has to be. There was a significant amount of syntax all hidden behind a small incorrect parse rule in dialect_ansi.py that treats WORD LITERAL as a typed literal every time (SELECT foo 'x' FROM t becomes type foo literal 'x' not column foo alias x), and fixing it requires actually implementing the missing syntax that it hid. This is ~160 lines of grammar not including comments but it also specifies lists of character sets, tests, etc. This behavior is nowhere in the ansi specification and should not be in dialect_ansi.py either. It also breaks other dialects so I'm fixing this in two parts. This is the first one. It includes the KILL patch I promised in #8584. Fixtures and rejection tests tested against MariaDB 11.8 (originally), and MySQL 8.4 and 9.7 (done later, worked fine, no changes required). Feel free to just look at the code here - the details tabs are only if you want more details you don't have to read them.
Where this is going in future patches I also want to clarify that I'm not failing to unify the things. I have planned a separate PR with a fix I've already tested locally. I just didn't want to put it in this PR because it's already a bit difficult to review. I can put it in this PR if you like. I have a tested fix for the workaround split on ansi's second inconsistent copy of the typed literal rule. Originally it had two copies, one in Expression_D_Grammar one in BaseExpressionElementGrammar that do not agree. (I extracted a part of Expression_D_Grammar's contents into TypedLiteralGrammar with no behavior change in order to be able to switch it off.) I've tested a fix locally that will unify these that changes nothing (all fixtures parse the same), but it does theoretically touch a lot of variants. The only things I can find that it might theoretically break are invalid things that don't even follow the syntax for them like invalid TYPE ARRAY stanzas in snowflake and bigquery: `SELECT INTEGER ARRAY[1]` and so forth, so I think this is safe, especially because the previous parsing of even the invalid stuff would have been incorrect. Upon further inspection, this exact same WORD LITERAL parse hits 14 dialects: ansi, ClickHouse, DB2, DuckDB, Flink, Greenplum, Materialize, Oracle, Postgres, SOQL, SQLite, Teradata, T-SQL and Vertica. It's wrong in SQLite and TSQL too, in Postgres it's actually correct, and I didn't check the rest. Once this and my planned unification fix merge, the fix appears to be just TypedLiteralGrammar=Nothing() in TSQL (I don't have a running TSQL server), and using ansi TypedLiteralGrammar then setting it to Nothing() in SQLite. I suspect its also easy in other variants with the same problem (though it ideally should be done by someone who works in that dialect to make sure something else didn't subtly break). I suspect other fixes will be similarly minor in other dialects after this PR and the planned fix follow up. The deeper problem is that Postgres leaked into ansi in a minor accident, an overly broad categorization in a pr #1338 (intent was `TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE ...` but ended up matching any type name) - but that has to wait until after this PR and my planned follow up, and will require more people than just me to fix because things depend on it.
--- Short version ended above --- Rest is description that you may choose to ignore and just look at the code. I did review and edit the part below, however. ---
The problem in detail In the mysql and mariadb dialects, any word followed by a literal parses as a typed literal: a value of a data type named by the word. MySQL only has this form for `DATE '2020-01-01'`, `TIME '10:00'` and `TIMESTAMP '2020-01-01 10:00'`, which have their own grammar and are unaffected. The general form comes from ansi's `Expression_D_Grammar`, but it is a PostgreSQL extension, not standard SQL: "SQL specifies this syntax only for a few data types, but PostgreSQL allows it for all types" ([PostgreSQL docs](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-syntax-lexical.html#SQL-SYNTAX-CONSTANTS-GENERIC)). So these parse silently wrong: | SQL | Parsed as | Actually | |---|---|---| | `SELECT foo 'x' FROM t` | a value of type `foo` | column `foo`, alias `'x'` | | `GROUP_CONCAT(v SEPARATOR ', ')` | a value of type `SEPARATOR` | the `SEPARATOR` clause | | `GROUP_CONCAT(v LIMIT 2)` (MariaDB) | a value of type `LIMIT` | a `LIMIT` clause | | `SELECT HARD 5`, `SELECT INT 5` | a value of type `HARD` / `INT` | syntax error | `SEPARATOR` is the common case in practice: tested against a large codebase, all (dozens) `GROUP_CONCAT ... SEPARATOR` sites parsed this way. sqlfluff already has grammar for `SEPARATOR` (in ansi's `FunctionContentsGrammar`), but the typed-literal reading wins the match. This came up in #8584 (`KILL`). The same rule made `KILL HARD 5` parse in the mysql dialect, which is why that PR's `KillIdGrammar` is narrower than the server's `KILL [CONNECTION | QUERY] expr`.
Full change list Changes: - **ansi**, with no behaviour change (every dialect's fixtures regenerate identically): - The typed-literal alternative in `Expression_D_Grammar` becomes a named `TypedLiteralGrammar`, so a dialect can switch it off. - The generic function path's `exclude=` list becomes a named `FunctionNameExclusionGrammar`, so a dialect with its own grammar for a function can keep the generic path from also matching it. - **mysql**: `TypedLiteralGrammar` is `Nothing()`, and ansi's second copy of the rule (`DatatypeSegment` + `LiteralGrammar`) is removed from `BaseExpressionElementGrammar`; see "Where this stops" for why there are two. - **mysql**: character set introducers, `_utf8mb4'x'` and `_latin1 X'41'` (`IntroducedLiteralSegment`). The server only treats `_word` as an introducer when `word` is a character set, so `_foo 'x'` is a column with an alias. The names are a `character_set_names` dialect set, from the [MySQL 8.4 list](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/charset-charsets.html). mariadb drops `GB18030`, which MariaDB doesn't have; there, `_gb18030'x'` is a column with an alias. - **mysql**: the national string `N'x'` is lexed as one token (`single_quote_with_n`, the same approach as T-SQL). mysql already does this for `X'41'` and `b'01'`. `N 'x'` and `N"x"` are both a column with an alias on the server. - **mysql**: `BINARY` becomes a unary prefix operator. This also fixes `SELECT BINARY col FROM t`, which main parses as a variable named `BINARY` with the alias `col`. - **mysql**: `GROUP_CONCAT` gets its own grammar, following MySQL's parser ([`sql_yacc.yy`](https://github.com/mysql/mysql-server/blob/99960bf74fa919347e4f4e3ca47672f333d6e91f/sql/sql_yacc.yy#L11077-L11080)): `[DISTINCT] expr, ... [ORDER BY ...] [SEPARATOR ...]` in that order, then an optional `OVER`. It is excluded from the generic function path. This also fixes `GROUP_CONCAT(DISTINCT (SELECT ...))`, which main parses as a function named `DISTINCT`. - **mariadb**: `GROUP_CONCAT` takes a trailing `LIMIT`, and `JSON_ARRAYAGG` gets its own grammar: `[DISTINCT] expr [ORDER BY ...] [LIMIT ...]`, then an optional `OVER`. MySQL has neither form.
Where the docs and the server's grammar disagree We read MySQL's parser source, not just the manual, and checked MariaDB's behaviour on a server. The grammar follows the parser where they differ: - **The `SEPARATOR` value** is documented as `str_val`. The parser takes `text_string`, which is a string, a hexadecimal literal or a bit-value literal ([`sql_yacc.yy`](https://github.com/mysql/mysql-server/blob/99960bf74fa919347e4f4e3ca47672f333d6e91f/sql/sql_yacc.yy#L14705-L14727)). So `SEPARATOR X'7C'` and `SEPARATOR 0b01111100` are accepted, while `SEPARATOR 5` and `SEPARATOR 'a' 'b'` are not. MariaDB behaves the same way. - **`OVER` on `GROUP_CONCAT`**: the manual says it is not a window function, but the parser accepts `opt_windowing_clause` after it ([`sql_yacc.yy`](https://github.com/mysql/mysql-server/blob/99960bf74fa919347e4f4e3ca47672f333d6e91f/sql/sql_yacc.yy#L11080)). The error comes later, as "not supported". MariaDB does the same, including for `JSON_ARRAYAGG`. - **`N'x'` vs `N"x"`**: the manual shows `N'literal'`. On the server, the double-quoted form is a column with an alias. - **`GROUP_CONCAT ... LIMIT`** in MariaDB must come after `SEPARATOR`; any other position is a syntax error on the server.
Where this stops, and why The line drawn is: match what the server's parser accepts, and stay loose about what it only rejects later, at execution. Grammar that mirrors the parser does not make sqlfluff fragile, because MySQL's parser grammar barely changes; grammar that mirrors runtime checks would. - **`OVER` on `GROUP_CONCAT`** is accepted, as above, although neither server can run it today. - **The generic function-argument grammar** (ansi's `FunctionContentsGrammar`) is left as it is. It accepts `SEPARATOR` and `ORDER BY` in any function, so `CONCAT(a SEPARATOR ',')` still parses. Tightening that affects every dialect. mysql's other dedicated functions (`CONVERT`, `JSON_VALUE`, `JSON_TABLE`) are not added to the new exclusion list either, so they keep their current fallback to it. That could be a follow-up, now that the hook exists. - **ansi defines the typed-literal rule twice.** Once in `Expression_D_Grammar` (now `TypedLiteralGrammar`), and once in `BaseExpressionElementGrammar` as `Sequence(Ref("DatatypeSegment"), Ref("LiteralGrammar"))`. The two disagree: the second accepts `QualifiedNumericLiteralSegment` (`INT -5`), which the first deliberately leaves out because it "looks like an arithmetic operation". mysql switches off the second with `copy(remove=[...])`. That works, but the `remove=` is only needed because of the duplication. The fix is one definition used in both places. It is left for its own change; it has since been tested and changes no fixture in any dialect (see the summary above). - **Reserved words as variable names** are not addressed. `LocalVariableNameSegment` accepts any word, so `SELECT CHAR 'x'` still parses, as a variable named `CHAR` with an alias. The fix would exclude reserved keywords there, but its correctness then depends on the reserved-keyword lists, and the mariadb list is not accurate. Testing each of its 253 words as a variable name on a MariaDB server, 12 are accepted there: - `DATABASE`, `SCHEMA`, `OPTION`, `WINDOW`, `GENERAL`, `SLOW`; - `CHANGED_PAGE_BITMAPS`, `CLIENT_STATISTICS`, `INDEX_STATISTICS`; - `IGNORE_SERVER_IDS`, `MASTER_HEARTBEAT_PERIOD`, `MASTER_SSL_VERIFY_SERVER_CERT`. The server also accepts those as unquoted column names. sqlfluff only parses `SELECT schema FROM t` today because of this same variable-name leniency, so tightening it first would break that. The list needs correcting first, which is a separate change. - **Rule CV10** leaves `N'x'` alone, which is correct (`N"x"` would change the meaning), but only because it doesn't recognise the `N` prefix, not because it knows the prefix requires single quotes.
### Are there any other side effects of this change that we should be aware of? - No existing fixture changes in any dialect.
More side effects - In the codebase mentioned above, the only parse-tree differences are corrections: the `SEPARATOR` and `LIMIT` clauses, and a `DISTINCT (subquery)`. No file changed between parsing and not parsing. Its `CREATE TABLE` statements parse identically before and after, so DDL is unaffected; column types go through their own grammar. - Every statement in the new fixtures was checked on a MariaDB server, and so was each rejected form in the new tests, apart from `GROUP_CONCAT(v LIMIT 2)` in the mysql dialect: MariaDB accepts that, and MySQL's parser has no `LIMIT` there. Executing `SELECT foo 'x' FROM (SELECT 1 AS foo) t` returns column `x` holding `1`, which confirms the alias reading. The mysql fixtures and rejection tests were later run on MySQL 8.4 and 9.7 too: every fixture statement parses, and every rejected form, `GROUP_CONCAT(v LIMIT 2)` included, is a syntax error on both. - The mysql dialect now rejects `LIMIT` inside `GROUP_CONCAT` and `JSON_ARRAYAGG`, which MySQL does not have. Main accepted it only as a typed literal.
### Pull Request checklist - [x] Please confirm you have completed any of the necessary steps below. - Included test cases to demonstrate any code changes, which may be one or more of the following: - `.sql`/`.yml` parser test cases in `test/fixtures/dialects`: `literal_introducer_alias` and `group_concat` for mysql and mariadb, and `group_concat_limit` and `json_arrayagg` for mariadb. - Tests in `test/dialects/mysql_test.py` that the word-then-number forms, and invalid `GROUP_CONCAT` / `JSON_ARRAYAGG` forms, are parse errors. - Added appropriate documentation for the change — none needed. - Created GitHub issues for any relevant followup/future enhancements if appropriate — none (plans below).
Follow-up plans My plan is to keep sending PRs for the follow-ups under "Where this stops", since writing each one up properly would take about as long as fixing it. The pace is set by review, because they build on each other: the variable-name fix needs the reserved-word list corrected first. So each one waits for the one before it to merge. If I stop before they're done, I'll open issues for what's left. I know of well over a dozen real holes not PRed yet, due to dependency issues and so that I don't flood your queue. I've already filed an issue for the one I don't plan to handle myself (#8564). I appreciate that you are doing the best you can with a high velocity of PRs.
### AI assistance disclosure Per CONTRIBUTING.md. The grammar change, the fixtures and the test runs were AI-assisted (Claude Opus 5.5). Manually validated by me: the diff, and each fixture and test statement against a running MariaDB server, and later the mysql ones against MySQL 8.4 and 9.7. Checks run locally: full test suite and all pre-commit hooks. The dbt templater tests were not run locally, as they need a running Postgres instance; CI covers them. --- ## Summary by cubic Fixes the mysql and mariadb dialects silently misparsing word-then-literal constructs as typed literals. The catch-all rule, a PostgreSQL generalization MySQL doesn't support, made `foo 'x'` parse as a value of type `foo` instead of the column `foo` with alias `'x'`, and swallowed valid clauses like `GROUP_CONCAT ... SEPARATOR ...`. **Bug fixes** - Adds real grammar for character set introducers (`_utf8mb4'x'`), national strings (`N'x'`), the `BINARY` unary operator, `GROUP_CONCAT`, and MariaDB's `JSON_ARRAYAGG`. - The ansi typed-literal rule is now a named grammar that mysql disables; the generic function-name exclusion is named so dialects can extend it. - `GROUP_CONCAT` follows the server parser: the separator is a string, hex, or bit literal, and MariaDB's trailing `LIMIT` must come after `SEPARATOR`. - MariaDB's aggregate `LIMIT` values are numbers, `?` placeholders, or routine variables; `ALL` and other expressions raise parse errors. - `KILL` now takes any expression as its id, matching the server; the old narrow grammar only existed to dodge the typed-literal misparse. - Word-then-number forms and invalid `GROUP_CONCAT` / `JSON_ARRAYAGG` layouts now raise parse errors. **Notes** - `OVER` on `GROUP_CONCAT` and `JSON_ARRAYAGG` is accepted, matching the parser, though neither server can execute it. - Reserved words as variable names stay lax, so `SELECT CHAR 'x'` still parses; tightening that first needs the mariadb reserved-word list corrected. - Every new fixture was checked against a running MariaDB server; only the existing `KILL` fixtures updated. Written for commit 6b48cccbcf2ed41730170ea7ef5a139142b7e270. Summary will update on new commits.

pulls.title: Oracle: only treat a line-starting slash as a batch delimiter
pulls.body: ### Brief summary of the change made Fixes #8373. A bare `/` in the SELECT of `CREATE VIEW ... AS SELECT ...` (Oracle dialect) was consumed as a SQL*Plus slash-buffer executor, so divisions like `1 / 100` or `sysdate - 1/24` left the rest of the statement unparsable. This regressed in 4.3.0 via #7945, which added `terminators=[Ref("BatchDelimiterGrammar")]` to the view's selectable grammar — a terminator that matched *any* slash, including division operators. The change: - Adds a `StartOfLineSlashParser` that matches `/` only when it is the first code token on its line (preceded, ignoring whitespace, by a newline or start of file) — matching SQL*Plus semantics, where only a line-starting `/` executes the buffer. - Registers it as a terminator on the oracle `StatementSegment`, so a statement never extends past a batch-delimiter slash, while division inside statements parses normally. - Removes the overly broad terminator from `CreateViewStatementSegment`. As a side effect, `CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT` followed by a lone `/` (previously broken on `main`) now parses too. ### Are there any other side effects of this change that we should be aware of? A `/` starting a line inside a statement now terminates it (this matches SQL*Plus, which treats such a `/` as buffer execution, so it cannot be division). Division whose `/` ends a line (`1 /` newline `24`) still parses as division. ### Pull Request checklist - [x] Please confirm you have completed any of the necessary steps below. - Included test cases: added division and delimiter cases to `test/fixtures/dialects/oracle/slash_batch_delimiter.sql` (yml regenerated with `python test/generate_parse_fixture_yml.py`); fails before / passes after. - Verification: `pytest test/dialects/dialects_test.py -k oracle` -> 309 passed; broader `test/core` + dialect suite green except 3 pre-existing `plugin_test.py` failures that also fail on unmodified `main`; `ruff check`, `ruff format --check`, and `mypy` clean on the changed file. --- ## Summary by cubic Fixes #8373. A `/` anywhere in `CREATE VIEW ... AS SELECT` was consumed as a SQL*Plus batch delimiter, breaking division like `1 / 100` or `sysdate - 1/24` and leaving the statement unparsable. Now a `/` only terminates a statement when it's the first code token on its line, matching SQL*Plus semantics; the overly broad terminator on the view grammar is replaced with a new `StartOfLineSlashParser` registered on Oracle's `StatementSegment`. As a side effect, `CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT` followed by a lone `/` now parses too. Written for commit 8fd8b7c806d4dad159e42a626c0868d3b0ab2716. Summary will update on new commits.

pulls.title: fix CP02: check the literal portion of identifiers mixing jinja and literal source
pulls.body: ### Brief summary of the change made Fixes #5616 CP02 (`capitalisation.identifiers`, formerly L014) skipped every templated segment, so an identifier like `{{ env_type }}_MY_DB` escaped the rule entirely, even though the literal `_MY_DB` portion violates the configured `extended_capitalisation_policy`. Changes: - Segments whose source is **entirely** templated (e.g. placeholder parameters like `:accountId`, or a fully templated `{{ db_name }}`) are still skipped, preserving the existing behaviour those cases rely on. - Identifiers that mix templated and literal source text are now checked against their **non-templated source text only** (computed from the templated file's literal raw slices, so it works for any templater). The rendered raw is deliberately not used, since the templated portion's casing is generated code outside the user's control. - For such mixed identifiers the rule emits a **source-level fix** (`SourceFix`) that recases only the literal portion, leaving jinja blocks untouched, e.g. `{{ env_type }}_MY_DB` → `{{ env_type }}_my_db`. To support this, `Rule_CP01` gains an overridable `_raw_for_capitalisation()` hook that supplies the text used for the capitalisation checks (defaults to `segment.raw`, so CP01/CP03/CP05 behaviour is unchanged). ### Are there any other side effects of this change that we should be aware of? - CP02 now sets `targets_templated = True` so violations on partially templated identifiers are not stripped by the linter's templated-error filter. Fully templated segments are still skipped inside the rule itself. - Existing CP01/CP02/CP03/CP05 behaviours are covered by the unchanged test suite (all pass). ### Pull Request checklist - [x] Please confirm you have completed any of the necessary steps below. - Included test cases to demonstrate any code changes, which may be one or more of the following: - [x] `.yml` rule test cases in `test/fixtures/rules/std_rule_cases` (added `test_fail_jinja_mixed_templated_identifier` and `test_pass_jinja_fully_templated_identifier` to `CP02.yml`). - [ ] `.sql`/`.yml` parser test cases in `test/fixtures/dialects`. - [ ] Full autofix test cases in `test/fixtures/linter/autofix`. - [x] Other: verified manually that `sqlfluff fix` rewrites `{{ env_type }}_MY_DB` to `{{ env_type }}_my_db` and that a fully templated identifier is left untouched. - [ ] Added appropriate documentation for the change. - [ ] Created GitHub issues for any relevant followup/future enhancements if appropriate. ### Testing - `pytest test/rules/yaml_test_cases_test.py -k "CP02 or CP01"` → 84 passed. - `pytest test/rules/` → 2696 passed, 101 skipped. - Repro from the issue (`{{ env_type }}_MY_DB`, snowflake dialect, jinja templater, `extended_capitalisation_policy = lower`) now raises CP02 and autofixes correctly; a fully templated identifier (`{{ pure }}`) is not flagged. --- ## Summary by cubic Fixes CP02 (`capitalisation.identifiers`) so identifiers mixing templated and literal source, like `{{ env_type }}_MY_DB`, no longer escape the rule; previously every templated segment was skipped. - Only segments whose source is entirely templated are now skipped; mixed identifiers are checked against their literal portion via a new overridable `_raw_for_capitalisation()` hook on `Rule_CP01`, leaving CP01/CP03/CP05 behaviour unchanged. - Violations on mixed identifiers get a source-level fix built from literal spans, so literals split by templated blocks are recased in full and jinja blocks are untouched; checks use the literal portion only, never the rendered templated casing. - CP02 sets `targets_templated = True`; tests cover mixed fail/fix (including split and empty-rendering templates), fully templated pass, and `ignore_words` on literals. Written for commit fcbc97eb8e15f2614d61b59ab739eadc6f258f60. Summary will update on new commits.

pulls.title: LT05: count unrendered Jinja source in the line length
pulls.body: ### Brief summary of the change made makes progress on #8603 `_source_char_len` in `reindent.py` counts a literal segment by its raw length. Literal source which the variant does not render has an empty raw, so it counts as 0 characters. Examples are a macro body, a skipped `if` or `else` branch and a loop with no iterations. Whitespace which a `-` marker removes is also unrendered, for example with `{%-`, `-%}`, `{{-` or `{#-`. LT05 then misses lines which are too long in the source file. The change has three parts: 1. `_source_char_len` takes an `include_unrendered` flag. With the flag, a literal segment with no raw counts by its source length. The default is `False`. On `main`, `lint_line_length` is the only caller. The `_fill_breaks` caller from #8580 keeps the measure from `main`. 2. `lint_line_length` uses the length with unrendered source to decide if a line is too long. If the line fits without the unrendered source, LT05 reports it with no fix. Every other line gets the same fixes as on `main`. 3. `lint_line_length` marks the result from part 2 with a new `defer_to_fix` flag on `LintResult` and `SQLLintError`. `LintedFile.deduplicate_in_source_space` drops a marked violation when an unmarked violation reports the same rule on the same line. Part 2 does not fix these lines because a break next to unrendered source can land inside the block. A variant which renders the block gives its own fix if its rendered line is too long. I also tried to fix these lines. Then a second `sqlfluff fix` pass with the default rules changed the file again on 8 of my 33 test inputs. On `main` and on this branch, this happens on 1 of them. Part 3 is for a block which only some variants or loop passes render. Examples are `{% if false %}` with no `else`, and `{% if loop.first %}` in a loop. One rendering reports the line with no fix, and the other reports it with a fix. The deduplication keeps both, because the fixes are part of the signature. Without part 3, `sqlfluff lint` prints the line twice. `sqlfluff fix` fixes the line, but it reports one unfixable violation and exits with 1. The two renderings can give the line a different length, for example with a trailing comment. On a long comment line the position differs too. So part 3 matches the rule and the line. If the unmarked violation has no fix, it keeps the line reported, and `sqlfluff fix` still exits with 1. Part 3 only drops a marked violation. On `main`, a violation with no fix next to a fixable copy can be the only sign that a fix is unsafe. For a leading comma in a loop, LT04 discards the fix on one pass. The fix spans two template blocks, and the check added for #3079 rejects it. `sqlfluff fix --rules LT04` then exits with 1. A check which drops every LT05 copy with no fix is wrong too. A long comment line with a skipped `if` on the same line is too long in every variant. The fix from the other variant does not shorten it. pulls.title: Postgres: accept PG 16-17 utility options and ON/OFF/0/1 option values
pulls.body: ### Brief summary of the change made fixes #8602 The postgres dialect reads a boolean option value with `BooleanLiteralGrammar`, which is only `TRUE` or `FALSE`. This change adds `OptionBooleanGrammar`, which also accepts `ON`, `OFF` and an unsigned number. It uses the new grammar in `EXPLAIN`, `ANALYZE`, `REINDEX` and `COPY`. It also uses the new grammar for `ALLOW_CONNECTIONS` and `IS_TEMPLATE` in `CREATE DATABASE` and `ALTER DATABASE`, and for `DETERMINISTIC` in `CREATE COLLATION`. PostgreSQL reads these values with `utility_option_arg`, `copy_generic_opt_arg` and `createdb_opt_item` in `gram.y`. `CREATE COLLATION` reads the value as a `def_arg` in `gram.y`, and `DefineCollation` converts it with `defGetBoolean`. The new grammar accepts the six values that the `EXPLAIN` page lists (`TRUE`, `ON`, `1`, `FALSE`, `OFF`, `0`) and any unsigned number. `VACUUM` keeps its own value grammar, which reads `on` as an identifier. The change also adds the options from PostgreSQL 16 and 17: - `EXPLAIN`: `GENERIC_PLAN [ boolean ]`, `SERIALIZE [ NONE | TEXT | BINARY ]` and `MEMORY [ boolean ]`. - `VACUUM`: `PROCESS_MAIN`, `SKIP_DATABASE_STATS`, `ONLY_DATABASE_STATS` and `BUFFER_USAGE_LIMIT`. - `ANALYZE`: `BUFFER_USAGE_LIMIT`, with a number or a quoted size such as `'1MB'`. The 7 new option names go into `postgres_nondocs_keywords` as non-reserved keywords: `BUFFER_USAGE_LIMIT`, `GENERIC_PLAN`, `MEMORY`, `ONLY_DATABASE_STATS`, `PROCESS_MAIN`, `SERIALIZE` and `SKIP_DATABASE_STATS`. They stay unreserved, so a column or a table with one of these names still parses. New fixture statements in `explain.sql` and `vacuum.sql` use them as column names. Measured with `sqlfluff lint --dialect postgres --rules LT01`, one statement at a time: | statement | `main` at `4d259e33f` | this branch | |---|---|---| | `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE ON, BUFFERS OFF) SELECT 1;` | unparsable | parses | | `EXPLAIN (GENERIC_PLAN) SELECT 1;` | unparsable | parses | | `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, SERIALIZE BINARY, MEMORY) SELECT 1;` | unparsable | parses | | `VACUUM (SKIP_DATABASE_STATS);` | unparsable | parses | | `VACUUM (PROCESS_MAIN FALSE, BUFFER_USAGE_LIMIT 256) t;` | unparsable | parses | | `ANALYZE (BUFFER_USAGE_LIMIT 256) t;` | unparsable | parses | | `ANALYZE (VERBOSE ON) t;` | unparsable | parses | | `REINDEX (VERBOSE 1) TABLE t;` | unparsable | parses | | `COPY t FROM STDIN WITH (FORMAT csv, HEADER ON);` | unparsable | parses | | `CREATE DATABASE d WITH IS_TEMPLATE ON;` | unparsable | parses | | `ALTER DATABASE d WITH ALLOW_CONNECTIONS OFF;` | unparsable | parses | | `CREATE DATABASE d IS_TEMPLATE = 1 ALLOW_CONNECTIONS = off CONNECTION LIMIT 5;` | unparsable | parses | | `ALTER DATABASE d IS_TEMPLATE ON CONNECTION LIMIT 5;` | unparsable | parses | | `CREATE COLLATION c (provider = icu, locale = 'und', deterministic = off);` | unparsable | parses | | `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE TRUE, COSTS FALSE) SELECT 1;` | parses | parses | | `CREATE DATABASE d WITH IS_TEMPLATE TRUE ALLOW_CONNECTIONS = false;` | parses | parses | | `SELECT memory, serialize, generic_plan, buffer_usage_limit FROM t;` | parses | parses | | `CREATE TABLE memory (serialize int, generic_plan text, process_main bool);` | parses | parses | The diff is 18 files: `dialect_postgres.py`, `dialect_postgres_keywords.py`, and new statements in 8 `.sql` fixtures with their `.yml` files. `pytest test/dialects -n 10` is 7144 passed on `main` and on this branch. The new statements sit in existing fixture files, so the count does not change. The fixture generator reports no change for `duckdb`, `greenplum`, `materialize` and `redshift`. `utils/build_parsers.py postgres --table-driven` exits 0. With the generated Rust parser installed, `pytest test/dialects -n 10` is also 7144 passed. I built it with Rust 1.98.1, not the pinned 1.96. ### Are there any other side effects of this change that we should be aware of? - RF04 (`references.keywords`) now flags an alias with one of the 7 new names in `postgres`, `duckdb`, `greenplum` and `materialize`. The test statement is `SELECT a AS memory, b AS generic_plan, c AS buffers FROM t;`. In each of these dialects, it gives 1 RF04 violation on `main` and 3 on this branch. `redshift` stays at 1. RF04 already treats `BUFFERS`, `COSTS` and `SETTINGS` the same way. - With the default configuration, RF04 also flags the new names in a column definition. `CREATE TABLE t (memory int, serialize text);` gives 0 RF04 violations on `main` and 2 on this branch in `postgres` and `materialize`. `CREATE TABLE t (buffers int, costs int, settings text);` already gives 3 on `main`. #7691 reports the same effect for `PROVIDER`, and open PR #7823 discusses a fix for it. - RF04 flags a plain column reference only with `unquoted_identifiers_policy = all`. With that setting, `SELECT memory, generic_plan FROM t;` gives 0 RF04 violations on `main` and 2 on this branch. - RF06 (`references.quoting`) with `prefer_quoted_keywords = True` now asks to quote these names. `SELECT memory, generic_plan FROM t;` gives 0 RF06 violations on `main` and 2 on this branch. - `OptionBooleanGrammar` accepts any unsigned number, so `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE 5) SELECT 1;` parses although PostgreSQL rejects it at run time. A signed value such as `-1` does not parse. ### Pull Request checklist - [x] Please confirm you have completed any of the necessary steps below. - Included test cases to demonstrate any code changes, which may be one or more of the following: - `.yml` rule test cases in `test/fixtures/rules/std_rule_cases`. - [x] `.sql`/`.yml` parser test cases in `test/fixtures/dialects` (note YML files can be auto generated with `tox -e generate-fixture-yml`): new statements in `alter_database.sql`, `analyze.sql`, `copy.sql`, `create_collation.sql`, `create_database.sql`, `explain.sql`, `reindex.sql` and `vacuum.sql`, with `.yml` files from `python test/generate_parse_fixture_yml.py -d postgres`. With the two dialect files reverted to `main`, 24 of these fixture tests fail: 16 with `Found unparsable section` and 8 with a parse tree mismatch. `ruff format --check .` and `ruff check .` are clean. - Full autofix test cases in `test/fixtures/linter/autofix`. - Other. - [x] Added appropriate documentation for the change. None needed. The segment docstrings now link the PostgreSQL 16 and 17 pages. - [ ] Created GitHub issues for any relevant followup/future enhancements if appropriate. `CLUSTER (VERBOSE) t;` is unparsable on `main` and on this branch. That is a separate gap: `ClusterStatementSegment` has no bracketed option list, so the cause is not the boolean value. I can file an issue for it. AI usage: Claude Code CLI with Opus 5.5. I checked the change with the `sqlfluff lint` comparison above, the fixture test runs on `main` and on this branch, and the revert test. --- ## Summary by cubic Fixes the postgres dialect so boolean utility options accept ON, OFF, 0, and 1 in addition to TRUE and FALSE, and adds the EXPLAIN, VACUUM, and ANALYZE options added in PostgreSQL 16 and 17. - Previously only TRUE and FALSE parsed as option values for EXPLAIN, ANALYZE, REINDEX, COPY, CREATE/ALTER DATABASE, and CREATE COLLATION. - Adds GENERIC_PLAN, SERIALIZE, and MEMORY to EXPLAIN; PROCESS_MAIN, SKIP_DATABASE_STATS, ONLY_DATABASE_STATS, and BUFFER_USAGE_LIMIT to VACUUM; and BUFFER_USAGE_LIMIT to ANALYZE. - The 7 new option names become non-reserved keywords, so they still parse as identifiers. - OptionBooleanGrammar accepts any unsigned number, so EXPLAIN (ANALYZE 5) parses even though PostgreSQL rejects it at runtime. - RF04 and RF06 now treat these names as keywords in postgres and derived dialects. Written for commit e715f58d40c00706d61675b939987df1c1135ddf. Summary will update on new commits.

pulls.title: fix(RF01): support case-insensitive table and alias references
pulls.body: ### Brief summary of the change made Fixes #8594. Rule `RF01` previously compared table references and aliases using raw/unescaped strings without dialect case-folding. In SQL dialects where unquoted identifiers are case-insensitive, referencing an alias or table using a different letter case (for example, `SELECT CI.id FROM source_table AS ci JOIN second_table AS b ON ci.id = b.id;`) resulted in a false-positive violation because `targets` contained the declared case while `possible_references` contained the reference case. This change includes dialect-normalized identifiers (via `raw_normalized()`) in: - `_alias_info_as_tuples` for aliased table expressions - `_table_ref_as_tuple` for table references - `_get_table_refs` for multipart and simple table references - `standalone_aliases` candidate targets This allows case-insensitive matching for unquoted identifiers while preserving exact case matching for quoted identifiers. ### Are there any other side effects of this change that we should be aware of? None. Quoted identifiers remain case-sensitive because their segments do not undergo casefolding. ### Pull Request checklist - [x] Please confirm you have completed any of the necessary steps below. - Included test cases to demonstrate any code changes, which may be one or more of the following: - `.yml` rule test cases in `test/fixtures/rules/std_rule_cases`. - `.sql`/`.yml` parser test cases in `test/fixtures/dialects` (note YML files can be auto generated with `tox -e generate-fixture-yml`). - Full autofix test cases in `test/fixtures/linter/autofix`. - Other. - Added appropriate documentation for the change. - Created GitHub issues for any relevant followup/future enhancements if appropriate. --- ## Summary by cubic Fixes RF01 false positives when table or alias references use a different letter case than the declared alias or table in dialects where unquoted identifiers are case-insensitive (issue #8594). **Bug Fixes** - Adds dialect-normalized identifiers via `raw_normalized()` so alias, table, and multipart schema.table references match case-insensitively. - Quoted identifiers remain case-sensitive. - Adds test cases for mixed-case alias, table, multipart schema.table, and standalone alias references. Written for commit 7f402a566794b6602c57d899ec1a3e10f6882d9b. Summary will update on new commits.

pulls.title: StarRocks: support PARTITION BY LIST (#8555)
pulls.body: ## Brief summary of the change made Fixes #8555. StarRocks [list partitioning](https://docs.starrocks.io/docs/table_design/data_distribution/list_partitioning/) (`PARTITION BY LIST`) failed to parse. A valid `CREATE TABLE` taken directly from the StarRocks docs produced an unparsable section: ```sql CREATE TABLE t_recharge_detail4 ( id BIGINT, city VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL, dt VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL ) ENGINE=OLAP DUPLICATE KEY(id) PARTITION BY LIST (dt, city) ( PARTITION p1 VALUES IN (("2022-04-01", "Los Angeles"), ("2022-04-02", "Los Angeles")), PARTITION p2 VALUES IN (("2022-04-01", "Houston"), ("2022-04-02", "Houston")) ) DISTRIBUTED BY HASH(id); ``` `PartitionSegment` handled `PARTITION BY RANGE` and expression partitioning, but not `LIST`. ## Change Add a `LIST` branch to the StarRocks `PartitionSegment`, matching `PARTITION BY LIST (columns)` followed by the partition definitions with `PARTITION VALUES IN (...)`. It covers both forms from the docs: - multi-column: `VALUES IN (("2022-04-01", "Los Angeles"), ...)` (tuples of literals) - single-column: `VALUES IN ("2022-04-01", "2022-04-02")` (bare literals) ## Dialect StarRocks. ## Tests Added `create_table_list_partition.sql` (multi-column and single-column cases) and its generated `.yml`. The full StarRocks dialect suite passes locally (`pytest test/dialects/dialects_test.py -k starrocks` -> 48 passed), and `ruff check` / `ruff format --check` are clean on the changed file. --- ## Summary by cubic Fixes #8555 so StarRocks `CREATE TABLE` statements using `PARTITION BY LIST` parse instead of failing. - Adds a `LIST` branch to the StarRocks `PartitionSegment`, covering `PARTITION ... VALUES IN (...)` for both multi-column tuples and single-column literals, and documents it in the segment docstring. - Adds parse fixtures for both forms. pulls.title: fix(ST01): keep comments inside a removed ELSE NULL clause
pulls.body: `ST01` removes a redundant `ELSE NULL` from a `CASE` expression by deleting the whole `else_clause` as a single unit. A comment written inside that clause is a child of the clause, not a sibling, so `sqlfluff fix` deletes the comment along with it. Nothing warns the user and nothing is recoverable afterwards. Fixes #8562. ## The failure ```sql select case when name = 'cat' then 'meow' when name = 'dog' then 'woof' else /* keep default */ null end from x ``` `sqlfluff fix --dialect ansi --rules ST01` on the above reports one fixable violation and rewrites the file to: ```sql select case when name = 'cat' then 'meow' when name = 'dog' then 'woof' end from x ``` `/* keep default */` is gone. There is no lint message, log line or diff hunk that mentions it. ## Root cause In `Rule_ST01._eval`, once a redundant `else null` is detected the rule emits ```python fixes=[LintFix.delete(else_clause[0])] + [LintFix.delete(seg) for seg in before_else], ``` `LintFix.delete(else_clause[0])` removes the `else_clause` segment and everything under it. The rule never inspects the clause's children, so a comment lexed between the `ELSE` keyword and the `NULL` literal is deleted as part of the clause. A comment placed *after* the `NULL` (`else null -- x`) is parsed as a sibling of the clause and was already safe, which is why this has gone unnoticed. ## Why preserve rather than decline to fix The other option would be to have `ST01` skip the autofix when a comment would be lost, leaving an unfixable lint error behind. I went with preserving the comment because that is what this codebase already does in the directly analogous case: `ST04` removes an `else_clause` from a `case_expression` too, and it deliberately carries the comments across, including the ones sitting between the `ELSE` and the nested `CASE` (`# Restore any comments that were deleted`, and the `after_else_comment` selection feeding `_rebuild_spacing`). Declining to fix would also regress the rule's usefulness for a common pattern, and "drop the user's prose" is never the better of the two options when a mechanical alternative exists. ## The fix When the clause contains comments, replace the `else_clause` with those comments instead of deleting it, and leave the preceding whitespace in place so the first comment lands exactly where `ELSE` was. Continuation lines are re-indented to the indent the `ELSE` had. When there is no comment the existing delete path is untouched, so the common case produces a byte-identical fix. ```sql select case when name = 'cat' then 'meow' when name = 'dog' then 'woof' /* keep default */ end from x ``` ## Tests Five cases added to `test/fixtures/rules/std_rule_cases/ST01.yml`: a comment between `ELSE` and `NULL`, a comment on its own line inside the clause, several comments spanning lines, the single-line form, and a comment after the `NULL` which pins the already-correct sibling behaviour so it cannot regress. Negative control, with the change to `ST01.py` reverted and the fixtures kept: ``` $ pytest test/rules/yaml_test_cases_test.py -k ST01 -q FAILED test/rules/yaml_test_cases_test.py::test__rule_test_case[ST01_redundant_else_null_with_comment] FAILED test/rules/yaml_test_cases_test.py::test__rule_test_case[ST01_redundant_else_null_with_comment_on_own_line] FAILED test/rules/yaml_test_cases_test.py::test__rule_test_case[ST01_redundant_else_null_with_several_comments] FAILED test/rules/yaml_test_cases_test.py::test__rule_test_case[ST01_redundant_else_null_with_comment_on_one_line] 4 failed, 6 passed, 2502 deselected in 46.88s ``` The fifth new case passes either way by design, since it documents behaviour that was already correct. With the fix applied: ``` $ pytest test/rules/yaml_test_cases_test.py -k ST01 -q 10 passed, 2502 deselected in 55.77s ``` The whole rule suite is green with the change in place: ``` $ pytest test/rules/ -q 2679 passed, 101 skipped in 2231.29s (0:37:11) ``` `ruff check`, `ruff format --check`, `yamllint -c .yamllint` and `mypy` are clean on both changed files. ## Question for a maintainer I left the comment where the `ELSE` was, on the grounds that it keeps it visually attached to the branch the author wrote it against. `ST04` instead anchors relocated comments after the last `WHEN` clause. Both land in the same place for the common single-line case, but they differ once the clause spans lines. If you would rather the two rules agree on anchoring, say so and I will move `ST01` onto the `ST04` placement. ## AI assistance Per the AI-assisted contribution guidelines: this change was AI-assisted. The diagnosis, the patch and the fixtures were drafted with an AI agent. Every command and every output quoted above was actually executed and read against this branch, including the reverted-fix negative control and the full `test/rules/` run; none of the figures are reconstructed or estimated. --- ## Summary by cubic Fixes `ST01` silently deleting comments written inside a redundant `ELSE NULL` clause when running `sqlfluff fix`. Previously the rule deleted the whole `else_clause` as a single unit, which also dropped any comment between the `ELSE` keyword and the `NULL` literal with no warning. Now, when the clause holds comments, the rule replaces the clause with those comments, anchoring the first one where the `ELSE` was and re-indenting continuation lines; the no-comment path is unchanged. Fixes #8562. - Keeps the line break that ends a kept line comment so a trailing comment can't swallow the following `END`, and lets continuation comments from an inline `ELSE` keep their own whitespace. - Adds seven test cases: comments inside the clause in various layouts, a comment after the `NULL`, a line comment directly before `END`, and an inline `ELSE`. Written for commit 08e95da231cd15a8bd1c53a75bf25565b9d786f1. Summary will update on new commits.
