pulls.title: Bound data type argument arity (reject DECIMAL(10, 2, 3) etc.)
pulls.body: ## What A data type's bracketed argument list is never validated for arity. In the shared ANSI grammar `BracketedArguments` is an unconstrained `Delimited` literal list, and `ColumnDefinitionSegment` also swallows any leftover bracket with `Bracketed(Anything(), optional=True)`. Both accept invalid SQL: ```sql CREATE TABLE t (a DECIMAL(10, 2, 3)); -- at most two arguments CREATE TABLE t (a NUMERIC(1, 2, 3)); CREATE TABLE t (a VARCHAR(3, 4)); -- at most one CREATE TABLE t (a CHAR(3, 4)); CREATE TABLE t (a INT(1, 2, 3)); -- actually takes none ``` All of the above parse with no violations on `ansi`, `sparksql`, `databricks`, `postgres` and `snowflake` on both engines. Reported in #8589. ## How Type-family argument productions replace the unconstrained list: * `NumericTypeArguments` — `( p [, s] )`: precision required, at most two arguments. `DECIMAL()`, `DECIMAL(, 2)` and `DECIMAL(10, )` are rejected too. * `LengthTypeArguments` — `( n )`: a single length. Empty brackets are still allowed (`snowflake` uses `VARCHAR()`), a second argument is not. * `SridTypeArguments` — `( srid | ANY )`: a single argument. `DatatypeSegment` matches the families explicitly and excludes their names from the generic (dialect-specific / user-defined) fallback, so a malformed argument list cannot fall through to the unconstrained bracket. The generic fallback keeps `BracketedArguments`, so `ENUM(...)`/`SET(...)` and user defined types with arguments are unaffected. Family names are matched by raw text rather than as dialect keywords because several dialects (e.g. `snowflake`) replace their keyword sets wholesale. The same treatment is applied to: * `sparksql`'s `PrimitiveTypeSegment` — and the documented `GEOGRAPHY` / `GEOMETRY` types are added there (Databricks Runtime 17.1+), so the `databricks` dialect now parses `GEOGRAPHY(4326)`/`GEOGRAPHY(ANY)` and rejects `GEOGRAPHY(4326, 1)` and bare `GEOGRAPHY`. * `postgres`' already-enumerated numeric/character/bit/vector families. * the redundant `Bracketed(Anything())` fallback is removed from `ColumnDefinitionSegment` in `ansi`, `mysql`, `sparksql`, `databricks` and `teradata` (and `doris`' copy index adjusted). This is the piece that makes `INT(1, 2, 3)` rejectable; across the whole 867-file Databricks corpus and the dialect suite it had no remaining legitimate use in those dialects. `DECIMAL(10, 2)`, `DECIMAL(10)`, `DECIMAL`, `VARCHAR(10)` and the aliases `DEC`/`NUMERIC`/`INTEGER` all still parse. ## Scope Fixes `ansi` (and the dialects that reuse its grammar: `snowflake`, `sqlite`, `bigquery`, `vertica`), plus `sparksql`/`databricks` and `postgres`. Dialects that redefine `DatatypeSegment` and still need the same treatment, left as follow-ups: `oracle`, `athena`, `hive`, `teradata`, `trino`, `clickhouse`, `tsql`, `exasol`, `redshift`, `mysql`. Known interaction, not fixed here: `CAST(x AS DECIMAL(10, 2, 3))` still parses on `main`, because ANSI's function-contents grammar accepts adjacent expressions and reads `(10, 2, 3)` as a second argument. That is addressed by the separate comma-delimited function-arguments work, not by this arity change. ## Tests - New `datatype_arguments.sql` fixtures and generated `.yml` for `ansi`, `sparksql`, `databricks` and `postgres`; rejection cases in `ansi_test.py`, `sparksql_test.py`, `databricks_test.py` and `postgres_test.py`, because a valid-parse fixture cannot express an over-acceptance. - Whole `test/dialects/` + Python/Rust parity: **9496 passed, 2 xfailed**. - `make reference`: four new pages (`decimal_type`, `int_type`, `geography_type`, `geometry_type`) transcribed from the Databricks SQL reference, all must-parse and must-reject cases conforming, controls ok. - `make corpus`: rejection **1327/1327 (100%)**, recall unchanged (the removed catch-all had zero uses across the corpus). ## AI assistance This pull request was co-authored with AI assistants: **Claude Opus 5** (Anthropic) and **DeepSeek V4.1 Flash**. They drafted the grammar, the fixtures and the rejection tests, and ran the measurements, under the contributor's direction. Every construct was checked against the Databricks SQL reference, and the changes were run through the whole `test/dialects/` suite, the Python/Rust parity tests, `make reference` and `make corpus` before submission. The human contributor remains responsible for the final pull request, including its correctness, tests and maintainability, as [CONTRIBUTING.md](https://github.com/sqlfluff/sqlfluff/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md#ai-assisted-contributions) requires. --- ## Summary by cubic Rejects data types with too many bracketed arguments so invalid SQL like `DECIMAL(10, 2, 3)`, `VARCHAR(3, 4)`, and `INT(1, 2, 3)` no longer parses silently on `ansi`, `sparksql`, `databricks`, and `postgres` (#8589). **Changes** - Numeric types now take a precision plus an optional scale, length types a single length, and geospatial types a single SRID or `ANY`; incomplete lists like `DECIMAL()` and `DECIMAL(, 2)` are rejected too. - Adds `GEOGRAPHY`/`GEOMETRY` to `sparksql`, so `databricks` parses `GEOGRAPHY(4326)` and rejects bare `GEOGRAPHY`. - Removes the redundant catch-all bracket from column definitions in `ansi`, `mysql`, `sparksql`, `databricks`, and `teradata`. **Notes** - `ENUM(...)`, `SET(...)`, and user-defined types keep unconstrained arguments. - `CAST(x AS DECIMAL(10, 2, 3))` still parses; that's handled by separate function-arguments work. - Dialects that redefine `DatatypeSegment` (`oracle`, `athena`, `hive`, `teradata`, `trino`, `clickhouse`, `tsql`, `exasol`, `redshift`, `mysql`) need the same treatment as follow-ups. Written for commit 3c5f72acb032749606db5701c684bd16473643e8. Summary will update on new commits.

pulls.title: Postgres: reject col_name_keywords (e.g. BETWEEN) as bare data types (#6430)
pulls.body: ## Brief summary of the change made Fixes #6430. Per the [PostgreSQL keyword appendix](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-keywords-appendix.html), `col_name_keyword`s (the "cannot be function or type name" class, e.g. `BETWEEN`, `COALESCE`, `NULLIF`) may not be used as bare type names. SQLFluff accepted them, so this parsed with no error: ```sql CREATE TABLE test_table ( type between NOT NULL ); ``` The ANSI `DatatypeIdentifierSegment` only excludes `NOT` from its identifier regex, so any other keyword fell through as a "user-defined type". ## Change Override `DatatypeIdentifierSegment` for Postgres to additionally exclude the `non-reserved-(cannot-be-function-or-type)` keyword class. Two deliberate scoping decisions: - **Built-in types are unaffected** — `INT`, `VARCHAR`, `TIMESTAMP`, etc. are matched by explicit branches in `DatatypeSegment` *before* this identifier fallback is reached. - **Reserved keywords are intentionally NOT excluded.** The `substring(... SIMILAR ... ESCAPE ...)` special form relies on matching reserved words as data-type identifiers, so excluding them would break it (verified against the existing `substring.sql` fixture). ## Dialect PostgreSQL. ## Tests Added `test_valid_column_types_parse` (built-in + user-defined types still parse) and `test_col_name_keyword_not_valid_datatype` (`between` as a type is now unparsable) to `test/dialects/postgres_test.py`. The full Postgres suite passes locally (`pytest test/dialects/dialects_test.py -k postgres test/dialects/postgres_test.py` → 538 passed), and `ruff check` / `ruff format --check` are clean on the changed files. --- ## Summary by cubic Fixes #6430 by making the Postgres dialect reject `col_name_keyword`s (e.g. `BETWEEN`) as bare data types, where it previously accepted invalid SQL like `CREATE TABLE t (x between NOT NULL)` as a user-defined type. The ANSI `DatatypeIdentifierSegment` only excluded `NOT` from its identifier regex, so other keywords fell through as type names. A Postgres override now also excludes the `non-reserved-(cannot-be-function-or-type)` keyword class. The exclusion lives in a dedicated `cannot_be_type_keywords` dialect set so child dialects can extend it; Greenplum now rejects its own keywords in that class too (`CUBE`, `ROLLUP`, `MEDIAN`). Built-in types (`INT`, `VARCHAR`, `TIMESTAMP`) are unaffected because they're matched by explicit `DatatypeSegment` branches before this fallback. `DEC` and `NCHAR`/`NATIONAL CHARACTER` (including their `VARYING` spellings) are `col_name_keyword`s that double as real built-in types, so they got explicit branches to stay parseable. Reserved keywords are intentionally not excluded — the `substring(... SIMILAR ... ESCAPE ...)` special form relies on them. Added tests confirm built-in and user-defined types still parse, and that keywords such as `between`, `values`, `setof`, and `row` are now unparsable as types. Written for commit 177b783d4a7bda30fd24688b5c7af3690cfa6398. Summary will update on new commits.

The full Snowflake dialect suite passes locally (`pytest test/dialects/dialects_test.py -k snowflake` → 750 passed). --- ## Summary by cubic Adds support for `ROW_TIMESTAMP_DEFAULT` in Snowflake `CREATE SCHEMA`, `ALTER SCHEMA ... UNSET` so they no longer produce "Found unparsable section". **Details** - `ROW_TIMESTAMP_DEFAULT = TRUE|FALSE` is parsed via the shared `SchemaObjectParamsSegment`, covering `CREATE SCHEMA` and `ALTER SCHEMA ... SET`. - Added to the `ALTER SCHEMA ... UNSET` parameter list. - Adds `ROW_TIMESTAMP_DEFAULT` to the Snowflake keyword list. - Adds parse fixtures for all statements and regenerates the expected output. pulls.title: fix(mysql): parse KILL statements
pulls.body: ### Brief summary of the change made The mysql and mariadb dialects have no `KILL` statement, so every `KILL` was unparsable. MySQL — https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.0/en/kill.html: ``` KILL [CONNECTION | QUERY] processlist_id ``` MariaDB adds three forms — https://mariadb.com/kb/en/kill/: ``` KILL [HARD | SOFT] { {CONNECTION|QUERY} thread_id | QUERY ID query_id | USER user_name } ``` Adds `KillStatementSegment` to `dialect_mysql.py` for the MySQL form, and overrides it in `dialect_mariadb.py` to add `HARD`/`SOFT`, `QUERY ID` and `USER`, so the mysql dialect still rejects the MariaDB-only forms. The id is deliberately not a general `ExpressionSegment`. The expression grammar accepts typed literals like `DATE '2020-01-01'`, and takes any word as the type name, so it would read `KILL HARD 5` in the mysql dialect as the literal `5` of a type called `HARD` — silently mis-parsing instead of reporting it as unparsable. `KillIdGrammar`, shared by both dialects, limits it to the shapes an id takes: a number, a variable, a function call such as `CONNECTION_ID()`, or a bracketed expression. ### Are there any other side effects of this change that we should be aware of? - No existing fixture changes across mysql, mariadb and starrocks. - `KILL USER` uses the existing `RoleReferenceSegment` for the account name, which #8463 changes. That PR is currently awaiting changes, so I haven't held this one for it. Whichever lands second only needs the mariadb `kill_statement.yml` regenerated — a one-command change with no grammar conflict. ### Pull Request checklist - [x] Please confirm you have completed any of the necessary steps below. - Included test cases to demonstrate any code changes, which may be one or more of the following: - `.sql`/`.yml` parser test cases in `test/fixtures/dialects` — new `kill_statement` fixtures for both mysql and mariadb. - Added appropriate documentation for the change — none needed. - Created GitHub issues for any relevant followup/future enhancements if appropriate — none. ### AI assistance disclosure Per CONTRIBUTING.md. The grammar change, the fixtures and the test runs were AI-assisted (Claude Opus 5.5). Manually validated by me: the diff, and each form in the fixtures against a running MariaDB server. Checks run locally: full test suite (11290 passed) and all pre-commit hooks. The dbt templater tests were not run locally, as they need a running Postgres instance; CI covers them. --- ## Summary by cubic Adds parsing support for `KILL` statements to the MySQL and MariaDB dialects, which previously rejected all `KILL` statements as unparsable. - Covers MySQL's `KILL [CONNECTION | QUERY] ` and MariaDB's extra `HARD`/`SOFT`, `QUERY ID`, and `USER` forms. - Restricts the id to numbers, variables, function calls, and bracketed expressions so MySQL rejects MariaDB-only forms instead of mis-parsing them; a regression test covers `KILL HARD 5`, `KILL SOFT CONNECTION 5`, `KILL QUERY ID 5`, and `KILL USER 'u'@'h'`. - `KILL USER` accepts account names including `CURRENT_USER()`; MariaDB also accepts an optional `CONNECTION`/`QUERY` before `USER`, matching the server. New fixtures cover both. - No existing fixtures change; `KILL USER` reuses `RoleReferenceSegment`, which an open PR also touches — whichever merges second only needs the MariaDB fixture regenerated. Written for commit 2bbde9ec36253ee060918519d93098d4a90e8dea. Summary will update on new commits.

pulls.title: fix(mysql): parse DO statements
pulls.body: ### Brief summary of the change made The mysql dialect has no `DO` statement, so every `DO` was unparsable — `DO SLEEP(1);`, `DO RELEASE_LOCK('x');` and so on, which are common in stored routines. https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.0/en/do.html: ``` DO expr [, expr] ... ``` Adds `DoStatementSegment` (`DO` followed by delimited expressions) and registers it in `StatementSegment` alongside `CALL`. The MariaDB syntax is the same, so it lives in `dialect_mysql.py` and mariadb inherits it. ### Are there any other side effects of this change that we should be aware of? - No existing fixture changes. Regenerating mysql, mariadb and starrocks reproduces every existing `.yml` unchanged. - `DO` is also the keyword that introduces a `CREATE EVENT` body. `create_event_do_statement` covers both sides of that: an event whose body is itself a `DO` statement (`... EVERY 1 DAY DO DO SLEEP(1);`) parses with one `do_statement`, and `... DO SELECT 1;` parses with none. ### Pull Request checklist - [x] Please confirm you have completed any of the necessary steps below. - Included test cases to demonstrate any code changes, which may be one or more of the following: - `.sql`/`.yml` parser test cases in `test/fixtures/dialects` — two new fixtures, `do_statement` and `create_event_do_statement`. - Added appropriate documentation for the change — none needed. - Created GitHub issues for any relevant followup/future enhancements if appropriate — none. ### AI assistance disclosure Per CONTRIBUTING.md. The grammar change, the fixtures and the test runs were AI-assisted (Claude Opus 5.5). Manually validated by me: the diff, and the syntax against the DO page in the MySQL manual. Checks run locally: full test suite (11290 passed) and all pre-commit hooks. The dbt templater tests were not run locally, as they need a running Postgres instance; CI covers them. --- ## Summary by cubic Adds parsing support for MySQL `DO` statements, which previously failed to parse. `DO SLEEP(1);`, `DO RELEASE_LOCK('x');`, and similar statements are common in stored routines and are now handled by a new `do_statement` segment registered alongside `CALL`. - MariaDB inherits the grammar since its `DO` syntax matches MySQL. - `CREATE EVENT` bodies that contain `DO` statements parse correctly, including nested `DO DO` cases. - Adds fixtures covering delimited expressions, variables, subselects, and case-insensitive keywords. Written for commit 174935886d73658a9f353d80e56fc2468826e0a4. Summary will update on new commits.

pulls.title: Oracle: fix division operator misparsed as SQL*Plus batch delimiter (#8373)
pulls.body: ## Summary Fixes #8373 — Oracle dialect regression where division operators ('/') inside CREATE VIEW statements were misparsed as SQL*Plus batch delimiters, causing PRS (unparsable) errors. ### Root Cause The Oracle dialect's `BatchDelimiterGrammar` used `Ref("SlashSegment")` as a terminator in `CreateViewStatementSegment`'s `OptionallyBracketed(SelectableGrammar)`. The parser's GREEDY matching uses `next_match()` for terminator lookahead, which calls the matcher directly without checking `Ref.exclude`, so ANY '/' token was treated as a batch delimiter boundary — including binary division operators inside SELECT expressions. ### Fix - Added `BatchDelimiterLookaheadMatcher` (a custom `Matchable`) that performs backward lookbehind to distinguish division operators from batch delimiters. A '/' is treated as a SQL*Plus batch delimiter only when it appears at a statement boundary: - at file start (no preceding code segment) - after a newline (with only whitespace between) - after a statement terminator (;), another batch delimiter, or start bracket - Replaced the old `SlashBufferExecutorSegment` with `OracleBatchDelimiterSegment` using this contextual matcher - Added regression test cases for division operators in CREATE VIEW ### Testing - All 306 Oracle dialect parser tests pass - Division operators in CREATE VIEW parse correctly as `binary_operator` - SQL*Plus slash batch delimiters (both with and without preceding semicolons) continue to work correctly - No PRS violations on affected queries ### AI Disclosure This fix was implemented with the assistance of AI coding tools. The diagnosis, root cause analysis, and solution approach were developed interactively, with all code changes manually verified through parser trace debugging and the full Oracle dialect test suite. ## Test Plan - [x] Run `python test/generate_parse_fixture_yml.py -d oracle` — all 102 fixtures regenerated successfully - [x] Run `python -m pytest test/dialects/dialects_test.py -k oracle` — 306 tests passed - [x] Verify division in CREATE VIEW: `select 1 / 100 as z from dual` parses without PRS errors - [x] Verify chained division: `nvl(bytes, 0) / 1024 / 1024` parses correctly - [x] Verify existing slash_batch_delimiter.sql fixture still parses three batches correctly - [x] Verify slash_buffer_executor_examples.sql and sqlplus_commands.sql fixtures still pass --- ## Summary by cubic Fixes #8373, an Oracle dialect regression where division operators (`/`) inside `CREATE VIEW` statements were misparsed as SQL*Plus batch delimiters, causing unparsable (PRS) errors. **Bug Fixes** - `/` is now recognized as a batch delimiter only at statement boundaries (file start, after a newline, or after a statement terminator or bracket), not when preceded by an operand. - Replaced `SlashBufferExecutorSegment` with `OracleBatchDelimiterSegment`, which uses a new `BatchDelimiterLookaheadMatcher` to distinguish division from batch delimiting. - Batch delimiter fixtures now emit `/` as `divide`; added regression tests for division operators in `CREATE VIEW`. Written for commit 6aa892d67694f1d7422c33385effdc77d139a210. Summary will update on new commits.

pulls.title: LT05: add a list_wrapping option to fill long lists
pulls.body: ### Brief summary of the change made fixes #5682 LT05 splits a long comma separated list at every comma. This change adds a `list_wrapping` option to the `indentation` section. The default is `one_per_line`, which keeps the current layout. With `fill`, LT05 puts as many list elements on each line as fit in `max_line_length`. alanmcruickshank supported this as point 2 in #5379. This PR fills lines with the normal indent, and does not bring back the hanging indent from point 1 of that comment. Measured with `sqlfluff format` and `max_line_length = 45`: ```sql -- list_wrapping = one_per_line (the default, same as main) SELECT a FROM tbl GROUP BY long_column_name1, long_column_name2, long_column_name3, long_column_name4 -- list_wrapping = fill SELECT a FROM tbl GROUP BY long_column_name1, long_column_name2, long_column_name3, long_column_name4 ``` How it works: - LT05 breaks a line at the points with the lowest balance. All the commas of one list share one balance, so LT05 breaks at all of them. - With `fill`, the new `_fill_breaks` helper in `reindent.py` walks those points in order. It takes a break only when the text up to the next point goes past the limit. The last point is measured against the whole line, which is already too long, so at least one break is always taken. - `fill` applies only when every target point is next to a comma. Operator chains such as `AND` and `+` still get one break each. - With `line_position = alone`, each comma has a break point on both sides. The helper takes both or neither, so the comma stays on its own line. - The config validator rejects any other value, with the same message shape as `implicit_indents`. The docs get a "Long Lists" section in `docsv/configuration/layout.md` and in `configuration/layout.rst`, and `default_config.cfg` documents the option. ### Are there any other side effects of this change that we should be aware of? - The default value changes nothing. The new LT05 code only runs when `list_wrapping = fill`. The full `test/` suite has 11306 passed. The same 8 plugin tests fail on `main` in my environment, because the example plugin is not installed. - When a select clause has more than one target, LT09 puts each target on its own line at any line length, and `sqlfluff format` applies LT09. So `fill` does not change a select clause with more than one target unless LT09 is excluded. With `exclude_rules = LT09` and `max_line_length = 45`, the select example in the issue formats to the requested layout. The docs note says this. I did not change LT09 in this PR. If you want LT09 to follow `list_wrapping`, I can do that as a follow-up. - LT05 counts the if/else branch that did not render as 0 characters. Main does the same. With `fill`, a fix can leave a line over the limit that LT05 does not report, at more limits than the default mode. My review reply has the measurements. ### Pull Request checklist - [x] Please confirm you have completed any of the necessary steps below. - Included test cases to demonstrate any code changes, which may be one or more of the following: - [x] `.yml` rule test cases in `test/fixtures/rules/std_rule_cases`: 8 new `test_fail_list_wrapping_fill*` cases in `LT05.yml`. They cover trailing, leading and alone commas, a function call, a nested list and an indented CTE. Two cases check that operator and boolean chains keep one break per operator. The trailing and alone cases sit exactly at the limit. 8 more cases cover Jinja templated lists: for loops, an if/else element, macro calls, variables with a rendered length different from the source length, and one tag that renders the whole list. - [x] Other: `test__rules__std_LT05_LT09_list_wrapping_fill` in `test/rules/std_LT05_LT09_combo_test.py` checks the LT09 interaction and that a second fix changes nothing. `test__validate_list_wrapping_invalid` in `test/core/config/validate_test.py` checks the validator. - [x] Added appropriate documentation for the change. - [x] Created GitHub issues for any relevant followup/future enhancements if appropriate. None yet, see the LT09 question above. AI usage: Claude Code CLI with Opus 5.5. I checked the change with the `sqlfluff format` runs above, the test run, and mutation tests on the new code. --- ## Summary by cubic Adds a `list_wrapping` option so LT05 fills long comma-separated lists instead of splitting at every comma. Fixes #5682. **New Features** - `list_wrapping = fill` puts as many list elements on each line as fit `max_line_length`; the default `one_per_line` keeps current behavior. - Only comma breaks are filled, with `line_position = alone` commas and their breaks treated as a group. - Config validation rejects invalid values, and docs cover the option in a new Long Lists section. - LT09 keeps a single select target on the SELECT line, so `sqlfluff format` won't fill multi-target select lists unless LT09 is excluded. Written for commit dedf18b6b02600cf5dbec3e8352aab600cec17e2. Summary will update on new commits.

pulls.title: Oracle: parse common SQL*Plus SET commands
pulls.body: ### Brief summary of the change made `SqlplusSetStatementSegment` only handled `SET SCAN ON|OFF`, so other SQL*Plus `SET` commands were unparsable. `SET DEFINE OFF` is really common at the top of Oracle scripts - it turns off substitution variables, so an `&` in a string literal is left alone - and because the unparsable section runs to the end of the file, a script like this didn't get linted at all: ```sql SET DEFINE OFF INSERT INTO tools (id, name) VALUES (1, 'Hammer & Tongs'); ``` This adds the `SET` system variables that come up most in deployment scripts: `DEFINE`, `ECHO`, `ESCAPE`, `FEEDBACK`, `FLAGGER`, `HEADING`, `LINESIZE`, `LONG`, `NULL`, `PAGESIZE`, `SERVEROUTPUT`, `SQLBLANKLINES`, `SUFFIX`, `TERMOUT`, `TIME`, `TIMING`, `TRIMSPOOL` and `VERIFY`, alongside the existing `SCAN`. Syntax is from the [SET System Variable Summary](https://docs.oracle.com/en/database/oracle/oracle-database/26/sqpug/SET-system-variable-summary.html). Names and values are plain keywords, with the new ones added to the Oracle unreserved keywords. Each variable takes its full name or its shortest documented abbreviation (e.g. `SERVEROUT`), one `SET` can set several of them (e.g. `SET ECHO OFF FEEDBACK OFF` - SQL*Plus accepts this even though the syntax summary shows one at a time), and it's still only tried at batch level. Each variable also only accepts its documented values rather than any tokens - SQL*Plus commands don't need a semicolon, so a looser grammar would end up swallowing the next line. Unquoted text values for `NULL` and `SUFFIX` are plain text tokens rather than identifiers, so reserved words work (`SET NULL NULL`) and capitalisation rules leave the text alone. Double-quoted text is a literal rather than a quoted identifier, so RF05 doesn't flag it. I've kept it to these variables so it's easy to review - happy to follow up with the rest of the list in another PR. ### Are there any other side effects of this change that we should be aware of? - `SET SCAN` parses the same as before, and no existing Oracle fixtures changed. - The new keywords are all unreserved, so they still work as identifiers. I compared parse trees against `main` with every new keyword used as a table, column, alias, bind and PL/SQL variable name (including `UPDATE t SET define = 1`), and they're identical. - As with any new unreserved keyword, RF04 will now flag these words when they're used as identifiers, e.g. a column called `echo` or `entry`. - Not covered here: - the rest of the `SET` variables; - abbreviations between the shortest form and the full name, e.g. `SET LINES` or `SET HEAD`; - SQL*Plus's `-` line continuation, e.g. a long `SET` split over two lines; - unquoted `\`, `$` and `#` values - `\` and `$` still give a lexer error and `#` is read as a comment, so they need quoting (e.g. `SET ESCAPE '\'`). ### Pull Request checklist - [x] Please confirm you have completed any of the necessary steps below. - Included test cases to demonstrate any code changes, which may be one or more of the following: - `.yml` rule test cases in `test/fixtures/rules/std_rule_cases`. - `.sql`/`.yml` parser test cases in `test/fixtures/dialects` (note YML files can be auto generated with `tox -e generate-fixture-yml`). - Full autofix test cases in `test/fixtures/linter/autofix`. - Other. - Added appropriate documentation for the change. - Created GitHub issues for any relevant followup/future enhancements if appropriate. ### Tested locally - all the `SET` lines in the new fixture parse on this branch, and all except the existing `SET SCAN OFF` fail on `main` - regenerated the fixtures for every dialect - only the new `sqlplus_set.yml` was added - the tox envs CI runs, on Linux: `py314` and `py310`, plus the `parse_suite`, `fix_suite` and `rules_suite` marks, each with and without the Rust parser, along with `linting`, `mypy`, `yamllint`, `doctests` and `doclinting` - Oracle dialect coverage is still 100% - `rustify.py build`, then `cargo fmt --check`, `cargo clippy -D warnings` and `cargo test` - `pre-commit` on the changed files I used Claude Code to help with this, and have reviewed and tested the change myself. --- ## Summary by cubic Extends Oracle's `SET` statement parsing beyond `SCAN ON|OFF` so common SQL\*Plus `SET` commands no longer fail to parse, which previously made entire scripts skip linting (e.g. `SET DEFINE OFF` at the top of a file). - Covers `DEFINE`, `ECHO`, `ESCAPE`, `FEEDBACK`, `FLAGGER`, `HEADING`, `LINESIZE`, `LONG`, `NULL`, `PAGESIZE`, `SERVEROUTPUT`, `SQLBLANKLINES`, `SUFFIX`, `TERMOUT`, `TIME`, `TIMING`, `TRIMSPOOL`, and `VERIFY`. - Accepts each variable's full name or its shortest documented abbreviation (including `TRU` for `TRUNCATED`), and lets one `SET` set multiple variables. - Values are restricted to documented options so the grammar doesn't swallow the next line; new words are unreserved keywords, so they remain usable as identifiers. - Unquoted text values (e.g. `SET NULL NULL`) are parsed as opaque text rather than keywords, so even reserved words work and capitalisation rules leave them alone. - Adds `TRU` to the Codespell ignore list, scoped to the uppercase keyword only. Written for commit c61954c6b9b2b05352caf8bb7307dc4d376bb87f. Summary will update on new commits.

pulls.title: Oracle: allow DELETE without the optional FROM keyword
pulls.body: ### Brief summary of the change made In Oracle `FROM` is optional in a `DELETE` ([docs](https://docs.oracle.com/en/database/oracle/oracle-database/26/sqlrf/DELETE.html)): ``` DELETE [ hint ] [ FROM ] { dml_table_expression_clause | ONLY (dml_table_expression_clause) } [ t_alias ] ... ``` The dialect required it, so these were unparsable, both on their own and inside PL/SQL blocks: ```sql DELETE employees; DELETE hr.employees WHERE employee_id = 100; ``` The unparsable section also runs to the end of the file, so nothing after one of these got linted either. The Oracle `DeleteStatementSegment` copied the ANSI grammar, which requires `FromClauseSegment`. I've added a `DeleteFromClauseSegment` with an optional `FROM` and used it instead. It subclasses `ansi.FromClauseSegment` and keeps the `from_clause` type, so `DELETE FROM ...` parses exactly the same as before. Linting the same statements with and without `FROM` gives the same results, apart from rules about the `FROM` keyword itself (like its capitalisation). While testing I also found that a `RETURNING` clause straight after the table, with no alias or `WHERE`, didn't parse even with `FROM`, because `RETURNING` was read as a table alias: ```sql DELETE FROM employees RETURNING last_name INTO :v_last_name; ``` `ReturningClauseSegment` is now in the Oracle `FromClauseTerminatorGrammar`, so it isn't taken as an alias when a returning clause follows. A table actually aliased `returning` still parses. ### Are there any other side effects of this change that we should be aware of? None that I've found. Regenerating the Oracle fixtures only added the new `delete.yml` - nothing else changed. I did look at making `FROM` a bare optional keyword like BigQuery and T-SQL do, but that drops the `from_clause` wrapper from every existing Oracle `DELETE FROM`, which felt like a bigger change than this needed. ### Pull Request checklist - [x] Please confirm you have completed any of the necessary steps below. - Included test cases to demonstrate any code changes, which may be one or more of the following: - `.yml` rule test cases in `test/fixtures/rules/std_rule_cases`. - `.sql`/`.yml` parser test cases in `test/fixtures/dialects` (note YML files can be auto generated with `tox -e generate-fixture-yml`). - Full autofix test cases in `test/fixtures/linter/autofix`. - Other. - Added appropriate documentation for the change. - Created GitHub issues for any relevant followup/future enhancements if appropriate. ### Tested locally - the statements without `FROM` in the new fixture fail on `main`, and everything in it parses on this branch - regenerated the fixtures for every dialect - only the new `delete.yml` was added - the tox envs CI runs, on Linux: `py314` and `py310`, plus the `parse_suite`, `fix_suite` and `rules_suite` marks, each with and without the Rust parser, along with `linting`, `mypy`, `yamllint`, `doctests` and `doclinting` - Oracle dialect coverage is still 100% - `rustify.py build`, then `cargo fmt --check`, `cargo clippy -D warnings` and `cargo test` - `pre-commit` on the changed files I used Claude Code to help with discovery and testing, I have of course reviewed and tested the change myself. --- ## Summary by cubic Allows Oracle `DELETE` statements without the optional `FROM` keyword, which the Oracle dialect previously rejected. Statements like `DELETE employees;` now parse correctly, both standalone and inside PL/SQL blocks, and no longer cause everything after them in a file to be skipped by the linter. - A new `DeleteFromClauseSegment` subclasses the ANSI `FromClauseSegment` and marks `FROM` as optional, so `DELETE FROM ...` parses exactly as before. - The `FROM` clause now terminates at `RETURNING`, so `RETURNING` is no longer misread as the delete target alias. - Linting results are unchanged except for rules targeting the `FROM` keyword itself. Written for commit 86168426c7e25549a3613a53b09b60428faf4b12. Summary will update on new commits.

pulls.title: Hive/Impala: support the NULL-safe equals operator `<=>`
pulls.body: ### Brief summary of the change made This supersedes #8409, which was closed for inactivity before I got back to it. Same change, rebased onto current `main` as a single commit, with the review feedback from @rubytobi already folded in. Hive has had the NULL-safe equality operator `<=>` since 0.9 ([LanguageManual UDF](https://cwiki.apache.org/confluence/display/Hive/LanguageManual+UDF) — "Returns same result with EQUAL(=) operator for non-null operands, but returns TRUE if both are NULL"), and Impala supports it as an alias for `IS NOT DISTINCT FROM` ([Impala operators](https://impala.apache.org/docs/build/html/topics/impala_operators.html)). SQLFluff currently reports both as unparsable: ``` $ sqlfluff parse --dialect hive <<< "SELECT a <=> b FROM t;" L: 1 | P: 10 | PRS | Line 1, Position 10: Found unparsable section: '<=> b' ``` This adds a `NullSafeEqualsSegment` to the Hive dialect, built from the raw `<`, `=` and `>` segments with `allow_gaps=False`, and inserts it into `ComparisonOperatorGrammar`. It deliberately mirrors the existing MySQL implementation from #6929, so no lexer change is needed and the resulting parse tree is identical to MySQL's: ``` comparison_operator: raw_comparison_operator: '<' raw_comparison_operator: '=' raw_comparison_operator: '>' ``` Because that shape matches, `ST09` — which already lists `<=>` among the operators it understands — handles it with no modification. ### Changes since #8409 - Rebased onto current `main`, so the `test/core/config/loader_test.py` failures that were blocking the old PR (fixed by #8461) are gone. - Added `SELECT * FROM tbl WHERE NOT a <=> b;` to the Impala fixture, matching the negated case already present in the Hive one, per review feedback. `NOT` applies to the boolean result, so it parses as `NOT (a <=> b)`. ### Are there any other side effects of this change that we should be aware of? **Impala is covered by the same change**, since `impala` inherits from `hive`. Fixtures are included for both dialects to lock that in. **Athena is deliberately unaffected**: it inherits from `ansi`, not `hive`, and Athena v3 is Trino-based with no `<=>`. Verified it still rejects the operator after this change. I swept the other dialects while I was here. `mysql`, `mariadb`, `doris`, `starrocks`, `sparksql`, `databricks`, `vertica`, `postgres` (pgvector's cosine distance) and `clickhouse` (since #8528 landed) already accept `<=>`. `duckdb`, `trino`, `sqlite` and `athena` reject it, which is correct — they use `IS NOT DISTINCT FROM` instead. So Hive/Impala looks like the remaining gap. ### Test results - `test/dialects/` — 7079 passed - `test/rules/` — 2674 passed, 101 skipped - `ruff format --check` and `ruff check` — clean - `mypy src/sqlfluff/dialects/dialect_hive.py` — Success ### Pull Request checklist - [x] Please confirm you have completed any of the necessary steps below. - Included test cases to demonstrate any code changes, which may be one or more of the following: - `.sql`/`.yml` parser test cases in `test/fixtures/dialects` — added `null_safe_equal.sql`/`.yml` for both `hive` and `impala`, with the `.yml` files generated by `test/generate_parse_fixture_yml.py`. - Added appropriate documentation for the change — the new segment carries a docstring linking the Hive reference; no user-facing docs list per-dialect operators. - Created GitHub issues for any relevant followup/future enhancements if appropriate — none needed. ### AI assistance disclosure Per the AI-Assisted Contributions section of `CONTRIBUTING.md`: this change was written with AI assistance (Claude). The AI drafted the grammar addition and the test fixtures, and ran the verification listed above. I reviewed the diff, confirmed the operator's semantics against the Hive and Impala documentation linked above, and confirmed the dialect inheritance behaviour (Impala covered, Athena unaffected) before submitting. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) --- ## Summary by cubic Adds support for the NULL-safe equals operator `<=>` in the Hive and Impala dialects, which SQLFluff previously reported as unparsable. **Bug Fixes** - The operator parses as a composite of raw `<`, `=`, `>` segments, matching the existing MySQL parse tree so rule ST09 handles it without changes. - Impala inherits support from Hive; Athena is deliberately unaffected since it inherits from ANSI. Written for commit a246b668c86bf3831ccb5045e6122b7060b9c4c0. Summary will update on new commits.

pulls.title: LT05: add option to ignore URL-only SQL comment lines
pulls.body: ### Brief summary of the change made Fixes #4881. Long reference URLs currently trigger LT05 unless users disable length checks for all comments. Add an opt-in setting that ignores a SQL comment line only when its entire content is a single URL with a `scheme://` prefix: ```ini [sqlfluff:rules:layout.long_lines] ignore_url_comment_lines = True ``` This covers dialect-specific line comments and URL-only lines in block comments. Comments containing prose, comments beside SQL, string literals, and template code on the same source line still receive length checks. The option is documented through the rule's configuration metadata and default config. ### Are there any other side effects of this change that we should be aware of? The default is `False`, preserving existing behavior. This setting applies to SQL comments; it does not exempt Jinja comments. ### Validation - End-to-end subprocess tests run `python -m sqlfluff lint`, `fix`, and lint again against temporary files and an on-disk configuration. They verify default/enabled behavior, preservation of URL text, exit codes, and continued diagnostics for nine ordinary or mixed-content long lines. - Negative control with the original LT05 implementation: **6 new cases fail, 4 pass**, including failure of the enabled CLI case. - `pytest test/rules test/cli test/core/config test/utils/reflow -n 4 -q`: **3,231 passed, 101 skipped** on Python 3.13. - `pre-commit run --all-files`: all checks passed. ### Pull Request checklist - [x] Added YAML rule regression cases and executable CLI regression tests. - [x] Documented the new setting and its default. - [x] Ran the relevant regression suites and all pre-commit checks. ### AI assistance and validation ownership This contribution was prepared with Codex at the submitting account owner's explicit request to fix an existing issue and verify it end to end. - **AI-assisted work:** Codex researched the issue, implemented the configuration and LT05 change, wrote the regression tests, prepared the commit and PR description, and ran the validation reported above. - **Validation performed by Codex:** CLI subprocess tests exercising lint, fix, and lint again; a negative control against the original implementation; the listed regression suites; and all pre-commit checks. - **Human manual validation:** No personal code review or manually executed testing by the submitting account owner has been confirmed in this description. The automated validation above should not be read as a claim of human review. Under the project's AI-assisted contribution guidelines, responsibility for the final contribution remains with the contributor. This submission still requires normal maintainer review and applicable CI checks; the local test results do not replace those requirements. --- ## Summary by cubic Adds an opt-in setting so LT05 no longer flags SQL comment lines whose entire content is a single URL with a `scheme://` prefix. Fixes #4881. - Previously, long URL comments triggered LT05 unless `ignore_comment_lines` disabled all comment length checks; the new `ignore_url_comment_lines` option defaults to `False`, preserving existing behavior. - URL-only lines in dialect-specific line comments and block comments are exempt; comments with prose, comments on the same line as SQL, string literals, and template code still receive length checks. Jinja comments are not exempted. Written for commit f468edb15463f42e0d3d8b19e77e86ed79847e45. Summary will update on new commits.

pulls.title: fix(sqlite): the column type is optional in a column definition
pulls.body: ### Brief summary of the change made SQLite's `column-def` is `column-name [type-name] [column-constraint]*` — the type name is optional ([syntax diagram](https://www.sqlite.org/syntax/column-def.html)). The dialect inherits the ANSI `ColumnDefinitionSegment`, which requires a `DatatypeSegment`, so every type-less column fails to parse: ```sql CREATE TABLE t (a, b, c); -- unparsable CREATE TABLE t (a PRIMARY KEY); -- unparsable CREATE TABLE t (a NOT NULL); -- unparsable CREATE TABLE t (a DEFAULT 1); -- unparsable CREATE TABLE t (a COLLATE NOCASE); -- unparsable CREATE TABLE t (a REFERENCES u (b)); -- unparsable CREATE TABLE t (b GENERATED ALWAYS AS (a + 1) VIRTUAL); -- unparsable CREATE TABLE t (b AS (a + 1) STORED); -- unparsable ALTER TABLE t ADD COLUMN b GENERATED ALWAYS AS (a + 1); -- unparsable ``` All of these are accepted by SQLite, and type-less columns are idiomatic there (SQLite has no mandatory column types outside `STRICT` tables). The generated-column forms are the same as the ones in the existing `create_table_constraint_generated.sql` fixture, just without the type. There is a second, quieter symptom: where the constraint keyword is also a valid type-name token, the statement parses but is analysed wrongly. `CREATE TABLE t (a UNIQUE)` produced ``` column_definition: naked_identifier: 'a' data_type: data_type_identifier: 'UNIQUE' ``` i.e. the constraint was swallowed as the column's type. Same for `a CHECK (...)`. ### The change Override `ColumnDefinitionSegment` in `dialect_sqlite.py` with the type made optional, and exclude a leading `ColumnConstraintSegment` from the type slot so that a constraint following the column name directly is not consumed as its type. `a UNIQUE` now yields a `column_constraint_segment`, and typed columns are unchanged. ### Are there any other side effects of this change that we should be aware of? The change is confined to `dialect_sqlite.py`; no other dialect derives from sqlite, and regenerating the fixture YAMLs touched only the sqlite directory. Existing sqlite fixtures parse unchanged (`pytest test/dialects/ -k sqlite` → 114 passed). ### Tests * `create_table_constraint_generated.sql` — added the type-less `GENERATED ALWAYS AS ... VIRTUAL/STORED` and `AS (...)` forms alongside the existing typed ones. * `create_table_no_datatype.sql` (new) — type-less columns with no constraint, and with `PRIMARY KEY`, `NOT NULL`, `DEFAULT`, `UNIQUE`, `CHECK`, `COLLATE`, `REFERENCES`, plus `ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN` with and without a generated expression. YAMLs generated with `test/generate_parse_fixture_yml.py --dialect sqlite`. ### Pull Request checklist - [x] Included test cases: `.sql`/`.yml` parser test cases in `test/fixtures/dialects`. - [x] Added appropriate documentation for the change — none needed beyond the dialect docstring. ### AI assistance disclosure Per CONTRIBUTING: this change was AI-assisted. The gap was found by running a corpus of dialect-documented statements through `sqlfluff parse` and collecting unparsable sections; the grammar change, the fixtures and the PR text were drafted with AI assistance. I validated manually: inspected the resulting parse trees for the type-less and typed forms (including the `a UNIQUE` mis-parse above), confirmed the change is scoped to the sqlite dialect, regenerated the fixture YAMLs, and ran the sqlite dialect tests. --- ## Summary by cubic Fixes SQLite parsing of type-less column definitions so columns without a type name are now accepted, matching SQLite's grammar. - Overrides `ColumnDefinitionSegment` in the SQLite dialect to make the type optional. - Excludes a leading column constraint from being parsed as the column type, so `a UNIQUE` yields a constraint instead of a type named `UNIQUE`. - Adds fixtures for type-less columns with and without constraints, plus generated columns. Written for commit 2bfa3414e6c4f7982cba73d0c477e32476cf754a. Summary will update on new commits.

pulls.title: test(parser): pin max_parse_depth safe direction across engines
pulls.body: ### Brief summary of the change made `max_parse_depth` is a DoS guard, but it is not enforced at the same nesting level by the two parsers. Python tracks nested `deeper_match` contexts (entering an extra one per segment match, plus algorithm wrappers such as `Bracket`, `GreedyUntil`, `Bracketed-StartBracket`/`-EndBracket` and `Delimited-Term`), while the Rust engine tracks its table-driven frame stack. Measured peak depth for nested brackets is `≈ 53 + 16d` (Python) vs `≈ 44 + 14d` (Rust), and the per-level rate differs by construct, so the boundary cannot be reconciled by tuning the default. Python is the stricter of the two. This adds a differential test that pins the *safe* invariant only — the Rust (default) engine must not reject input that the Python engine accepts — across a matrix of nested and flat shapes. It deliberately does not assert the exact gap, so it does not enshrine the current boundary. A note is also added where the guard is enforced, recording that the trip level is engine-dependent. Exact parity is tracked in #8570; this change is a safeguard, not a fix for it. ### Are there any other side effects of this change that we should be aware of? No. There is no behaviour change: the source edit is a comment, and the new test only reads behaviour. Like the existing `test_max_parse_depth_rust_parser_exceeds_limit`, the test is skipped when the Rust extension is not importable. ### Trade-offs considered The test asserts `rust_threshold <= python_threshold` rather than an exact value. Asserting an exact gap would pin a divergence that is expected to change (and would need editing by whichever fix lands); asserting the direction pins the property that actually matters — the default engine never being the stricter one — and will fail loudly if a future grammar change flips it. ### Pull Request checklist - [x] Included test cases to demonstrate any code changes (`test_max_parse_depth_rust_is_never_stricter_than_python`, five shapes, both engines). - [ ] Added appropriate documentation for the change — not user-facing; the note lives at the point of enforcement in `context.py`. As this is a known, pre-existing divergence rather than a fix, it may be worth landing alongside the discussion in #8570 rather than on its own. Tests run locally against the fork with the Rust extension installed: `test/core/parser/` (2778 passed, 2 xfailed), including the five new cases. ### AI disclosure AI-assisted. The investigation, test and comment were produced with DeepSeek V4.1 Flash; Claude Opus 5 was used for planning and review. Validated by confirming the Rust engine is genuinely engaged (its measured threshold is strictly below Python's on every shape) and by the parser suite above. --- ## Summary by cubic Pins the safe direction of `max_parse_depth`: the Rust (default) engine must never reject input that the Python engine accepts. The two engines measure parse depth differently — Python tracks nested `deeper_match` contexts, Rust its table-driven frame stack — so the guard trips at different levels, and Python is currently the stricter. The new differential test asserts only the direction across nested and flat shapes, not the exact gap, so it won't enshrine the current boundary. No behavior change: the source edit is a comment, and the test skips when the Rust extension isn't importable. Exact parity is tracked in #8570. Written for commit dcdf57c23b47ad6aec0ed85fcb061056406e807c. Summary will update on new commits.

pulls.title: parser: make max_parse_nodes accounting identical across Python and Rust
pulls.body:
### Brief summary of the change made

`core.max_parse_nodes` bounds the parse tree, but the Python and Rust engines
counted it differently, so the Rust engine rejected files the Python engine
accepted just under the limit. Reproduced on the public Spark
`typeCoercion/native/decimalPrecision.sql` (1448 lines): ~96k nodes in Python,
~108k in Rust.

Two differences:

- Python charged inserted segments (Indent/Dedent/implicit) only for
  zero-length matches, while Rust charged them unconditionally. For the
  reproduction file that is ~11,826 nodes of difference.
- The engines seeded the budget from different bases: Python from the full
  lexed segment count (`len(segments)`, including leading/trailing non-code),
  Rust only from the trimmed code slice.

### What changed

- `match_result.py`: charge inserted segments in non-empty matches too, so
  Python counts the same nodes as Rust.
- `core.rs` / `python.rs` / `rust_parser.py`: pass the Python-side base count
  (`len(segments)`) into the Rust parser so both limits share a base. The Rust
  binding takes an optional `base_node_count`.
- `rust_parser.py` detects whether the installed `sqlfluffrs` accepts
  `base_node_count` and passes it only when supported, so a wheel that predates
  the parameter (e.g. installing `sqlfluff` from a branch while the released
  `sqlfluffrs==4.3.0` is already present) keeps working rather than raising
  `TypeError` on every Rust parse. CI builds `sqlfluffrs` from source, so it
  would not have caught that skew.
- Raise the default `core.max_parse_nodes` from 100000 to 200000. With the
  corrected (higher) accounting the reproduction file's true budget is ~108k,
  so the old default would newly reject a file the Python engine previously
  parsed. 200000 keeps ~1.85x headroom above it.

The two engines now compute identical node budgets: the same input gives the
same number, and the same accept/reject decision, on both.

### Are there any other side effects of this change that we should be aware of?

Raising the default only affects files whose true node budget sits between
100000 and 200000: they now parse instead of being rejected. Nothing that
parsed before starts failing — the Python engine can only ever count *more*
than it used to, and the cap is the same or higher.

### Pull Request checklist

- [x] Included test cases:
  - `test/core/parser/max_parse_nodes_test.py`: a Python/Rust agreement test
    parametrised over limits that straddle the reproduction file's count (some
    of which used to fall in the band the two engines disagreed on), plus a
    check that the file parses under the shipped default.
  - `test/fixtures/parser/max_parse_nodes_repro.sql`: a synthesized
    reproduction (60 wide `CAST` statements, ~5.4k nodes) whose header explains
    the original manifestation.
  - A Rust unit test pinning `MatchResult::node_count` (classed children plus
    inserts on non-empty matches).
  - Updated the default-value assertion.
- [x] Added appropriate documentation: no prose change needed — the security
  docs reference the defaults generically rather than restating the number.

### Verification

Rebuilt `sqlfluffrs` and measured the two engines reporting identical totals
(10,952 nodes for 120 statements; 27,332 for 300). The reproduction file now
rejects on both engines at limit 100000 and parses on both at the new default.

- `test/core/parser` + `test/core/config`: 2916 passed, 2 xfailed.
- `test/dialects`: 7061 passed.
- `test/rules`: 2774 passed.
- `test/core` + `test/api` + `test/cli`: 3780 passed (only the pre-existing
  example-plugin failures in `test/core/plugin_test.py`).
- Rust: `cargo test -p sqlfluffrs_parser --lib` (22 passed),
  `cargo fmt --all --check`, and
  `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --features python -- -D warnings`
  all clean.
- Python: `ruff check`, `ruff format --check`, `mypy` all clean.

### AI disclosure

This contribution is **AI-assisted and explicitly disclosed**, in line with
[CONTRIBUTING.md](https://github.com/sqlfluff/sqlfluff/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md#ai-assisted-contributions):

- Tools used: **DeepSeek V4.1 Flash** drafted the implementation (the Python
  change plus the Rust and PyO3 changes) and the tests; **Claude Opus 5** was
  used for planning and review.
- The human contributor directed the work, reproduced the bug against both
  engines, chose the fix approach and the new default, verified it by
  rebuilding `sqlfluffrs` and measuring identical node totals, and ran the
  suites above. The human contributor remains responsible for the final pull
  request, including its correctness, tests and maintainability.

pulls.title: fix(RF03): only skip templated refs for the placeholder templater
pulls.body: ### Brief summary of the change made Fixes #8556. `RF03` (`references.consistent`) unconditionally skips consistency checking for any unqualified reference where `ref.is_templated` is `True`. That guard was added in #7615 to stop the `placeholder` templater's colon-style bind parameters (e.g. `:colname`) — rendered as a bare identifier that is not a real column — from being wrongly qualified/flagged. `ref.is_templated` is a generic marker shared by every templater though, so the same guard also silently exempted Jinja/dbt `{{ var }}`-rendered column names — genuine identifiers the user intends to select — from ever being checked. This threads `templater_name` (`context.config.get("templater")`) down through `_visit_queries`/`_check_references` and narrows the skip to apply only when the active templater is `placeholder`, matching what #7615 itself scoped the exemption to in its PR body, review thread, and tests. **Impact: silent-wrong-result.** **Entry point / who reaches this:** any user running `sqlfluff lint` or `sqlfluff fix` with `RF03` enabled (it is on by default in the base rule set) against SQL rendered by the Jinja templater — the default templater, and the one used by every dbt project (`sqlfluff` is dbt's most common SQL linter integration). A single-table query with one qualified and one unqualified column reference, where the unqualified reference comes from a Jinja variable/macro (e.g. `{{ my_col }}`, or any dbt `{{ ref(...) }}`-style macro that expands to a bare column name), silently produces zero `RF03` violations instead of the two violations the byte-identical non-templated query correctly reports. The user sees a clean lint pass on code the rule is supposed to flag — the rule is not merely weaker here, it is inverted from "flag both qualified and unqualified in the same select" to "flag neither," specifically for the common Jinja/dbt path. ### Are there any other side effects of this change that we should be aware of? None expected. The `placeholder` templater's exemption (the case #7615 actually addressed) is unchanged — this only narrows the condition that already existed from "any templater" to "the templater #7615's own PR scoped it to." Negative control — reverted only `src/sqlfluff/rules/references/RF03.py` to `upstream/main` (regression fixture kept) and re-ran the targeted test: ``` $ pytest test/rules/yaml_test_cases_test.py -k RF03 -q FAILED test/rules/yaml_test_cases_test.py::test__rule_test_case[RF03_test_fail_jinja_templated_unqualified_reference_inconsistent] 1 failed, 60 passed, 2436 deselected in 5.44s ``` Restored the fix and re-ran the identical command: ``` $ pytest test/rules/yaml_test_cases_test.py -k RF03 -q 61 passed, 2436 deselected in 5.82s ``` The new case fails without the fix and passes with it; the other 60 pre-existing RF03 cases are unaffected in both directions. ### Pull Request checklist - [x] Included test cases to demonstrate any code changes: added `RF03_test_fail_jinja_templated_unqualified_reference_inconsistent` to `test/fixtures/rules/std_rule_cases/RF03.yml`, which fails without this fix (`1 failed, 60 passed`) and passes with it (`61 passed`). - [ ] Added appropriate documentation for the change (behavior-narrowing bug fix; no public API or documented-behavior change to update). - [ ] Created GitHub issues for any relevant followup/future enhancements (none identified). ### AI-assisted contribution disclosure AI-assisted. The defect was located and the mechanism (the `#7615` guard's generic `ref.is_templated` check vs. its own PR-scoped intent) diagnosed with AI assistance; the fix, the regression fixture, and the negative control (reverting only `RF03.py` and confirming the new test fails while the other 60 remain green) were manually validated by execution before this PR was opened. Signed-off-by: Udaya Tejas --- ## Summary by cubic Fixes RF03 (`references.consistent`) silently skipping consistency checks for any templated unqualified reference, hiding real violations in Jinja/dbt queries. The existing skip was meant for `placeholder` templater bind parameters like `:colname`, which render as bare identifiers that aren't real columns. Since `ref.is_templated` is a generic marker shared by all templaters, the skip also exempted genuine Jinja/dbt `{{ my_col }}` references from ever being checked. - Narrowed the skip to the `placeholder` templater by threading its name through the rule. - Stopped attaching autofixes to templated references: a single `{{ cols }}` template (e.g. `dbt_utils.star()`) can render to multiple columns, so inserting or deleting a qualifier would touch only the first rendered column and silently corrupt the SQL. Such references are still flagged and left for the user to fix by hand. - Added regression tests verifying that Jinja-rendered unqualified references are still flagged and never autofixed. Written for commit 0d8518cd295f726799ab4f55c046284ba4da7199. Summary will update on new commits.

pulls.title: parser: opt-in anchoring of parse failures at the furthest failure
pulls.body:
### Brief summary of the change made

A root-shape parse failure is anchored at the start of the enclosing unparsable
section - often line 1, position 1 - which tells the user nothing about where
the statement actually broke.

Record the furthest token index at which a *required* element failed (a
monotonic high-water mark kept on the parse context; both the Python and the
Rust engine keep one) and attach the segment at that index to the root
`UnparsableSegment`. With the new opt-in `core.furthest_failure_anchor` the
linter then anchors the violation - and the position in its message - at that
point. For example:

```
WITH cte AS (SELECT 1)
SELEC id
FROM cte
```

is reported at `L: 1 | P: 1` by default, and at `L: 2 | P: 1` (the `SELEC`
line) when the option is enabled.

The anchor is bounded to the unparsable section and to its first statement
terminator, so a failure recorded in a *following* statement is never used.

### Engine parity

The feature is only useful if both engines report the same position, and the two
parsers backtrack differently, so the recorded "furthest failure" had to be
reconciled:

- Python no longer records a failure in `AnyNumberOf`/`OneOf`. Those
  alternatives are speculative: the position they reach can sit in a discarded
  branch or even in the next statement.
- Rust now records a required content-element failure *inside* brackets (at the
  content position), which Python already did by descending into the bracket.
- The linter only accepts an anchor that falls inside the unparsable section and
  no later than its first statement terminator.

A differential test
(`test__linter__furthest_failure_anchor_engine_agreement`) asserts that the two
engines anchor a set of representative failures at exactly the same position.
Measured over the unparsable subset of the public Databricks corpus, the engines
now agree on every file; the only remaining difference is a pre-existing
Rust-only `max_parse_nodes` failure, unrelated to this feature.

### Are there any other side effects of this change that we should be aware of?

The anchor is opt-in because it moves violation positions, which is a
user-visible (if minor) behaviour change. The default is unchanged: the
`UnparsableSegment` always carries the recorded failure, but the linter only
uses it when the option is set. The Rust engine's new property is only read when
the option is enabled (and via `getattr`), so an older `sqlfluffrs` wheel cannot
break the default path.

### Trade-offs considered

The recorder is a **side table on the parse context** (Python `ParseContext`,
Rust `Parser`) rather than a field on `MatchResult`. Keeping it off the frozen
`MatchResult` avoids threading a new field through `append()`/`wrap()` (whose
early-return passthroughs can silently drop it) and keeps the hot path to an
integer comparison. It is also cache-sound: the recorder is a monotonic
high-water mark living for the duration of one file parse, so a cache hit that
does not re-enter the handler cannot move the anchor. A unit test pins that the
anchor is identical across two parses.

### Pull Request checklist
- [x] Included test cases to demonstrate any code changes
  (`test__linter__furthest_failure_anchor*`: pinned positions, both engines
  agreeing, graceful degradation against a wheel without the property, and cache
  stability).
- [x] Added appropriate documentation for the change (the option is documented
  in `default_config.cfg` alongside the other `core` options).

As this makes a backwards-incompatible (opt-in) change to reported positions,
it should probably be raised as an issue for discussion before merge.

Tests run locally against the fork (Rust extension rebuilt via `maturin develop
--release`): `test/core` + `test/api` + `test/cli` (3790 passed, 3 skipped, 2
xfailed) and full `test/dialects/` (7054 passed). The only failures are the
pre-existing example-plugin tests in `test/core/plugin_test.py`.

### AI disclosure

AI-assisted. The implementation (Python and Rust, including the PyO3 getter and
the engine-parity reconciliation) and the tests were produced with DeepSeek
V4.1 Flash; Claude Opus 5 was used for planning and review. Validated by
rebuilding `sqlfluffrs` and checking that both engines anchor at the same
position, and by the full suites above.

pulls.title: parser: name the unexpected token in leftover unparsable messages
pulls.body: ### Brief summary of the change made When a `GREEDY`/`GREEDY_ONCE_STARTED` Sequence matches all of its elements but leaves unclaimed code behind, it marks that code unparsable with the generic `"Nothing here."` message. Name the first unexpected token instead: ``` ... Found unparsable section: '2 3'. Expected: Nothing here. Found ``` This mirrors the sibling `"Found ..."` messages on the same code path and the `AnyNumberOf` `"Nothing else before ..."` message, and it is by far the most common `Expected:` value in real-world parse failures. The change is applied to both engines - Python's `Sequence.match` GREEDY mop-up and the Rust table-driven `sequence.rs` / `bracketed.rs` fallbacks - so the parity suite's byte-exact `stringify()` comparison stays green. The Rust `sequence.rs` block also had a dead `segment_kwargs` map that duplicated the message but was never used; it is removed. ### Are there any other side effects of this change that we should be aware of? The parity regression fixture that pins the optional-content-failure wording is updated to describe the new message. No grammar or match behaviour changes. ### Pull Request checklist - [x] Included test cases to demonstrate any code changes (the parity regression fixture, plus the Rust unit/parity suites). - [x] Added appropriate documentation for the change (troubleshooting guide and its `docsv` mirror). Tests run locally against the fork (Rust extension rebuilt via `maturin develop --release`): parity suite `test/core/parser/parity/` (2358 passed, 2 xfailed), full `test/dialects/` (7054 passed), `test/core/parser/` (2771 passed). ### AI disclosure AI-assisted. The implementation (Python and Rust) and the fixture updates were produced with DeepSeek V4.1 Flash; Claude Opus 5 was used for planning and review. Validated by rebuilding `sqlfluffrs` and running the full parity suite, which compares the two engines byte-for-byte on `stringify()` output. --- ## Summary by cubic Names the first unexpected token in leftover unparsable sections, so `Expected:` reads `Nothing here. Found ` instead of the generic `Nothing here.` when a `GREEDY`/`GREEDY_ONCE_STARTED` sequence leaves unclaimed code. - Applied to Python's `Sequence.match` and the Rust table-driven `sequence.rs`/`bracketed.rs` fallbacks to keep the parity suite's byte-exact `stringify()` comparison green. - Removes a dead `segment_kwargs` map in `sequence.rs` that duplicated the message. - Updates the doc troubleshooting guides and the parity regression fixture for the new wording. Written for commit 67276dfaad8d25be8a7a90da68ac9601f8ab790c. Summary will update on new commits.

pulls.title: linter: surface the expected grammar in unparsable messages
pulls.body: ### Brief summary of the change made The parser already records what it was expecting on every `UnparsableSegment` (via `_expected`), but the linter discarded it and reported only `Found unparsable section: ''`. Surface it: ``` Line 1, Position 1: Found unparsable section: 'SELECT'. Expected: ]> after . Found nothing. ``` - The raw section is now capped at 80 chars, and the old `len(raw) < 40` comparison (which appended an ellipsis to exactly-40-char sections) is fixed. - The `expected` string is curtailed to 80 chars so the message stays on one line. - When no expected string was recorded the message is unchanged. This is the difference between knowing *that* something failed and knowing *what* was expected. In a 150-file sample of real-world published Databricks SQL, 85% of parse failures reported an uninformative expected string, and 0% of root-shape failures gave any hint of the cause. The position, by contrast, was already correct in the common (nested) cases, which is why the message and not the anchor is the first change. ### Are there any other side effects of this change that we should be aware of? Existing fixture expectations that pin the exact message text are updated. The GitLab Code Quality fingerprint hashes `filepath:code:line:pos` and does not include the description, so it is unaffected. ### Pull Request checklist - [x] Included test cases to demonstrate any code changes (`parse_test.py`, `simple_test.py`, `commands_test.py`, plus updated fixtures). - [x] Added appropriate documentation for the change (troubleshooting guide and its `docsv` mirror). The change was validated by running the affected suites and the full `test/dialects/` suite locally, and by inspecting the resulting messages against the real engine. --- ## Summary by cubic Surfaces the expected grammar in unparsable parse violations so the message explains what the parser was looking for instead of just reporting the failure. - Caps the raw section at 80 chars, fixing the old comparison that appended an ellipsis to exactly-40-char sections. - Curtails the expected string to 80 chars to keep the message on one line; messages without an expected value are unchanged. - Updates fixtures that pin the exact message text. pulls.title: fix(AM07): restore CTE after resolving an unaliased wildcard
pulls.body: ### Brief summary of the change made `AM07` resolves a bare `SELECT * FROM cte` through `Query.lookup_cte()`, whose `pop` argument defaults to `True`, so the CTE is deleted from its scope once found. The sibling path for *aliased* wildcards goes through `Query.crawl_sources()`, whose own `pop` default is `False`. That asymmetry means the second of two unaliased references to the same CTE in one set expression cannot resolve. Because AM07 only reports when every branch resolved, a genuine column count mismatch is discarded entirely: ```sql with cte as (select a, b from t) select * from cte union select * from cte union select c, d, e from t2 ``` `sqlfluff lint --dialect ansi --rules AM07` reports `All Finished!` on this query. The same query with one `select * from cte` branch removed is correctly flagged, so the bug is specifically the repeated unaliased reference. The rule's own debug output shows the mechanism — two textually identical branches resolving differently: ``` [AM07] Resolved N=2: 'select * from cte' [AM07] Unresolved N=0: 'select * from cte' [AM07] Resolved select sizes (resolved wildcard: False) : {0, 2, 3} ``` Three distinct sizes are computed and then discarded, because one branch did not resolve. The pop exists to stop a CTE that references itself from recursing forever while it is being resolved, so this change keeps it and restores the CTE to its owning scope once that resolution has finished. Restoring afterwards rather than not popping at all preserves the guard: passing `pop=False` instead reintroduces `maximum recursion depth exceeded` on `with cte as (select * from cte union all select 1 as n) select * from cte union select 1`, which I checked before settling on this approach. ### `AM04`, and the reason it is in this pull request `AM04` calls `lookup_cte` in the same way and shows the mirrored symptom on the same query — a false *positive* "Query produces an unknown number of result columns" on the second reference, where AM07 gives a false negative: ```sql with cte as (select a, b from t) select * from cte union select * from cte union select c, d from t2 ``` `AM04` is fixed here rather than in a follow-up. An earlier revision of this description deferred it to keep the pull request to a single concern; that was changed at review, and this section records why the two changes belong together. They are the same defect and the same two-line fix — leaving one rule half-fixed would mean the remaining bug stayed reachable through whichever rule the user happened to run, and the AM04 half is a false *positive*, which is the more annoying of the two symptoms to ship around. `AM04` and `AM07` are the only callers of `lookup_cte()` in the tree. `RF03` reaches the same CTEs via `crawl_sources()`, which defaults to `pop=False`, so it is unaffected and is not touched here. ### Pull Request checklist Six cases were added across `test/fixtures/rules/std_rule_cases/AM07.yml` and `AM04.yml`: | Case | Rule | Kind | Fails without the fix? | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | `test_fail_repeated_unaliased_cte_wildcard_reference` | AM07 | fail, pinned violations | yes | | `test_fail_repeated_unaliased_cte_wildcard_reference_nested_scope` | AM07 | fail, pinned violations | yes | | `test_pass_repeated_unaliased_cte_wildcard_reference_matching` | AM07 | pass, branches genuinely agree | no (guards a false positive) | | `test_pass_self_referencing_cte_wildcard` | AM07 | pass, recursion guard | no (locks in the chosen fix) | | `test_pass_repeated_unaliased_cte_wildcard_reference` | AM04 | pass, the false positive above | yes | | `test_fail_self_referencing_cte_wildcard` | AM04 | fail, recursion guard | no (locks in the chosen fix) | With the production change reverted and all six fixtures present, exactly the three marked above fail and nothing else — the two AM07 fail cases have no violation left to find at all, and the AM04 pass case trips the false positive: ``` $ pytest test/rules/yaml_test_cases_test.py -k "AM04 or AM07" -q FAILED test/rules/yaml_test_cases_test.py::test__rule_test_case[AM04_test_pass_repeated_unaliased_cte_wildcard_reference] FAILED test/rules/yaml_test_cases_test.py::test__rule_test_case[AM07_test_fail_repeated_unaliased_cte_wildcard_reference] FAILED test/rules/yaml_test_cases_test.py::test__rule_test_case[AM07_test_fail_repeated_unaliased_cte_wildcard_reference_nested_scope] 3 failed, 110 passed, 2398 deselected ``` With the fix restored: `114 passed` for `-k "AM04 or AM07"`, `257 passed` for the full `AM0*` family, and `2823 passed, 104 skipped` for `test/rules/ test/core/rules/ test/utils/analysis/`. Coverage stays at 100% on both `AM04.py` and `AM07.py`. `ruff check`, `ruff format --check` and `yamllint -c .yamllint` are all clean. The recursion guard is a real test rather than a comment: swapping the restore for `pop=False` makes `test_pass_self_referencing_cte_wildcard` fail with `RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded`, which is what ruled that simpler option out. AM04 gets the same guard for the same reason, since its restore could reintroduce the same recursion. `AM07`'s `if cte.parent is not None` guard is now an `assert`, to answer the question raised in review. Yes, it is always true: `Query.from_segment()` constructs every CTE with its owning query as `parent` (`query.py:434`), and `Query.__post_init__` re-asserts it for CTEs present at construction (`query.py:224-225`). The `assert` also gives mypy the narrowing it needs to reach `cte.parent.ctes`. ### How this was verified Everything quoted above is from runs I made on the branch. Specifically: - I reproduced the bug before the fix and confirmed the false negative, then confirmed the same query is flagged after the fix. - I ran the negative control: with the production change reverted and all six fixtures present, exactly the three cases marked above fail and the rest pass. - I ran the self-referencing CTE case and confirmed it completes without recursing, and separately confirmed that the `pop=False` alternative does recurse, which is what ruled that option out. - I confirmed the `parent` invariant by reading `Query.from_segment` and `Query.__post_init__` rather than assuming it. - I ran the rule and analysis suites in full, plus `ruff` and `yamllint`. To be precise about the diagnosis: I did not derive the root cause independently. I confirmed it by running the behaviour it predicts, and each of the claims above has a command behind it. ### Review comments addressed - @rubytobi — "please update AM04 as well for consistency": done, and this description now says so rather than deferring it. - @rubytobi — nested-scope test: `test_fail_repeated_unaliased_cte_wildcard_reference_nested_scope`, with the CTE defined and referenced inside another CTE's body so the restore lands in the nested owning scope. - @rubytobi — "add a passing case where the repeated references genuinely match": `test_pass_repeated_unaliased_cte_wildcard_reference_matching`. - @rubytobi — "pin the expected violations in the fail case": both AM07 fail cases now pin full `violations:` blocks, as does the AM04 counterpart. - @rubytobi — "Isn't this always true?": yes; the guard is now an `assert` with the invariant documented above. - cubic — AM04 fix not reflected in the description: fixed above, this is the accurate account of what the branch does. - cubic — nested-scope fail case does not pin its violations: fixed in `96752b3`. Both findings were valid; both are addressed. --- ## Summary by cubic Fixes AM07 and AM04 giving false results when a CTE referenced by unaliased wildcards appears in multiple branches of a set expression. `lookup_cte()` pops the CTE from scope, so later branches failed to resolve; the CTE is now restored after resolution, keeping the recursion guard for self-referencing CTEs. - Switches AM07's `if cte.parent is not None` guard to an assert, since the parent is always set for CTEs reachable via `lookup_cte()`. - Adds regression tests for repeated references, nested CTE scopes, self-referencing CTEs, and matching column counts; AM04's mirrored false positive is fixed here instead of deferred to a follow-up. Written for commit aa98d37cc136dd37bdb2d981213f91f140d52ae4. Summary will update on new commits.

pulls.title: Databricks: support the Unity Catalog governance surface
pulls.body:
## Summary

Adds the Unity Catalog governance surface:

- **`SHOW`** for the Unity Catalog objects: `CATALOGS`, `CONNECTIONS`,
  `[STORAGE | SERVICE] CREDENTIALS`, `EXTERNAL LOCATIONS`, `GROUPS`,
  `EFFECTIVE POLICIES` / `POLICIES`, `PROCEDURES`, `PROVIDERS`, `RECIPIENTS`,
  `SHARES`, `TABLES DROPPED`, `USERS`, `ALL IN SHARE`, `COLUMNS`, and
  `GRANTS ON SHARE` / `GRANTS TO RECIPIENT`.
- **`DESCRIBE`** for the same objects plus the `CATALOG` and `QUERY` forms,
  with a guarded DESCRIBE table reference so a bare object keyword is not read
  as a table name.
- The complete Unity Catalog **securable list**, with `ALL PRIVILEGES` bound
  against a privilege list (the reference makes them exclusive alternatives).
- **`CREATE GROUP` / `DROP GROUP`**, **`DENY`**, **`GRANT` / `REVOKE ON
  SHARE`**, and **`MSCK REPAIR ... PRIVILEGES`**.
- The **`READ FILES`** privilege and the **`ANY FILE`** securable.

  than parsed as a principal named `RECIPIENT`.

pulls.title: Databricks: support INSERT, RESTORE and flow statements
pulls.body:
## Summary

Adds the Databricks ingestion and flow surface:

- **`INSERT WITH SCHEMA EVOLUTION`** and the **`REPLACE ON`** alternative,
  including the parenthesised query source, which a general expression grammar
  mis-reads as a function call
  ([docs](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/sql/language-manual/sql-ref-syntax-dml-insert-into)).
- **`RESTORE [TABLE] <target> [TO] { TIMESTAMP AS OF | VERSION AS OF }`**,
  with the table name and `TO` optional and an arithmetic timestamp expression
  ([docs](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/sql/language-manual/delta-restore)).
- **Inline `FLOW`** on a pipeline `CREATE TABLE`, and on a `STREAMING` table
  ([docs](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/ldp/developer/ldp-sql-ref-create-table-flow)).
- Bind **`REPLACE USING (...)` and `SEQUENCE BY` together** in the append-flow
  spec, so a standalone `CREATE FLOW` rejects either half on its own. This is
  the over-acceptance [#8509](https://github.com/sqlfluff/sqlfluff/pull/8509)
  shipped: it took `REPLACE USING (...)` without the required `SEQUENCE BY`,
  and rejected the documented pair
  ([docs](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/ldp/developer/ldp-sql-ref-create-flow)).

Adds fixtures for each and rejection cases for the partial forms a valid-parse
fixture cannot express.

## Note on scope

The inline-`FLOW` machinery overlaps the open draft
[#8520](https://github.com/sqlfluff/sqlfluff/pull/8520) (inline `FLOW` on a
streaming table). They are the same statement family and share the `FLOW`
clause, so whichever lands second should drop the overlap; this branch carries
both the streaming and the plain pipeline form so it is measurable on its own.

## Tests

## Summary

- **`OFFSET`** without the ANSI `ROW`/`ROWS` keyword

  `OFFSET` remains a legal column name, so it is removed from the
  `FromClauseTerminatorGrammar` set and excluded from the alias grammar
  explicitly instead.
