  ([docs](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/sql/language-manual/sql-ref-syntax-qry-select-sampling)).
- **`MATCH_RECOGNIZE`**, including the trailing table alias it allows
  ([docs](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/sql/language-manual/sql-ref-syntax-qry-select-match-recognize)).
- **`WITH ( ... )` options** on a table reference
  ([docs](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/sql/language-manual/sql-ref-syntax-qry-select-table-reference)).
- **`MAX RECURSION LEVEL`** on a CTE definition
  ([docs](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/sql/language-manual/sql-ref-syntax-qry-select-cte)).
- The **SQL pipeline `|>`** in its `FROM` / `TABLE` / `SELECT` forms, including
  a pipeline with zero operations (`FROM t`)
  ([docs](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/sql/language-manual/sql-ref-syntax-qry-pipeline)).
- **`ORDER BY ALL`**

- **`USE [DATABASE|SCHEMA] name`**, with a bare `USE SCHEMA` rejected.

pulls.title: SparkSQL/Databricks: identifier and keyword false positives, JSON paths, set operands
pulls.body:
## Summary

Fixes a set of parser false positives and gaps in the SparkSQL and Databricks
dialects, all found by an independent doc-derived conformance corpus:

- **`IDENTIFIER(...)` as a column, `IDENTIFIER()` rejected.** A Databricks
  column reference now inherits the object reference, so the identifier clause
  can appear as a column (`SELECT IDENTIFIER('col')`), and `IDENTIFIER` is
  excluded from function names, so the argument-less `IDENTIFIER()` is
  rejected.
- **`LEFT` and `RIGHT` are unreserved again.** The SparkSQL `LEFT`/`RIGHT`
  join keywords had made them illegal as identifiers. `KEYS`, `PIVOT` and
  `WINDOW` are legal *explicit* aliases (`AS PIVOT`) while still excluded from
  implicit aliases.
- **`DESCRIBE history.tbl`.** The general `DESCRIBE` no longer excludes the
  `HISTORY`/`DETAIL` keywords, and the Delta `DESCRIBE HISTORY`/`DESCRIBE
  DETAIL` statements are tried first, so an unqualified `DESCRIBE HISTORY tbl`
  still binds to them.
- **A table named `stream`** can be referenced in `FROM` (`SELECT * FROM
  stream`), which the streaming `STREAM` prefix previously made unparsable.
- **JSON path** `[*]` wildcard and delimited identifiers
  (`raw:store.book[*]`, ``raw:`full name` ``).
- **A parenthesised subquery is a set-operation operand**
  (`EXCEPT (SELECT ...)`); only `EXCEPT (col, ...)` is treated as a wildcard
  exclusion.

Fixes the reference cases `identifier-clause.without-argument`,
`array-sort.lambda-keyword-parameters`, `json-path.star`,
`json-path.delimited-identifier` and `set-operators.parenthesised-operands`,
and the published files `spark-tpcds/q87.sql` and

pulls.title: Databricks: keep notebook magic-cell boundaries out of the lexer
pulls.body:
## What

Fixes two boundary errors in the Databricks notebook `-- MAGIC` lexer, both of
which end a magic cell early and leave the following statement unparsable:

- `magic_start` consumed its trailing newline, and the `[^%]` in
  `magic_single_line` / `magic_line` was allowed to match one. A `-- MAGIC`
  line with a **trailing space**, or a cell whose last line is a **standalone
  directive**, therefore swallowed the blank line that separates the cell from
  its `-- COMMAND` separator. The lexer now matches only non-newline
  characters in the body of a magic line and leaves the newline to the lexer.

A second commit fixes the related grammar boundary: a cell's language comes
from its first directive, so a later directive-shaped line — an `%md` cell
quoting `%pip`, for example — is body text. The grammar previously allowed only
plain `magic_line` body lines after the directive and ended the cell instead.

## Tests

- `test/dialects/databricks_test.py::test_magic_cell_boundaries` pins both
  whitespace boundaries as **clean-parse** checks, not rejections: trailing
  whitespace is stripped from `.sql` fixtures, and one boundary is exactly a
  trailing space, so a fixture cannot express it.
- The affected published notebook (`my_streaming_table.sql`) now parses; the
  SCD notebook advances past its magic cells — it now fails later, on the
  separately queued `COPY INTO`.
- Whole `test/dialects/` **7032 passed**; corpus mutation stays **100%**

pulls.body:
## What

Adds a `databricks` style to the placeholder templater for notebook widget and
dashboard parameters:


pulls.title: Parser: treat a closing bracket as a code boundary for keyword terminators
pulls.body:
## What

A keyword terminator was only honoured when preceded by whitespace, so a
keyword glued to a closing bracket was read as an **implicit alias** instead of
ending the clause:

```sql
SELECT (a)FROM t;   -- unparsable: `FROM` taken as the alias of `(a)`
SELECT (a) FROM t;  -- parses
```

The two differ only by a whitespace token. The same shape appears in real SQL —
`count(DISTINCT sk)FROM t` in a published notebook, and `(a)WHERE`,
`(a)ORDER BY`, `(a)LIMIT` — and the keyword is swallowed as a naked identifier
alias, so the rest of the statement is unparsable. It reproduces on `ansi`,
`sparksql` and `databricks`, and on released 4.3.0, so it is core rather than
dialect-specific.

`greedy_match()` requires whitespace before an all-alphabetic terminator to
avoid a keyword being matched mid-expression. But a closing bracket is already
an unambiguous code boundary — nothing can absorb the keyword into the
preceding token — so the requirement is dropped after `)`, `]` and `}`.

The Rust parser mirrors the same rule (`is_preceded_by_whitespace`), so it is
updated too; without that the Python-vs-Rust parity corpus test fails on the
new fixture.

## Tests

- New `ansi/select_bracket_then_keyword.sql`: `(a)FROM`, `(a)WHERE`,
  `(a)ORDER BY`, `(a)LIMIT` and `count(DISTINCT sk)FROM`. Every case fails to
  parse before the change.
- `test/dialects/` and `test/core/parser/` in full, which includes the
  `python-vs-rust` parity corpus test, both engines green.
- The whole `test/` suite: no new failures.
- The published notebook whose `count(DISTINCT sk)FROM` motivated this now
  parses.

pulls.title: fix(mysql): allow CALL without parentheses
pulls.body: ### Brief summary of the change made `CALL` requires parentheses in sqlfluff, but the mysql manual allows without parens too — https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.0/en/call.html says: ``` CALL sp_name([parameter[,...]]) CALL sp_name[()] ``` The `[()]` means the parentheses themselves are optional, not just the arguments, so `CALL p;` is valid and was unparsable. `CallStoredProcedureSegment` matched `Ref("FunctionSegment")`, which always expects a bracketed argument list. It now accepts a bare `FunctionNameSegment` as an alternative. Qualified names work either way — `CALL db.p;` and `CALL db.p();` both parse. ### Are there any other side effects of this change that we should be aware of? - No existing fixture changes; `call_statement.yml` is untouched, since the parenthesised form still matches `FunctionSegment` first. - No other dialect is affected. ### Pull Request checklist - [x] Please confirm you have completed any of the necessary steps below. - Included test cases to demonstrate any code changes, which may be one or more of the following: - `.sql`/`.yml` parser test cases in `test/fixtures/dialects` — two new fixtures, `call_no_parentheses` and `call_qualified_no_parentheses`, alongside the existing `call_statement`. - Added appropriate documentation for the change — none needed; this widens an existing segment rather than adding one. - Created GitHub issues for any relevant followup/future enhancements if appropriate — none. ### AI assistance disclosure Per CONTRIBUTING.md. The grammar change, the fixtures and the test runs were AI-assisted (Claude Opus 5). Manually validated by me: the diff, and the syntax against the CALL page in the MySQL manual; I've also written a lot of procedural code using this syntax. Checks run locally: full test suite (11231 passed) and all pre-commit hooks. Fixture regeneration across all dialects reproduces every `.yml` in this branch byte for byte. The dbt templater tests were not run locally, as they need a running Postgres instance; CI covers them. --- ## Summary by cubic Allows MySQL `CALL` statements without parentheses, so `CALL p;` and `CALL db.p;` parse instead of failing, matching the MySQL manual. - Adds parse fixtures for unqualified and qualified `CALL` without parentheses. - Leaves the parenthesized form and all other dialects unchanged. pulls.title: fix(mysql): support multiple variables and expression defaults in DEC…
pulls.body: ### Brief summary of the change made Two gaps in the local variable branch of `DeclareStatement`, per https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.0/en/declare-local-variable.html: ``` DECLARE var_name [, var_name] ... type [DEFAULT value] ``` `DECLARE a, b, c INT;` was unparsable — only a single variable was accepted. And the `DEFAULT` clause accepted only a quoted literal, a numeric literal or a function, so `DECLARE x INT DEFAULT NULL;` was unparsable, as was any expression such as `DEFAULT 1 + 2`. The manual states the default "can be specified as an expression; it need not be a constant". Both are fixed by `Delimited(Ref("LocalVariableNameSegment"))` for the name list and `Ref("ExpressionSegment")` for the default, which makes the grammar slightly smaller than before. All five forms were checked against a running MariaDB server, which accepts each of them: ```sql BEGIN NOT ATOMIC DECLARE a INT DEFAULT 1 + 2; DECLARE b INT DEFAULT NULL; DECLARE c INT DEFAULT GREATEST(1, 2); DECLARE d INT DEFAULT -1; DECLARE e, f, g INT DEFAULT 0; SELECT a, b, c, d, e, f, g; END ``` returns `3, NULL, 2, -1, 0, 0, 0`. `DEFAULT -1` was also unparsable before this change, not just `DEFAULT NULL`. `DEFAULT greatest(1, 2)` already parsed via the `FunctionSegment` branch being removed here, so `declare_default_function.sql` is regression cover for that rather than a new capability. ### Are there any other side effects of this change that we should be aware of? - `DEFAULT 1` now parses as `expression: numeric_literal: '1'` rather than a bare `numeric_literal`, so four existing fixtures are regenerated: `declare_default_numeric` and `declare_default_quotedliteral`, in both `mysql` and `mariadb`. Deeper tree, but it matches the documented grammar. - No other dialect is affected; fixture generation across all dialects shows no further changes. - A note on the fixtures themselves: `DECLARE` is only valid at the start of a `BEGIN ... END` block, so these bare statements are not valid MySQL on their own — and neither are the existing `declare_*` fixtures they sit alongside, such as `declare_local_variable.sql` and `declare_cursor.sql`. I have followed that existing convention rather than changed it, partly for consistency and partly to keep this change independent of #8531, which alters how compound bodies parse. Moving the whole `declare_*` family into block context looks worth doing, but as its own change rather than folded into this one. Happy to do it if you would like it. ### Pull Request checklist - [x] Please confirm you have completed any of the necessary steps below. - Included test cases to demonstrate any code changes, which may be one or more of the following: - `.sql`/`.yml` parser test cases in `test/fixtures/dialects` — six new fixtures: `declare_default_null`, `declare_default_expression`, `declare_default_negative`, `declare_default_function`, `declare_multiple_variables` and `declare_multiple_variables_default`. The `function` one covers behaviour that already worked, so the branch being removed does not regress. - Added appropriate documentation for the change — no docstring or user facing documentation changes seemed needed, since this corrects an existing segment rather than adding one. Happy to add some if you would like. - Created GitHub issues for any relevant followup/future enhancements if appropriate — none opened for this; the fixture placement point above is the only followup I can see, and it is noted here rather than filed separately. ### AI assistance disclosure Per CONTRIBUTING.md. The grammar change, the new fixtures and the test runs were AI-assisted (Claude Opus 5). Manually validated by me: the full diff, the implemented syntax against the DECLARE grammar in the MySQL manual, and the accepted forms against a running MariaDB server. Checks run locally: full test suite (11237 passed), all pre-commit hooks, and `lint-imports`. Fixture regeneration across all dialects reproduces every `.yml` in this branch byte for byte. The dbt templater tests were not run locally, as they need a running Postgres instance; CI covers them. --- ## Summary by cubic Fixes MySQL `DECLARE` so it accepts comma-separated variable lists and expression defaults, matching the documented grammar. - `DECLARE a, b INT` now parses; previously only a single variable was allowed. - `DEFAULT` now accepts any expression, including `NULL`, `-1`, and `1 + 2`; previously only quoted literals, numeric literals, and function calls were allowed. - `DEFAULT` values now parse as expression nodes, so four existing MySQL and MariaDB fixtures regenerate. No other dialects are affected. Written for commit bb3ae156ddf476eae8262d9fcb492527f2999c83. Summary will update on new commits.

pulls.title: fix(AM02): preserve UNION's existing case instead of forcing a hardcoded one
pulls.body: ## Summary `AM02` (`ambiguous.union` / `L033`) flags a bare `UNION` and offers a fix that inserts `DISTINCT`. To do that, its fix currently **replaces** the existing `UNION` keyword segment with a hardcoded `KeywordSegment("UNION")` or `KeywordSegment("union")`, chosen only by checking whether the raw text is *exactly* all-lowercase `"union"`. Any other casing - `Union`, `UnION`, `UNioN`, etc. - falls into the "else" branch and is silently rewritten to all-caps `UNION`, even though nothing about that casing was wrong and this rule has nothing to do with keyword capitalisation (that is `CP01`'s job). Impact: silent-wrong-result **Entry point / who reaches it:** any user who runs `sqlfluff lint --fix` (or `sqlfluff fix`) with the default rule set - `AM02` is in the `core` group and enabled by default for the dialects it targets (`ansi`, `bigquery`, `clickhouse`, `databricks`, `db2`, `hive`, `mysql`, `redshift`, `snowflake`, `trino`). It is triggered whenever a `UNION` (without `ALL`/`DISTINCT`) is written with any casing other than pure lower-case, e.g. `Union` (a common style from IDE auto-capitalisation or hand formatting). **What they observe:** ```sql SELECT a FROM t1 Union SELECT a FROM t2 ``` is auto-fixed to ```sql SELECT a FROM t1 UNION DISTINCT SELECT a FROM t2 ``` The user asked only to have `DISTINCT` made explicit; the fixer also silently forced their `Union` to shout-case `UNION`, with no lint message ever mentioning capitalisation. On a project configured to lint/format lower-case or mixed-case SQL, this recasing fights the project's own style (and can even flap against `CP01` if that rule is also enabled with a different policy). ## Fix Instead of replacing the `UNION` keyword, insert `DISTINCT` **after** it via `LintFix.create_after`, leaving the original keyword's text untouched. The new `DISTINCT`/`distinct` keyword's case is chosen from whether the existing `UNION` keyword is all upper-case, matching the same case-inference pattern already used a few rules over in `AM05` for `INNER`/`OUTER` insertion. ## Testing - Added `test_fail_mixed_case_union_preserves_case` to `test/fixtures/rules/std_rule_cases/AM02.yml` (`Union` -> `Union distinct`). - Negative control: reverted only the production file (`src/sqlfluff/rules/ambiguous/AM02.py`) and re-ran `pytest test/rules/yaml_test_cases_test.py -k AM02 -q`: **1 failed (exactly the new case), 10 passed**. Restored the fix: **11 passed**. - All 4 pre-existing fixtures continue to pass unchanged (`UNION` -> `UNION DISTINCT`, `union` -> `union distinct`, the Redshift/triple-join cases), confirming this is not a behaviour change for the cases the rule was already tested against. - `ruff check`, `ruff format --check`, `yamllint -c .yamllint`, and `mypy -p sqlfluff.rules.ambiguous.AM02` all pass clean. ## AI-assisted disclosure This change was AI-assisted: an LLM-based coding agent located the bug by reading `AM02.py`'s two branches, drafted the fix, and wrote the regression fixture. I manually validated it before opening this PR: I reproduced the original bug live (`sqlfluff fix` on a mixed-case `Union` sample, confirming the unwanted recasing), read `git log -S` on the affected branch to confirm this was oversight rather than a deliberate choice (the file has not touched this logic since it was introduced whole-cloth in the original rule bundle), read every existing `AM02.yml` fixture to confirm none of them exercised mixed casing, ran the negative control myself (reverting only the production file and observing the new test go red, then restoring it and seeing it go green), and re-ran the full `ruff`/`yamllint`/`mypy` checks on the changed files myself rather than trusting the agent's report. Signed-off-by: Udaya Tejas --- ## Summary by cubic AM02's auto-fix previously rewrote any `UNION` written in mixed casing (e.g. `Union`) to all‑caps `UNION` when inserting `DISTINCT` – an unwanted recasing that fights project style and overlaps with `CP01`. The fix now inserts `DISTINCT` after the existing keyword, preserving its original casing and matching the case of the new keyword to it. - Added a regression fixture for mixed‑case `UNION`. Written for commit 201e7557f356197c3ff48337ab4c6573f7e9bb92. Summary will update on new commits.

pulls.title: ClickHouse: accept the DISTINCT qualifier on INTERSECT and EXCEPT
pulls.body: ### Brief summary of the change made `INTERSECT DISTINCT` and `EXCEPT DISTINCT` are unparsable in the `clickhouse` dialect today, while `UNION DISTINCT` parses fine: ```sql -- ok today SELECT c FROM number1 UNION DISTINCT SELECT c FROM number2; -- "Found unparsable section" today SELECT c FROM number1 INTERSECT DISTINCT SELECT c FROM number2; SELECT c FROM number1 EXCEPT DISTINCT SELECT c FROM number2; ``` ClickHouse documents the qualifier for all three. From the EXCEPT page: "The result of `EXCEPT` can contain duplicate rows. Use `EXCEPT DISTINCT` if this is not desirable." The INTERSECT page says the same for `INTERSECT DISTINCT`, and the UNION page documents `UNION ALL` and `UNION DISTINCT`. - https://clickhouse.com/docs/sql-reference/statements/select/except - https://clickhouse.com/docs/sql-reference/statements/select/intersect Worth noting for reviewers: in ClickHouse the default for `INTERSECT` and `EXCEPT` keeps duplicates, the opposite of standard SQL, so `DISTINCT` there changes the result rather than restating the default. That makes it a qualifier users have a real reason to write. The docstring now says so. This adds one keyword to the existing `INTERSECT`/`EXCEPT` branch. I did not collapse the branches as I did for `trino` in #8532, because here `UNION` goes through `Ref("UnionGrammar")`, which is shared with the ANSI dialect, and `MINUS` stands on its own; merging them would mean inlining shared grammar for no benefit. This is the `clickhouse` follow-up to #8532 (`trino`) and #8523 (`sparksql`). ### Are there any other side effects of this change that we should be aware of? The grammar accepts one extra keyword in one place, so it is strictly more permissive; no previously valid statement parses differently. I checked all eleven relevant forms against unmodified `main` and against this branch. Only the two `DISTINCT` forms change, from unparsable to parsing: ``` before after SELECT * EXCEPT (c1) FROM t1 parses parses SELECT * EXCEPT (c1, c2) FROM t1 parses parses UNION / UNION ALL / UNION DISTINCT parses parses INTERSECT / INTERSECT ALL parses parses INTERSECT DISTINCT unparsable parses EXCEPT / EXCEPT ALL parses parses EXCEPT DISTINCT unparsable parses MINUS parses parses ``` The `exclude` that keeps `SELECT * EXCEPT (...)` wildcard exclusions out of set operators is untouched, and the existing `clickhouse/select_except.sql` fixture that covers it still passes. ### Two things I left alone on purpose The ClickHouse documentation does not mention `ALL` on `INTERSECT`/`EXCEPT`, nor `MINUS` at all, yet the grammar accepts both today. I have not touched either. Absence from the documentation is not evidence that the server rejects them, and narrowing a grammar would break files that lint cleanly now; that deserves its own change with its own evidence rather than riding along here. For the same reason the new fixture covers the nine `UNION`/`INTERSECT`/`EXCEPT` forms but deliberately omits `MINUS`: it parses, but I did not want to enshrine in a test a form the vendor does not document. Happy to open an issue for either if you would like one. ### Pull Request checklist - [x] Please confirm you have completed any of the necessary steps below. - Included test cases to demonstrate any code changes, which may be one or more of the following: - `.sql`/`.yml` parser test cases in `test/fixtures/dialects` (`clickhouse/select_set_operators.sql`, with the `.yml` generated). - Added appropriate documentation for the change: the segment docstring now states the rule, links both ClickHouse pages and records the inverted default. - Created GitHub issues for any relevant followup/future enhancements if appropriate: the remaining dialect is `ansi`, noted below. ### Remaining follow-up The same qualifier is still missing from `INTERSECT`/`EXCEPT` in the `ansi` base grammar, and therefore in the 18 dialects that inherit it, including `postgres`, `mysql` and `hive`, none of which define a `SetOperatorSegment` of their own. PostgreSQL documents `{ UNION | INTERSECT | EXCEPT } [ ALL | DISTINCT ]`, MySQL 8.4 the same for all three, and Hive added the `distinct`/`all` variants in 2.3.0 (HIVE-12764). I am keeping that separate because widening the baseline for 18 dialects at once deserves its own discussion. `exasol` and `redshift` are narrower still, but correctly so, since neither vendor supports `INTERSECT ALL`/`EXCEPT ALL`. ### AI assistance Per the AI-assisted contributions section of `CONTRIBUTING.md`: this change was written with Claude Opus 5 in Claude Code. The gap was found by reading each dialect's `SetOperatorSegment` and checking it against the vendor documentation, then probing the parser with the documented forms. Manually validated: the ClickHouse pages quoted above; the eleven-form before/after table; that the wildcard exclusion and `MINUS` are unaffected; the generated fixture; `pytest test/dialects/dialects_test.py -k clickhouse` locally on Python 3.14, 180 passed, including the parse-tree hash check for the new fixture; and `ruff format --check` and `ruff check` on the changed file. --- ## Summary by cubic Accepts the `DISTINCT` qualifier on `INTERSECT` and `EXCEPT` in the ClickHouse dialect, so these statements parse instead of failing with "Found unparsable section". - ClickHouse's default for `INTERSECT`/`EXCEPT` keeps duplicates, unlike standard SQL, so `DISTINCT` changes the result rather than restating it. - The change is strictly additive; no previously valid statements parse differently, and `SELECT * EXCEPT (...)` wildcard exclusions are unaffected. - `ALL` and `MINUS` support is unchanged, and the new fixture covers the nine `UNION`/`INTERSECT`/`EXCEPT` forms. Written for commit 7dbdcc97d605e8b223daf59a72b58f832ba3efe7. Summary will update on new commits.

pulls.title: Trino: accept the DISTINCT qualifier on INTERSECT and EXCEPT
pulls.body: ### Brief summary of the change made `INTERSECT DISTINCT` and `EXCEPT DISTINCT` are unparsable in the `trino` dialect today, while `UNION DISTINCT` parses fine: ```sql -- ok today SELECT c FROM number1 UNION DISTINCT SELECT c FROM number2; -- "Found unparsable section" today SELECT c FROM number1 INTERSECT DISTINCT SELECT c FROM number2; SELECT c FROM number1 EXCEPT DISTINCT SELECT c FROM number2; ``` The Trino documentation gives the same optional quantifier for all three operators: ``` query UNION [ALL | DISTINCT] [CORRESPONDING] query query INTERSECT [ALL | DISTINCT] [CORRESPONDING] query query EXCEPT [ALL | DISTINCT] [CORRESPONDING] query ``` https://trino.io/docs/current/sql/select.html `SetOperatorSegment` had `UNION` in one branch with `OneOf("DISTINCT", "ALL")` and `INTERSECT`/`EXCEPT` in another with `Ref.keyword("ALL")` only. Since the documented grammar is identical for all three, the two branches collapse into one. Trino has no `MINUS`, so nothing else is involved. This is the follow-up for `trino` that I mentioned in #8523, which does the same thing for `sparksql`. `trino` had no fixture covering set operators at all, so this adds `test/fixtures/dialects/trino/select_set_operators.sql` with all nine forms (bare, `ALL` and `DISTINCT` for each of the three operators) and the generated `.yml`. ### Are there any other side effects of this change that we should be aware of? The grammar accepts one extra keyword in two places, so it is strictly more permissive; no previously valid statement parses differently. I checked bare `UNION`/`INTERSECT`/`EXCEPT`, all three with `ALL`, all three with `DISTINCT`, and the bracketed forms, before and after the change. One pre-existing limitation is worth flagging, since the new fixture is the first `trino` test to use `EXCEPT` at all and therefore the first to exercise the `exclude`: ```sql -- unparsable both before and after this change SELECT c FROM number1 EXCEPT (SELECT c FROM number2); -- parses fine SELECT c FROM number1 EXCEPT ALL (SELECT c FROM number2); ``` `exclude=Sequence("EXCEPT", Bracketed(Anything()))` keeps wildcard exclusions out of set operators, and as a side effect it also rejects a bare `EXCEPT` followed by a bracketed query. I verified on unmodified `main` that this already failed, so it is not a regression, and I have left it alone rather than widening the scope of this pull request. Happy to open a separate issue for it if you would like. The fixture deliberately uses unbracketed right-hand operands so that it documents what the dialect actually accepts. ### Follow-ups, not included here The same qualifier is still missing from `INTERSECT`/`EXCEPT` in: - `clickhouse`, which overrides the segment and whose docs state "The result of `EXCEPT` can contain duplicate rows. Use `EXCEPT DISTINCT` if this is not desirable" (note its default is `ALL`, unlike the standard). - the `ansi` base grammar, and therefore the 18 dialects that inherit it, including `postgres`, `mysql` and `hive`, which do not define a `SetOperatorSegment` of their own. PostgreSQL documents `{ UNION | INTERSECT | EXCEPT } [ ALL | DISTINCT ]`, MySQL 8.4 the same for all three, and Hive added the `distinct`/`all` variants in 2.3.0 (HIVE-12764). I have kept those separate on purpose: the `ansi` change widens the baseline for 18 dialects at once and deserves its own discussion rather than riding along here. `exasol` and `redshift` are narrower still, but correctly so, since neither vendor supports `INTERSECT ALL`/`EXCEPT ALL`. ### Pull Request checklist - [x] Please confirm you have completed any of the necessary steps below. - Included test cases to demonstrate any code changes, which may be one or more of the following: - `.sql`/`.yml` parser test cases in `test/fixtures/dialects` (`trino/select_set_operators.sql`, with the `.yml` generated). - Added appropriate documentation for the change: the segment docstring now states the rule and links the Trino docs. - Created GitHub issues for any relevant followup/future enhancements if appropriate: happy to file the `ansi`/`clickhouse` follow-up and the `EXCEPT (` one noted above. ### AI assistance Per the AI-assisted contributions section of `CONTRIBUTING.md`: this change was written with Claude Opus 5 in Claude Code. The gap was found by reading each dialect's `SetOperatorSegment` and checking it against the vendor documentation, then probing the parser with the documented forms. Manually validated: the Trino documentation quoted above; that the nine forms fail before the change and pass after; that `EXCEPT (SELECT ...)` already failed on unmodified `main`; the generated fixture; and `pytest test/dialects/dialects_test.py -k trino` locally on Python 3.14, 75 passed, including the parse-tree hash check for the new fixture. The full `test/dialects` run was still going when I opened this, so I am relying on CI for that. --- ## Summary by cubic Makes the Trino dialect accept the DISTINCT qualifier on INTERSECT and EXCEPT, so all three set operators now support both ALL and DISTINCT as documented. - Previously only UNION parsed DISTINCT; INTERSECT and EXCEPT only accepted ALL or no qualifier. - The grammar change is strictly more permissive; no previously valid statement parses differently. - Adds fixture coverage for all nine forms of UNION, INTERSECT, and EXCEPT with no qualifier, ALL, and DISTINCT. - EXCEPT followed by a bracketed query remains unparsable due to an existing exclude rule; this was already the case before this change. Written for commit 3a816e9722012feb05074054fa282a7b51b58f2b. Summary will update on new commits.

pulls.title: fix(mysql): parse BEGIN...END bodies as compound statements
pulls.body: ### Brief summary of the change made Makes progress on #901, and related to #3599. Every MySQL/MariaDB routine body with more than one statement is currently mis-parsed, silently: `BEGIN` is read as a transaction start and the remaining statements escape to file scope, so rules run against a tree that doesn't represent the SQL. Three existing fixtures encode that wrong tree, so CI enforces the bug on every run. They are corrected here. **Size, for triage:** the grammar change is 83 lines added and 63 removed, all in `dialect_mysql.py`. The other 98 files are 12 new fixtures (`.sql` and `.yml` each) and 74 regenerated `.yml` trees; most of the regenerated trees differ only because bodies now nest inside `compound_statement`. MySQL compound statement bodies were not contained in the parse tree. `FunctionDefinitionGrammar` matched `TransactionStatementSegment`, so `BEGIN` was parsed as a transaction start and the statements that followed escaped to file scope rather than nesting inside the routine. No error was raised, so rules ran against a tree that did not represent the SQL. ```sql CREATE FUNCTION f1(p1 INT) RETURNS INT DETERMINISTIC BEGIN DECLARE v1 INT; SET v1 = p1 * 2; RETURN v1; END ``` `create_function_statement` ended at the first internal `;`, and `SET` and `RETURN` appeared as top level statements beside it. The underlying cause is that `BEGIN` is two unrelated keywords in MySQL: transaction control, closed by `COMMIT` or `ROLLBACK`, and a compound statement, closed by `END`. Only the first was modelled, so blocks existed as a side effect of transaction parsing rather than in their own right. This adds `CompoundStatementSegment` — optional label, `BEGIN`, a delimited statement list, `END`, optional end label, per https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.0/en/begin-end.html — and uses it for `CREATE PROCEDURE` and `CREATE FUNCTION` bodies, `CREATE TRIGGER` bodies, and as a statement in its own right so nested and standalone blocks parse the same way. Label handling is not new: it moves here from `TransactionStatementSegment`, which carried the begin label on its `BEGIN` branch and the end label on a separate standalone `END` branch. `TransactionStatementSegment` is narrowed to transaction control only: its `BEGIN` branch becomes a bare `BEGIN [WORK]`, and its standalone `END` branch is removed now that compound statements consume their own `END`. Without the first change a nested block still matched the transaction segment, consumed a single statement, and left the enclosing block to terminate at the inner `END` — so the outer body ended in the wrong place. The same flat shape turned out to affect the loop constructs, which the review bot spotted. With blocks properly nested, `WHILE`, `LOOP` and `REPEAT` could no longer close, because the block's `END` matched the `END` of `END WHILE`. All three now consume their own bodies and closing clauses. `LEAVE` moves to its own `LeaveStatementSegment` alongside the existing `IterateStatementSegment`, since it is flow control for labelled blocks and loops rather than transaction control. Worth noting the shape of this bug, since it may be useful beyond this PR: the opening clause and the matching `END` were separate alternatives of the same `OneOf` in every block construct — `BEGIN...END`, `WHILE`, `LOOP` and `REPEAT` — so none of them could contain anything. `IF` had already been fixed in #8380. With this change no block construct in the dialect retains that shape. It stayed invisible because every procedural fixture had a single statement body, and a containment bug cannot manifest with one statement in the block: there is nothing that can escape. The three corrected `.yml` files are the only pre-existing fixtures with more than one. ### Are there any other side effects of this change that we should be aware of? - The three fixtures named above are corrected: `mysql/create_trigger.yml`, `mysql/create_event.yml` and `mariadb/create_trigger.yml`. - Parse tree shape changes for compound and loop bodies, so 74 existing `.yml` fixtures in `mysql` and `mariadb` are regenerated. Running fixture generation across all dialects shows no other dialect affected. - `LEAVE` now parses as `leave_statement` rather than `transaction_statement`. - Bare `BEGIN;` and `BEGIN WORK;` now parse as `transaction_statement`. They were unparsable before, because the old `BEGIN` branch required a statement to follow it. `START TRANSACTION` is unaffected. This PR adds no transaction fixtures, deliberately. Both meanings of `BEGIN` were broken; this PR fixes the compound statement, and the transaction side comes out less broken only as a side effect of the split. Transaction control as a whole is still largely missing from the dialect. Of 52 forms from the MySQL manual, 35 are still unparsable: - `START TRANSACTION` with characteristics (`READ ONLY`, `READ WRITE`, `WITH CONSISTENT SNAPSHOT`) - `COMMIT … [NO] RELEASE` - every `ROLLBACK` option, including `AND [NO] CHAIN`, which `COMMIT` already accepts - `SAVEPOINT`, `ROLLBACK [WORK] TO [SAVEPOINT]`, `RELEASE SAVEPOINT` - `LOCK TABLES` / `UNLOCK TABLES`, which appear in every `mysqldump` file - `LOCK INSTANCE FOR BACKUP` / `UNLOCK INSTANCE` - all of `XA` Fixing that is a separate piece of work, and its fixtures belong with it rather than here. - Deliberately out of scope: routine characteristics such as `MODIFIES SQL DATA` only parse in the single order used by the existing fixtures. I have that fix ready locally and will open it once this one lands — sending them together would collide on the regenerated fixtures. ### Pull Request checklist - [x] Please confirm you have completed any of the necessary steps below. - Included test cases to demonstrate any code changes, which may be one or more of the following: - `.sql`/`.yml` parser test cases in `test/fixtures/dialects` — twelve new fixtures covering multi statement bodies, nesting, an empty body, a labelled block, a function body, two trigger bodies, procedure and trigger bodies written without `BEGIN`/`END`, and `WHILE`, `REPEAT` and `LOOP` bodies inside a block. - Added appropriate documentation for the change — docstrings on the new and changed segments. The stale `begin-end.html` link on `TransactionStatementSegment` is removed, since that syntax is no longer handled there. No user facing documentation changes seemed needed for a parser fix, but happy to add some if you would like them. - Created GitHub issues for any relevant followup/future enhancements if appropriate — the remaining gaps are listed under side effects above. I have not opened issues for them yet; happy to do that, or to send them as follow-up PRs, whichever you prefer. ### AI assistance disclosure Per CONTRIBUTING.md. The grammar changes, the new fixtures and the test runs were AI-assisted (Claude Opus 5). Manually validated by me: the full diff, the reasoning for narrowing `TransactionStatementSegment` together with its effect on standalone and nested blocks, the loop nesting and `LEAVE` changes made in response to review, and the implemented syntax against the compound statement grammar in the MySQL manual. Checks run locally: full test suite (11320 passed), all pre-commit hooks, and `lint-imports`. Fixture regeneration across all dialects reproduces every `.yml` in this branch byte for byte. The dbt templater tests were not run locally, as they need a running Postgres instance; CI covers them. --- ## Summary by cubic Parses MySQL `BEGIN...END` compound statements as their own segment so routine and trigger bodies are contained in the parse tree. Loop, `REPEAT`, and `WHILE` bodies now nest the same way, and `LEAVE` gets its own segment instead of being misparsed as transaction control. **Side effects** - Statements inside `BEGIN...END` now nest under `compound_statement`; `LOOP`, `REPEAT`, and `WHILE` bodies nest under their loop segments. - `LEAVE` now parses as `leave_statement` instead of `transaction_statement`. - MySQL and MariaDB fixtures were regenerated, including three that had encoded the old incorrect tree. - `TransactionStatementSegment` now covers only transaction control, so bare `BEGIN`, `BEGIN WORK`, and `START TRANSACTION` are unchanged. - `create_database.sql` and `create_table_column_charset.sql` now parse. - `DECLARE a, b INT` and `DECLARE x INT DEFAULT NULL` remain unparsable. Written for commit 84f47e7aafb17d0c50de75bb8fa7c080718c8722. Summary will update on new commits.

pulls.title: fix(RF04/RF05/CP02): scope column_aliases/table_aliases to the SELECT an alias belongs to
pulls.body: ### Brief summary of the change made `identifiers_policy_applicable()` (shared by CP02, RF04, RF05) decides whether an identifier is a "table alias" by checking if *any* ancestor of the identifier is a `from_clause`: ```python is_inside_from = any(p.is_type("from_clause") for p in parent_stack) ``` This misclassifies a **column alias that belongs to a derived table's own `SELECT`**, because that inner `SELECT` is itself nested inside the *outer* `from_clause`. For example, in `SELECT * FROM (SELECT 1 AS date) x`, the alias `date` is a column alias of the inner `SELECT`, but its ancestor chain does pass through the outer `from_clause`, so it is wrongly treated as a table alias. Impact: contract-violation. Entry point / who reaches it: any user of the documented `references.keywords.unquoted_identifiers_policy` / `references.keywords.quoted_identifiers_policy` (RF04) or `references.special_chars.unquoted_identifiers_policy` / `references.special_chars.quoted_identifiers_policy` (RF05) config keys in `.sqlfluff`, a documented, user-facing config surface. Triggered by linting any SQL file containing a derived-table subquery (`FROM (SELECT ... AS alias) ...`) with `column_aliases` or `table_aliases` set. `RF04`'s `unquoted_identifiers_policy` and `RF05`'s `quoted/unquoted_identifiers_policy` document `column_aliases` and `table_aliases` as distinct, targeted settings. In practice, for a column alias inside a derived-table subquery: - `unquoted_identifiers_policy: column_aliases` **silently misses** a real violation (a keyword used as that column alias is never flagged). - `unquoted_identifiers_policy: table_aliases` **wrongly flags** it (a perfectly fine column alias is reported as if it were a table alias). Reproduced on current `main` (`90b975dfa`): ``` $ echo "SELECT * FROM (SELECT 1 AS date) x" | sqlfluff lint --dialect ansi --rules RF04 \ --config <(printf '[sqlfluff:rules:references.keywords]\nunquoted_identifiers_policy = column_aliases\n') - All Finished! # false negative: `date` is a keyword used as a column alias, never flagged $ echo "SELECT * FROM (SELECT 1 AS date) x" | sqlfluff lint --dialect ansi --rules RF04 \ --config <(printf '[sqlfluff:rules:references.keywords]\nunquoted_identifiers_policy = table_aliases\n') - == [stdin] FAIL L: 1 | P: 28 | RF04 | Keywords should not be used as identifiers. # false positive: `date` isn't a table alias ``` Same asymmetry reproduces for RF05's `quoted_identifiers_policy` with a special-character column alias (`"a b"`). Fix: instead of scanning the whole ancestor chain for *any* `from_clause`, walk outward from the identifier and stop at the first `select_clause` or `from_clause` encountered. A column alias always hits its own `select_clause` first; a genuine table/CTE alias hits `from_clause` first. This keeps a nested derived table's column aliases correctly scoped to the `SELECT` they belong to, without changing behaviour for any existing (non-nested) case. Checked provenance (`git log -S` on the `is_inside_from` line, and on every `column_aliases`/`table_aliases` fixture in `RF04.yml`/`RF05.yml`/`CP02.yml`): the check was introduced whole-cloth with the `references` rule bundle (#4446) and extended for `table_aliases` in #6273; every existing fixture uses a flat `SELECT x AS a FROM tbl AS a` or `FROM VALUES(...) AS a` shape, none exercise a derived-table subquery, so this is an oversight, not a tested/pinned decision. No open issue or PR covers this specific case (checked `is_inside_from`, `identifiers_policy_applicable`, and `column_aliases`+`table_aliases`); it's distinct from the still-open #5487 (CTE names not recognised as aliases at all), which is a different code path in the same helper. ### Are there any other side effects of this change that we should be aware of? None. The fix only changes classification for identifiers nested inside a derived table's own `SELECT`; all existing `aliases`/`column_aliases`/`table_aliases`/`all`/`none` fixture cases (CP02, RF04, RF05 - 141 cases) still pass unchanged. ### AI disclosure AI-assisted: an agent did the initial deep read of `src/sqlfluff/rules/references/` and proposed this candidate with a repro. What I manually validated myself, independent of the agent's report: re-ran both repro commands against a clean worktree and confirmed the exact output shown above; walked the actual parse tree (`sqlfluff parse`) to confirm *why* the ancestor chain includes the outer `from_clause`; wrote the fix and both sets of regression tests myself; ran the negative control myself (`git stash` the production file, confirmed the new cases fail - 4 failed, 141 passed - then restored and confirmed 145 passed); independently ran `git log -S` for provenance and searched GitHub issues/PRs for duplicates rather than trusting the agent's claims on those points; and ran `ruff`, `mypy`, `yamllint`, and `lint-imports` myself before opening this PR. ### Pull Request checklist - [x] Please confirm you have completed any of the necessary steps below. - Included test cases to demonstrate any code changes, which may be one or more of the following: - `.yml` rule test cases in `test/fixtures/rules/std_rule_cases`. - Added appropriate documentation for the change. - Created GitHub issues for any relevant followup/future enhancements if appropriate. --- ## Summary by cubic Fixes RF04/RF05 alias classification so column aliases in derived-table subqueries are no longer mistaken for table aliases. `identifiers_policy_applicable()` previously treated any identifier nested under a `from_clause` as a table alias, so `SELECT * FROM (SELECT 1 AS date) x` caused `column_aliases` to miss the violation and `table_aliases` to flag it incorrectly. It now stops at the nearest `select_clause` or `from_clause`, scoping each alias to the `SELECT` it belongs to. Adds regression tests for RF04 and RF05, including positive controls confirming a derived table's own alias is still treated as a table alias. This also corrects the same misclassification for CP02, which shares the helper. No migration or rollout steps are required. Written for commit 0bd4b58746a5e31c000976c7110133efa3a5e88c. Summary will update on new commits.

pulls.title: SparkSQL: accept the DISTINCT qualifier on EXCEPT and MINUS
pulls.body: ### Brief summary of the change made `EXCEPT DISTINCT` and `MINUS DISTINCT` are currently unparsable in the `sparksql` and `databricks` dialects, while `INTERSECT DISTINCT` and `UNION DISTINCT` parse fine: ```sql -- ok today (SELECT c FROM number1) INTERSECT DISTINCT (SELECT c FROM number2); -- "Found unparsable section" today SELECT c FROM number1 EXCEPT DISTINCT (SELECT c FROM number2); ``` The Spark docs page that `SetOperatorSegment` already links to gives the same optional qualifier for every set operator: ``` [ ( ] relation [ ) ] EXCEPT | MINUS [ ALL | DISTINCT ] [ ( ] relation [ ) ] [ ( ] relation [ ) ] INTERSECT [ ALL | DISTINCT ] [ ( ] relation [ ) ] [ ( ] relation [ ) ] UNION [ ALL | DISTINCT ] [ ( ] relation [ ) ] ``` and `EXCEPT` explicitly documents the form: "`EXCEPT` (alternatively, `EXCEPT DISTINCT`) takes only distinct rows". Spark's own grammar agrees, since `setOperation` in `SqlBaseParser.g4` allows one `setQuantifier` after any of the operators. So the two branches of the grammar collapse into one, which is what this change does. `EXCEPT`/`MINUS` gain the `DISTINCT` qualifier and nothing else changes; the `exclude` that keeps `SELECT * EXCEPT (col)` wildcard exclusions out of set operators is untouched. Databricks inherits the segment, so it is fixed too. Test cases are added to `test/fixtures/dialects/sparksql/select_set_operators.sql`, which mirrors that documentation page and already covered `INTERSECT DISTINCT`, alongside the regenerated `.yml`. ### Are there any other side effects of this change that we should be aware of? The grammar now accepts one extra keyword in two places, so it is strictly more permissive for `sparksql` and `databricks`; no previously valid statement parses differently. I checked that `SELECT * EXCEPT (c) FROM t`, `EXCEPT ALL`, `MINUS ALL`, bare `EXCEPT`/`MINUS`, `INTERSECT DISTINCT` and `UNION DISTINCT` all still parse in both dialects. While looking into this, I noticed the same `DISTINCT` qualifier is missing from `INTERSECT`/`EXCEPT` in other dialects whose vendors document it, including the ANSI base grammar (standard SQL allows `[ALL | DISTINCT]` there), and therefore `postgres`, `mysql`, `trino`, `hive` and `clickhouse`. I have deliberately left those out of this pull request to keep it reviewable. I am happy to open a follow-up issue, or a separate pull request per dialect, if that is useful. ### Pull Request checklist - [x] Please confirm you have completed any of the necessary steps below. - Included test cases to demonstrate any code changes, which may be one or more of the following: - `.sql`/`.yml` parser test cases in `test/fixtures/dialects` (`sparksql/select_set_operators.sql`, with the `.yml` regenerated). - Added appropriate documentation for the change: the segment docstring now states the actual rule. - Created GitHub issues for any relevant followup/future enhancements if appropriate: happy to file the cross-dialect follow-up noted above. ### AI assistance Per the AI-assisted contributions section of `CONTRIBUTING.md`: this change was written with Claude Opus 5 in Claude Code. The bug was found by probing dialects with documented SQL and comparing which forms parse; the tool does not report a reasoning level. Manually validated: the Spark documentation and `SqlBaseParser.g4` quoted above, that `INTERSECT DISTINCT`/`UNION DISTINCT` already worked while `EXCEPT`/`MINUS DISTINCT` did not, the regenerated fixture, and `pytest test/dialects` locally on Python 3.14 (7030 passed), plus `ruff format --check` and `ruff check` on the changed file. --- ## Summary by cubic Makes `EXCEPT DISTINCT` and `MINUS DISTINCT` parse in the `sparksql` and `databricks` dialects, matching the documented Spark grammar. These forms previously raised an unparsable section error, while `INTERSECT DISTINCT` and `UNION DISTINCT` already worked; the grammar now accepts the same optional `DISTINCT` qualifier after all four set operators. - Adds fixture cases for the new forms in `test/fixtures/dialects/sparksql/select_set_operators.sql` and regenerates the expected `.yml` output. - No previously valid statement parses differently, including `SELECT * EXCEPT (col)` wildcard exclusions and `ALL`-qualified forms. Written for commit 01ee72ed8ede5586f7c744cd6e128e92b6349950. Summary will update on new commits.

pulls.title: SparkSQL/Databricks: accept NOT NULL and COLLATE on a struct field
pulls.body:
### Brief summary of the change made

Databricks documents a `STRUCT` field as

```
STRUCT < [fieldName [:] fieldType [NOT NULL] [COLLATE collationName] [COMMENT str] [, …] ] >
```

([STRUCT type](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/sql/language-manual/data-types/struct-type))

`StructTypeSchemaSegment` had the identifier, the optional colon, the type
and the comment — but neither clause in between. So
`STRUCT<a: INT COMMENT 'c'>` parsed while `STRUCT<a: INT NOT NULL>` and
`STRUCT<a: STRING COLLATE UTF8_LCASE>` were unparsable, even though all
three sit in the same production.

**`NOT NULL` is Spark's, so it is fixed in `sparksql`.** Spark's grammar has
it:

```
complexColType
    : errorCapturingIdentifier COLON? dataType (errorCapturingNot NULL)? commentSpec?
    ;
```

`databricks` inherits this segment, so it is fixed there too.

**`COLLATE` is Databricks', so it activates only there** — without a second
copy of the segment. ANSI already defines `CollateGrammar` as `Nothing()`,
`sparksql` does not override it, and `dialect_databricks.py` already defines
it as `Sequence("COLLATE", Ref("CollationReferenceSegment"))`. Adding
`Ref("CollateGrammar", optional=True)` in the documented position is
therefore inert for `sparksql` and every other dialect inheriting the
segment, and live for `databricks` alone. Restating the whole segment in
`dialect_databricks.py` would have worked too, but a restated segment is how
this dialect lost `LIVE` views in #7405, so the extension point seemed the
safer shape.

`STRING COLLATE UTF8_LCASE` already parsed as a top-level column and inside
a `CAST`; it just could not be nested.

### Are there any other side effects of this change that we should be aware of?

Narrow by construction. `NOT` and `NULL` are bound together as one optional
`Sequence` rather than two independent optional keywords, and both clauses
are positionally bound rather than floating:

| statement | `sparksql` | `databricks` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `STRUCT<a: INT NOT NULL>` | **now parses** | **now parses** |
| `STRUCT<a INT NOT NULL>` (no colon) | **now parses** | **now parses** |
| `STRUCT<a: INT NOT NULL COMMENT 'c'>` | **now parses** | **now parses** |
| `STRUCT<a: STRING COLLATE UTF8_BINARY>` | still rejected | **now parses** |
| `STRUCT<a: STRING NOT NULL COLLATE UTF8_LCASE COMMENT 'c'>` | still rejected | **now parses** |
| `STRUCT<a: INT NOT>` | rejected | rejected |
| `STRUCT<a: INT NULL>` | rejected | rejected |
| `STRUCT<a: STRING COLLATE>` | rejected | rejected |
| `STRUCT<a: INT COMMENT 'c' NOT NULL>` (wrong order) | rejected | rejected |
| `STRUCT<a: STRING COLLATE UTF8_LCASE NOT NULL>` (wrong order) | rejected | rejected |
| `STRUCT<NOT NULL>` | rejected | rejected |
| `ARRAY<STRING COLLATE UTF8_LCASE>` | rejected | rejected |
| `MAP<STRING COLLATE UTF8_LCASE, INT>` | rejected | rejected |

`ARRAY` and `MAP` element types are deliberately untouched: they are rejected
today, and I could not find a reference page that documents a collation in
either position, so widening them would not have been evidence-backed.

Regenerating the parse fixtures for **every** dialect leaves all 2277
unchanged apart from the two files this PR touches, so nothing that parsed
before parses differently now.

On the Rust parser: `sqlfluffrs/sqlfluffrs_dialects/build.rs` generates the
dialect sources from the Python dialect at build time and re-runs when a
dialect file changes, so the `-rust` CI suites build this grammar rather than
a stale copy. Nothing generated is checked in.

### How this was tested

- `pytest test/dialects/` in full — 7033 passed. Not a `-k` subset, which
  would skip the hand-written rejection tests in `sparksql_test.py` and
  `databricks_test.py`.
- The probe set in the table above, run against both dialects, with a
  deliberately broken control statement in the same batch so a silently
  broken check could not read as success.
- `ruff check`, `ruff format --diff`, `mypy src/sqlfluff` (268 files) and
  `yamllint` on the changed files — all clean.
- Measured against a corpus of 867 files of published Databricks SQL, with a
  control run on the branch's own base commit rather than an older `main`:
  recall is unchanged at 761/866, and the mutation corpus still rejects
  1327/1327 guaranteed-invalid inputs, so nothing was widened in exchange.
- Against a set of cases transcribed from the Databricks SQL reference,
  documented syntax accepted goes from 104/170 to 107/170, with no case
  flipping the other way.

## AI assistance

This pull request was co-authored with AI assistants: **Claude Opus 5**
(Anthropic) and **DeepSeek V4.1 Flash**. They drafted the grammar, the
fixtures and the rejection tests, and ran the measurements, under the
contributor's direction. Every construct was checked against the Databricks SQL
reference, and the changes were run through the whole `test/dialects/` suite,
the Python/Rust parity tests, `make reference` and `make corpus` before
submission. The human contributor remains responsible for the final pull
request, including its correctness, tests and maintainability, as
[CONTRIBUTING.md](https://github.com/sqlfluff/sqlfluff/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md#ai-assisted-contributions)
requires.

pulls.title: fix(CV07): guard one-sided liftable-whitespace fix independently
pulls.body: ### Brief summary of the change made Rule `CV07` (`convention.statement_brackets`, aliased `L053`) crashes with an unhandled `AssertionError` on ordinary, valid SQL whenever a bracket-wrapped top-level statement has liftable content (whitespace or an inline comment) on only *one* side of its inner content — e.g.: ```sql ( SELECT foo FROM bar) ``` `CV07._eval` computes `leading`/`trailing` (liftable segments at the start/end) separately, but gates `LintFix.create_before`/`create_after` on their *combination* (`lift_nodes = leading + trailing`). Both calls assert a non-empty edit list (`src/sqlfluff/core/rules/fix.py:78-80`), so whenever exactly one side is empty — the common case, since most bracketed statements don't have matching whitespace/comment on both sides — the empty side still gets called and raises `AssertionError: A create fix must have an edit.` Entry point: any `sqlfluff lint`/`sqlfluff fix` (CLI or the public API) with `CV07`/`L053` enabled (default rule set) over such a file. Before the fix, linting the example above raises the `AssertionError` with a full traceback, and `sqlfluff fix` silently drops the fix instead of correcting the file. A second bug in the same block: when `trailing` is empty, `filtered_children[len(leading) : -len(trailing)]` evaluates `-len(trailing)` as `-0 == 0`, truncating to an empty slice whenever `leading` is non-empty — so patching only the assertion would make `fix()` silently drop the statement's real content instead of crashing. Fix: guard `create_before`/`create_after` independently on whether that side's list is non-empty, and compute the trailing slice bound as `len(filtered_children) - len(trailing)` so it degrades correctly to "keep everything" when `trailing` is empty. ### Are there any other side effects of this change that we should be aware of? None. All 10 pre-existing `CV07` fixtures (which all happen to have liftable content on both sides, or none) pass unchanged with identical fix output. ### Pull Request checklist - [x] Included test cases to demonstrate any code changes: - Two `.yml` rule test cases in `test/fixtures/rules/std_rule_cases/CV07.yml` (`test_fail_leading_whitespace_only_no_trailing`, `test_fail_trailing_whitespace_only_no_leading`). - [x] No documentation change needed (bugfix, no contract change to already-passing cases). Impact: crash-on-valid-input — legitimate, common SQL raises an unhandled `AssertionError` instead of linting/fixing normally. Negative control — reverting only `src/sqlfluff/rules/convention/CV07.py` and re-running: ``` $ pytest test/rules/yaml_test_cases_test.py -k CV07 -q # pre-fix (production file reverted, new fixtures kept): 2 failed, 10 passed # post-fix (fix restored): 12 passed ``` ### AI-assisted contribution disclosure AI-assisted, disclosed per CONTRIBUTING.md. What was AI-assisted: locating the asymmetric-lift gap while reading `CV07.py`'s `_eval`, drafting the guard fix, the two new fixtures, and this description. What I manually validated myself: reproduced the crash by executing `sqlfluff lint --dialect ansi --rules CV07 -` against the example above on the pre-fix code and read the full traceback; independently confirmed why the trailing side is empty for that input by walking the actual parse tree (`sqlfluff parse`), not by trusting a description; confirmed the existing fixtures don't already cover this by reading the yaml file myself; ran the negative control above by hand; ran `ruff check`, `ruff format --check`, `yamllint`, `mypy -p sqlfluff`, and `lint-imports`, all clean; confirmed via `gh api search/issues` that no existing issue reports this crash. --- ## Summary by cubic Fixes `CV07`/`L053` crashing on valid SQL when a bracketed top-level statement has liftable whitespace or a comment on only one side of its inner content, and ensures fixes don't drop the statement's content when only the trailing side is empty. Bug Fixes: - Calls `create_before`/`create_after` only when that side actually has liftable nodes, avoiding the internal assertion on an empty edit list. - Computes the trailing slice bound with `len(filtered_children) - len(trailing)` so an empty trailing list preserves all children. - Adds regression fixtures for leading-only and trailing-only liftable whitespace; all existing `CV07` fixtures pass unchanged. Written for commit f3e82854fff804f0eca391c139600de0332b8d61. Summary will update on new commits.

pulls.title: Databricks: parse inline FLOW clauses on streaming tables
pulls.body: ### Brief summary of the change made A streaming table can declare its flow inline instead of an `AS` query. The [reference](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/ldp/developer/ldp-sql-ref-create-streaming-table) has four forms (`INSERT [ONCE] BY NAME`, `AUTO CDC`, `REPLACE WHERE ... BY NAME`, `REPLACE USING (...) SEQUENCE BY ... BY NAME`) and none parsed: CREATE OR REFRESH STREAMING TABLE t FLOW INSERT BY NAME SELECT * FROM STREAM s; This adds `FlowClauseSegment` for the four forms. `AUTO CDC` reuses `CDCSpecificationSegment` without `INTO`, since the table is the target. ### Are there any other side effects of this change that we should be aware of? Inline `FLOW` is only accepted with `STREAMING` (`CREATE TABLE t FLOW ...` is rejected), and `REPLACE USING` and `SEQUENCE BY` must appear together. Plain `CREATE STREAMING TABLE ... AS` is unchanged. ### Tests New fixture `databricks/create_streaming_table_flow` covers all four forms, including `INSERT ONCE` and a private target. Full `test/dialects/` passes. ### AI assistance Written with Claude and DeepSeek. I checked each form against the Databricks reference and ran the dialect suite myself. --- ## Summary by cubic Adds support for inline `FLOW` clauses on Databricks streaming tables. Previously `CREATE OR REFRESH STREAMING TABLE t FLOW INSERT BY NAME ...` was unparsable; now all four documented alternatives parse. - Adds `FlowClauseSegment` for `INSERT [ONCE] BY NAME`, `AUTO CDC`, `REPLACE WHERE ... BY NAME`, and `REPLACE USING ... SEQUENCE BY ... BY NAME`. - Inline `FLOW` requires `STREAMING`; the grammar rejects partial specs like `REPLACE USING` without `SEQUENCE BY` or `INSERT` without `BY NAME`. - Wraps the grammar override in `Sequence` to satisfy mypy without changing parsing. Written for commit 063b3df83f03dfb2066058d65b05db835b4ddb9e. Summary will update on new commits.

pulls.title: Databricks: parse DROP MATERIALIZED VIEW
pulls.body: ### Brief summary of the change made `DROP MATERIALIZED VIEW` is unparsable in the `databricks` dialect. The [reference](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/sql/language-manual/sql-ref-syntax-ddl-drop-view) gives: ``` DROP [ MATERIALIZED ] VIEW [ IF EXISTS ] view_name ``` and its own example uses `DROP MATERIALIZED VIEW employeeView`. The dialect inherited the ANSI segment, which accepts only `DROP VIEW`, so the documented materialized form fails: ```sql DROP MATERIALIZED VIEW employeeview; -- was unparsable ``` The fix inserts `MATERIALIZED` as an optional keyword ahead of `VIEW` in a `databricks`-only override of `DropViewStatementSegment`. Apache Spark has no materialized views, so `sparksql` is deliberately left alone. ### Are there any other side effects of this change that we should be aware of? None beyond the widening: `DROP VIEW` and `DROP VIEW IF EXISTS` parse exactly as before, and `DROP MATERIALIZED` with no view is still rejected. The fixture covers the plain, `IF EXISTS` and schema-qualified forms, and `DROP VIEW` remains covered by the existing sparksql fixture this dialect shares. ### What tests/validation did you carry out? - `DROP MATERIALIZED VIEW mv`, `DROP MATERIALIZED VIEW IF EXISTS mv` and `DROP MATERIALIZED VIEW cat.sch.mv` parse; the `DROP VIEW` forms are unchanged. - `DROP MATERIALIZED` (dangling, no view) is still rejected. - Whole `test/dialects/` directory: **7021 passed**. - `ruff check` and `ruff format --check` clean on the changed file. The syntax is taken from the reference page linked above, and the statement was found against a corpus of published Databricks SQL. 🤖 AI disclosure: written with AI assistance (DeepSeek v4.1 Flash via opencode); the validation above was run and reviewed by me. ## AI assistance This pull request was co-authored with AI assistants: **Claude Opus 5** (Anthropic) and **DeepSeek V4.1 Flash**. They drafted the grammar, the fixtures and the rejection tests, and ran the measurements, under the contributor's direction. Every construct was checked against the Databricks SQL reference, and the changes were run through the whole `test/dialects/` suite, the Python/Rust parity tests, `make reference` and `make corpus` before submission. The human contributor remains responsible for the final pull request, including its correctness, tests and maintainability, as [CONTRIBUTING.md](https://github.com/sqlfluff/sqlfluff/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md#ai-assisted-contributions) requires. --- ## Summary by cubic Databricks now accepts `DROP MATERIALIZED VIEW`, which was previously unparsable even though it's part of the documented Databricks syntax. The change is scoped to the `databricks` dialect; `sparksql` is untouched, and `DROP VIEW` / `DROP VIEW IF EXISTS` parse exactly as before. `DROP MATERIALIZED` without a view name is still rejected. Written for commit 62b890328aae2b9e0a08df91b1bd95715aafc4bd. Summary will update on new commits.

pulls.title: fix(snowflake): parse key=>value USING params in EXECUTE IMMEDIATE FROM
pulls.body: ### Brief summary of the change made `EXECUTE IMMEDIATE FROM ` (running a SQL script staged at a file path) takes a `USING ( key => value [, ...] )` clause for template substitution — documented at https://docs.snowflake.com/en/sql-reference/sql/execute-immediate-from. This is a different clause from the non-`FROM` forms' `USING ( bind_variable [, ...] )`, which binds `?` placeholders to a plain variable list, documented at https://docs.snowflake.com/en/sql-reference/sql/execute-immediate. `ExecuteImmediateClauseSegment`'s grammar only ever implemented the bind-variable-list shape for `USING`, so any `FROM`-form statement carrying a `USING (key => value, ...)` clause reports an unparsable section instead of parsing. This is the documented, common form of the statement (running a staged deployment script with parameters), not an edge case. Entry point: triggered by any `sqlfluff parse` / `sqlfluff lint` / `sqlfluff fix` invocation with `--dialect snowflake` (or the public `sqlfluff.parse()` / `sqlfluff.lint()` API) over a file containing `EXECUTE IMMEDIATE FROM '/scripts/foo.sql' USING (env => 'prod');` — valid, documented Snowflake syntax that sqlfluff currently cannot parse. Fix: accept `NamedParameterExpressionSegment` (already used elsewhere in this dialect for `key => value` arguments, e.g. `CHANGES(INFORMATION => ...)`) as an alternative to `LocalVariableNameSegment` inside the `USING (...)` bracket, so both shapes parse. Impact: contract-violation — sqlfluff's own docstring/comment on this segment (and Snowflake's own docs, linked above) describe `EXECUTE IMMEDIATE FROM` plus a `USING` clause as valid syntax, and actual behaviour disagrees: it raises a parse violation and refuses to process the file. Negative control — reverting only `src/sqlfluff/dialects/dialect_snowflake.py` to its pre-fix state and re-running the new fixture case fails without the fix, and passes with it: ``` $ pytest test/dialects/dialects_test.py -k "snowflake and execute_immediate" -q # pre-fix (production file reverted, new fixture case kept): 3 failed, 6827 deselected # post-fix (fix restored): 3 passed, 6827 deselected ``` ### Are there any other side effects of this change that we should be aware of? None. The change only widens what is accepted inside the existing `USING (...)` bracket for this one clause; the non-`FROM` bind-variable-list forms (`EXECUTE IMMEDIATE $pie USING (one, two);` etc.) still parse identically — re-verified against the full existing `execute_immediate.sql` fixture, no change to its parse tree. ### Pull Request checklist - [x] Included test cases to demonstrate any code changes: - `.sql`/`.yml` parser test case added to `test/fixtures/dialects/snowflake/execute_immediate.sql`, regenerated with `test/generate_parse_fixture_yml.py -d snowflake`. - [x] No documentation change needed (dialect grammar only). ### AI-assisted contribution disclosure AI-assisted, disclosed per CONTRIBUTING.md. What was AI-assisted: locating the mismatch between the two `EXECUTE IMMEDIATE` `USING` shapes while reading `dialect_snowflake.py`, and drafting the grammar edit and this description. What I manually validated myself: read Snowflake's own docs for both `EXECUTE IMMEDIATE` and `EXECUTE IMMEDIATE FROM` to confirm the two USING shapes really do differ; reproduced the parse failure by executing `sqlfluff parse` against the pre-fix code; ran the negative control above by hand (reverting only the production file, not the test fixtures) and read its full failure output; confirmed the fix resolves it and that all 243 existing Snowflake dialect fixtures still regenerate cleanly with no unrelated diff. --- ## Summary by cubic Fixes Snowflake `EXECUTE IMMEDIATE FROM` so `USING (key => value)` template parameters parse instead of raising an unparsable section. The grammar previously only accepted `USING (bind_variable, ...)`, but the `FROM` form uses `key => value` substitutions. Both shapes now parse; non-`FROM` `EXECUTE IMMEDIATE` statements are unaffected. **Tests** - Adds a Snowflake parser fixture for `EXECUTE IMMEDIATE FROM '/scripts/foo.sql' USING (env => 'prod', region => 'us')`. Written for commit 22da15b69dc84f60428169403ee5bc88e3287b0b. Summary will update on new commits.

pulls.title: SparkSQL: accept a table identifier as the CONVERT TO DELTA target
