issues.title: RF03: unqualified Jinja-rendered column references are silently exempted from consistency checking
issues.body:
## Bug

`RF03` (`references.consistent`) silently skips consistency checking for a
Jinja-templated, unqualified column reference, even though the rendered
identifier is a completely ordinary column name a user wrote themselves.

## Repro

```
$ cat jinja_case.sql
{% set my_col = 'customer_id' %}
SELECT {{ my_col }}, orders.total FROM orders

$ sqlfluff lint --dialect ansi --templater jinja --rules RF03 jinja_case.sql
All Finished!

$ cat plain_case.sql
SELECT customer_id, orders.total FROM orders

$ sqlfluff lint --dialect ansi --rules RF03 plain_case.sql
L:   1 | P:   8 | RF03 | Unqualified reference 'customer_id' found in single
                       | table select. [references.consistent]
L:   1 | P:  21 | RF03 | Qualified reference 'orders.total' found in single table
                       | select which is inconsistent with previous references.
                       | [references.consistent]
```

Both files describe the exact same query (`customer_id` unqualified,
`orders.total` qualified, single table). The byte-identical query flags two
`RF03` violations when written plainly, and zero when the same identifier is
rendered through Jinja. Reproduces on current `main`.

## Why this happens

`_check_references()` in `src/sqlfluff/rules/references/RF03.py` skips any
unqualified reference where `ref.is_templated` is `True`:

```python
if this_ref_type == "unqualified" and ref.is_templated:
    continue
```

That guard was added in #7615 to stop the `placeholder` templater's
colon-style bind parameters (e.g. `:colname`, rendered as a bare identifier
that is not a real column) from being wrongly qualified/flagged — the PR
body, review thread and added tests are all scoped explicitly to the
`placeholder` templater. `ref.is_templated` is a generic marker shared by
every templater, though, so the same guard also silently exempts Jinja/dbt
`{{ var }}`-rendered column names — genuine identifiers the user intends to
select — from ever being checked. Nothing in #7615's discussion considers
Jinja; this is scope drift in an unconditional check, not a decision anyone
made about the Jinja/dbt case.

## Expected

The Jinja-rendered case should report the same two violations as the
non-templated equivalent. The `placeholder`-templater exemption #7615 added
should stay scoped to that templater.

I have a fix + regression fixture ready and will open a PR shortly.

issues.title: StarRocks: PARTITION BY LIST is not supported, and fails to parse valid CREATE TABLE DDL
issues.body:
## Bug

`sqlfluff parse`/`lint` with `--dialect starrocks` fails to parse an ordinary
StarRocks `CREATE TABLE` statement that uses `LIST` partitioning
(`PARTITION BY LIST ... VALUES IN (...)`).

## Repro

```
$ cat t.sql
CREATE TABLE t_recharge_detail4
(
    id BIGINT,
    city VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
    dt VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL
)
ENGINE=OLAP
DUPLICATE KEY(id)
PARTITION BY LIST (dt, city)
(
    PARTITION p1 VALUES IN (("2022-04-01", "Los Angeles"), ("2022-04-02", "Los Angeles")),
    PARTITION p2 VALUES IN (("2022-04-01", "Houston"), ("2022-04-02", "Houston"))
)
DISTRIBUTED BY HASH(id);

$ sqlfluff parse --dialect starrocks t.sql
...
==== parsing violations ====
L:   9 | P:  29 |  PRS | Line 9, Position 29: Found unparsable section: '(\n   PARTITION
                       | p1 VALUES...'
```

Reproduces on current `main`. This is taken directly from StarRocks's own
list-partitioning documentation
(https://docs.starrocks.io/docs/table_design/data_distribution/list_partitioning/),
not a contrived edge case.

## Why this happens

`PartitionSegment` in `src/sqlfluff/dialects/dialect_starrocks.py` only
implements `RANGE` partitioning (`LESS THAN` / fixed-range / dynamic
`START`/`END`/`EVERY`) and two "expression partitioning" shapes (a function
call, or a bare bracketed column list). It has no branch for `LIST`
partitioning's `PARTITION name VALUES IN (...)` syntax. This segment was
added whole in #6415 ("Initial support for Starrocks dialect") and has
never been touched since; no existing fixture exercises `LIST`
partitioning, so the gap was never caught by the test suite.

StarRocks's own public ANTLR grammar
(`fe/fe-grammar/src/main/antlr/com/starrocks/grammar/StarRocks.g4`,
`partitionDesc`/`listPartitionDesc` rules) confirms `LIST` partitioning is
a first-class, separate form from `RANGE` partitioning, with `VALUES IN`
accepting either a flat list of string/`NULL` values (single partitioning
column) or a list of parenthesized tuples (multiple columns).

## Expected

`PARTITION BY LIST (...) (PARTITION ... VALUES IN (...), ...)` should
parse, matching StarRocks's documented grammar.

I have a fix + regression fixtures ready and will open a PR shortly.

issues.title: AM07 silently misses a column-count mismatch when a CTE is wildcard-referenced twice in one set expression
issues.body:
## Summary

`Rule_AM07` (`ambiguous.set_columns`) checks that every branch of a set expression (`UNION`/`INTERSECT`/etc.) selects the same number of columns, resolving any `SELECT *` by looking up the underlying CTE. If the *same* CTE is referenced by an unaliased wildcard more than once in one set expression, only the first reference resolves — the second silently reports "unable to resolve", and since AM07 requires every branch to resolve before it reports anything, a real, unambiguous column-count mismatch goes completely unreported.

**Impact: silent-wrong-result**

Entry point / who reaches it: any user running `sqlfluff lint` (or `fix`) with `AM07`/`ambiguous.set_columns` enabled (it's in the default `all` rule group) on a query with a `WITH` CTE. Triggered when a set expression (`UNION`, `UNION ALL`, `INTERSECT`, `EXCEPT`) references the same CTE via a bare, unaliased `SELECT * FROM <cte>` more than once.

Reproduction:
```sql
WITH cte AS (
    SELECT a, b FROM t
)
SELECT * FROM cte
UNION
SELECT * FROM cte
UNION
SELECT c, d, e
FROM t2
```
Before this fix, `sqlfluff lint --dialect ansi --rules AM07` on the above reports `All Finished!` — no violation — even though the three branches visibly select 2, 2, and 3 columns. A single-reference version of the same query (drop the second `SELECT * FROM cte` branch) is correctly flagged, which is what exposes the asymmetry: the bug is specifically the *repeated* unaliased reference.

## Root cause

`Rule_AM07.__resolve_selectable_wildcard` (`src/sqlfluff/rules/ambiguous/AM07.py`) resolves a bare wildcard's CTE via `root_query.lookup_cte(cte_name)`. `Query.lookup_cte` (`src/sqlfluff/utils/analysis/query.py`) defaults `pop=True`, deleting the CTE from the query's CTE scope once found. The sibling path used for *aliased* wildcard references (`SELECT cte_al.* FROM cte AS cte_al`) goes through `Query.crawl_sources`, whose own `pop` default is `False` — non-destructive. Both paths exist to answer the same question ("how many columns does this CTE-backed wildcard expand to?"), but only one of them consumes the CTE, for a reason that has nothing to do with AM07's own logic — it's a mismatched default carried over from a 2023 refactor (`70c4f8b05`, #5112), never revisited. None of the 39 existing fixtures in `test/fixtures/rules/std_rule_cases/AM07.yml` reference the same bare CTE name via wildcard twice in one set expression, which is why this was never caught.

## Fix

Keep the pop-then-resolve behaviour — it exists to stop a CTE that (invalidly) references itself from recursing forever while it's being resolved — but put the CTE straight back into its owning scope once that resolution finishes, so a *different* selectable in the same set expression can still resolve a repeated reference to it.

I checked this doesn't reopen the recursion case it protects against: a CTE that references itself via an unaliased wildcard (invalid SQL, but sqlfluff's grammar still parses it, e.g. `WITH cte AS (SELECT * FROM cte UNION ALL SELECT 1 AS n) SELECT * FROM cte UNION SELECT 1`) still resolves without recursing, because the CTE is only restored *after* its own resolution completes, not during it. Added that case as a regression test too.

## Testing (negative control — Lessons on reproducing by execution)

Added two cases to `test/fixtures/rules/std_rule_cases/AM07.yml`: the double-unaliased-wildcard mismatch above, and the self-referencing-CTE no-crash case.

With the production fix reverted (and only the new fixtures present), running the fixture suite fails exactly the new mismatch case and nothing else — proving the test actually depends on the fix, not merely that it passes:
```
$ pytest test/rules/yaml_test_cases_test.py -k AM07 -q
.......................................F.                                [100%]
FAILED test/rules/yaml_test_cases_test.py::test__rule_test_case[AM07_test_fail_repeated_unaliased_cte_wildcard_reference]
1 failed, 40 passed, 2467 deselected in 4.13s
```
With the fix restored:
```
$ pytest test/rules/yaml_test_cases_test.py -k AM07 -q
.........................................                                [100%]
41 passed, 2467 deselected in 5.38s
```
Also ran the full `AM0*` rule family (254 cases, all pass) to check for cross-rule regressions, plus `ruff check`, `ruff format --check`, `yamllint -c .yamllint`, and `mypy -p sqlfluff.rules.ambiguous.AM07` — all clean.

## AI assistance disclosure

This change was AI-assisted: an AI agent located the bug by reading `AM07.py` and its fixtures, proposed the initial diagnosis, and drafted the fix and regression tests. I manually validated it before submitting: I independently re-read the `lookup_cte`/`crawl_sources` default-parameter asymmetry in `query.py` myself rather than trusting the diagnosis as given; I ran the reproduction SQL through `sqlfluff lint` myself and read the actual output; I independently constructed and ran the self-referencing-CTE case to check the fix doesn't reintroduce unbounded recursion (confirmed no crash, both before designing the fix and after); and I ran the full test suite (negative control, full `AM0*` family, ruff/yamllint/mypy) myself and read the results shown above rather than taking a report of them at face value.

Signed-off-by: Udaya Tejas <udayatejas2004@gmail.com>

issues.title: `pip install sqlfluff-templater-dbt` silently breaks a dbt-oss 2.x environment
issues.body:
### Search before asking

- [x] I searched the [issues](https://github.com/sqlfluff/sqlfluff/issues) and found no similar issues.


### What Happened

Installing `sqlfluff-templater-dbt` into an environment that has **dbt-oss** silently breaks dbt. The templater requires `dbt-core>=1.4.1`, which dbt-oss does not satisfy, so pip installs dbt-core 1.x alongside it — and because both wheels own the same `site-packages/dbt/` path and overlap on 10 files, dbt-core's modules overwrite dbt-oss's. The install prints no warning, `pip check` passes, and `pip list` still reports `dbt-oss 2.0.4` as installed, but the `dbt` command is now dbt-core 1.12.5 and dbt-oss's engine is unreachable. Install order decides which one survives, so the reverse order breaks sqlfluff instead. I'm not asking for dbt-oss support here, only that the incompatibility fail loudly instead of quietly downgrading the user's dbt by a major version.

### Expected Behaviour

Installing `sqlfluff-templater-dbt` into an environment it cannot support should fail loudly — a pip resolution error, or a clear error when the templater loads.

### Observed Behaviour

In an environment with **dbt-oss**, the install succeeds, prints no warning, and leaves dbt broken. The user's `dbt` command silently becomes a different dbt at a different major version.

### How to reproduce

```
python -m venv env
./env/bin/pip install dbt-oss==2.0.4
./env/bin/dbt --version          # -> dbt-oss 2.0.4
./env/bin/pip install sqlfluff-templater-dbt==4.3.0
./env/bin/dbt --version          # -> Core: installed: 1.12.5
```
Nothing in the second install signals a problem. Afterwards:

- **No pip conflict warning**, and `pip check` reports "No broken requirements found".
- **`pip list` still shows `dbt-oss 2.0.4` as installed**, so anything that inspects the environment rather than running it — CI checks, lockfile audits, a human reading `pip list` — sees a healthy env.
- **The `dbt` CLI is now dbt-core 1.12.5.** dbt-oss's Rust engine (`dbt/_core.abi3.so`) is still on disk but unreachable: `import dbt.runner` fails with `ImportError: cannot import name 'Manifest' from 'dbt.artifacts.schemas.manifest'`, because dbt-core's modules now shadow it.
- `mashumaro` is downgraded 3.22 -> 3.17 as a side effect.

Install order decides the winner, so the reverse order breaks sqlfluff instead. A `pip install -r requirements.txt` containing both is a coin flip.

### Dialect

Databricks

### Version

- sqlfluff 4.3.0, sqlfluff-templater-dbt 4.3.0
- dbt-oss 2.0.4; dbt-core 1.12.5 (pulled in by the install)
- Python 3.12, macOS 15 (arm64), pip 26.2.1

n/a

issues.title: Keyword terminators need preceding whitespace, so `SELECT *FROM t` is unparsable
issues.body:
### Search before asking

- [x] I searched the issues and found no similar issues.

### What Happened

`SELECT *FROM table_a` (no space between `*` and `FROM`) is reported as unparsable. It fails in ansi, postgres, mysql, snowflake, sparksql, databricks and hive. `SELECT t.*FROM table_a t` also fails. bigquery parses it.

This was first reported downstream in reata/sqllineage#776, where the maintainer confirmed Spark accepts this syntax and pointed to sqlfluff's grammar.

### Expected Behaviour

`SELECT *FROM table_a` parses the same way as `SELECT * FROM table_a`.

### Observed Behaviour

```
Line 1, Position 9: Found unparsable section: 'FROM table_a'
```

The cause looks like `greedy_match` in `src/sqlfluff/core/parser/match_algorithms.py`. It only accepts an alphabetical terminator such as `FROM` when whitespace precedes it. Here the previous segment is `*`, so the `FROM` terminator is skipped and the select clause claims the rest of the statement. The comment there already has a TODO to review this rule. The Rust parser applies the same check (`is_preceded_by_whitespace` in `sqlfluffrs/sqlfluffrs_parser/src/parser/table_driven/match_algorithms.rs`), so a fix would likely need to be mirrored there.

Would you accept allowing a keyword terminator when the preceding code segment is a symbol such as `*`, while keeping the whitespace requirement otherwise? I'm happy to open a PR once the intended behaviour is agreed.

### How to reproduce

```python
import sqlfluff

sqlfluff.parse("SELECT * FROM table_a", dialect="ansi")  # parses
sqlfluff.parse("SELECT *FROM table_a", dialect="ansi")   # APIParsingError
```

### Dialect

ansi (also postgres, mysql, snowflake, sparksql, databricks and hive)

### Version

4.3.0. The whitespace rule in `greedy_match` is unchanged on `main`.

### Configuration

None, default configuration.

### Are you willing to work on and submit a PR to address the issue?

- [x] Yes I am willing to submit a PR!

issues.title: sqlfluff parse --dialect doris fails on ordinary aggregate-type column with DEFAULT/COMMENT/NOT NULL
issues.body:
## Bug

`sqlfluff parse`/`lint` with `--dialect doris` fails to parse an ordinary
Apache Doris `CREATE TABLE` column that combines an aggregate-key type
(`SUM`, `MAX`, `MIN`, `REPLACE`, `BITMAP_UNION`, `HLL_UNION`,
`QUANTILE_UNION`) with `DEFAULT`, `COMMENT`, or `NOT NULL` on the same
column.

## Repro

```
$ cat t.sql
CREATE TABLE t3
(
  id INT,
  v1 BIGINT SUM DEFAULT "0" COMMENT "running total",
  v2 INT MAX NOT NULL,
  v3 STRING REPLACE DEFAULT "n/a"
)
AGGREGATE KEY (id)
DISTRIBUTED BY HASH (id)
PROPERTIES (
  'replication_num' = '1'
);

$ sqlfluff parse --dialect doris t.sql
...
[L:  4, P:  1]      |unparsable: ...
Found unparsable section: 'CREATE TABLE t3\n(\n  id INT,\n  v1 BIGINT SUM DEFAULT "0" COMMENT "running total",\n...'
```

Reproduces on current `main` (`818243e2f`). Removing the agg-type keyword,
or removing the trailing `DEFAULT`/`COMMENT`/`NOT NULL`, parses fine — only
the combination fails.

## Why this happens

`ColumnDefinitionSegment` in `src/sqlfluff/dialects/dialect_doris.py:70-83`
extends MySQL's `ColumnDefinitionSegment.match_grammar` with
`.copy(insert=[OneOf("MAX", "MIN", "REPLACE", "SUM", "BITMAP_UNION",
"HLL_UNION", "QUANTILE_UNION", optional=True)])` and no `at=`/`before=`
argument. Per `BaseGrammar.copy()`'s own docstring, that inserts at the END
of the sequence. MySQL's base `ColumnDefinitionSegment` grammar is
`[SingleIdentifierGrammar, OneOf(datatype), Bracketed(Anything, optional),
AnyNumberOf(ColumnConstraintSegment, optional)]` (4 elements) — so the
agg-type keyword lands AFTER the constraint clauses instead of before them.

Apache Doris's own documented column syntax
(https://doris.apache.org/docs/table-design/data-model/aggregate) is
`col_name col_type [agg_type] [NULL|NOT NULL] [DEFAULT default_value]
[comment]` — agg-type comes immediately after the data type, before those
clauses. This dialect was added whole in #6979 with no comment indicating
an intentional append-at-end, and none of the five committed Doris fixtures
that use an agg-type combine it with a trailing constraint, so the gap was
never exercised by the existing suite.

## Expected

The agg-type keyword should be accepted immediately after the column's data
type, ahead of any `NULL`/`NOT NULL`/`DEFAULT`/`COMMENT` clause, matching
Doris's documented grammar.

I have a small fix (`at=3` on the same `.copy()` call) + a regression
fixture ready and will open a PR shortly.

issues.title: Snowflake dialect does not parse EXECUTE DBT PROJECT command

### What Happened

SQLFluff fails to parse Snowflake's EXECUTE DBT PROJECT command and returns a parser (PRS) error indicating an unparsable section.

The SQL executes successfully in Snowflake, but SQLFluff cannot parse the statement when using the Snowflake dialect.

EXECUTE DBT PROJECT should be recognized as valid Snowflake syntax and parse successfully under the Snowflake dialect.

SQLFluff reports:

Found unparsable section: 'EXECUTE DBT PROJECT ...'

sqlfluff, version 4.3.0

Create a SQL file named example.sql containing an EXECUTE DBT PROJECT statement:
EXECUTE DBT PROJECT ILFS_PROJECT;
Run:
sqlfluff lint example.sql --dialect snowflake

Then, observe the parser error.

This syntax is part of Snowflake's native dbt integration and executes successfully within Snowflake. Because SQLFluff cannot parse the statement, users are currently forced to:

Skip linting database deployment scripts containing this command

issues.title: AssertionError instead of a clean config error when pyproject.toml sets a non-table `rules` value
issues.body:
## Bug

`sqlfluff` crashes with a raw, uncaught `AssertionError` (instead of a clean
config-loading error) when a `pyproject.toml` sets `rules` directly under
`[tool.sqlfluff]` to something that isn't a table.

## Repro

```
$ cat pyproject.toml
[tool.sqlfluff]
dialect = "ansi"
rules = "all"

$ echo "select 1" > test.sql
$ sqlfluff lint test.sql
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
  File ".../sqlfluff/core/config/toml.py", line 119, in load_toml_file_config
    assert isinstance(rules_section, dict), (
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
AssertionError: Expected to find section in `rules` section of config, but instead found all
```

This reproduces on current `main` (`818243e2f`) with any command that loads
config (`lint`, `fix`, `parse`, even `version`).

## Why this happens

`load_toml_file_config` (`src/sqlfluff/core/config/toml.py`) narrows the
`rules` section with a bare `assert isinstance(rules_section, dict)`. That
assert was added incidentally during a 2024 strict-typing pass (#6206), not as
a deliberate design decision.

`.sqlfluff` ini files support a top-level scalar `rules = all` under
`[sqlfluff]` (see `default_config.cfg`), so it's an easy mistake to write the
toml equivalent as `[tool.sqlfluff]` + `rules = "..."` instead of the actually
required `[tool.sqlfluff.rules.<rule_name>]` per-rule tables. When that
happens, the assert trips.

`get_config()` in the CLI (`src/sqlfluff/cli/commands.py`) only catches
`SQLFluffUserError` around config loading, so the `AssertionError` is never
caught and the user gets a full Python traceback instead of the clean
"Error loading config: ..." message every other malformed-config case (e.g.
an invalid `layout` section) produces.

## Expected

A `SQLFluffUserError` with a message pointing at the correct
`[tool.sqlfluff.rules.<rule_name>]` syntax, matching how other config
sections are validated.

I have a small fix + regression test ready and will open a PR shortly.

ansi (reproduces with any dialect - the bug is in output formatting, not

issues.title: RF06 replaces function/procedure names with a segment type the grammar cannot match, so the fix is silently dropped
issues.body:
Reporting this because the warning text asks for it, verbatim: *"Please report this as a bug with a minimal query which demonstrates this warning."*

## What happens

`sqlfluff fix` declines to apply an RF06 fix, saying the result would be unparsable. The result parses fine.

```sql
-- mysql
CREATE PROCEDURE `testprocedure`(in test int)
BEGIN
END~
```

```
$ sqlfluff fix --dialect mysql --rules RF06 procedure_in_param.sql
Fixes for RF06 not applied, as it would result in an unparsable file.
Please report this as a bug with a minimal query which demonstrates this warning.
```

The file is left unchanged, and the violation stays:

```
L: 1 | P: 18 | RF06 | Unnecessary quoted identifier `testprocedure`.
```

## The output would not have been unparsable

Both forms parse cleanly through the same API path, on `main` (`85dfbdff`):

```python
from sqlfluff.core import Linter, FluffConfig
L = Linter(config=FluffConfig(overrides={"dialect": "mysql"}))

for sql in ["CREATE PROCEDURE `testprocedure`(in test int)\nBEGIN\nEND~\n",
            "CREATE PROCEDURE  testprocedure (in test int)\nBEGIN\nEND~\n"]:
    p = L.parse_string(sql)
    print(len([v for v in p.violations if v.rule_code().startswith(("PRS", "LXR"))]),
          len(list(p.tree.recursive_crawl("unparsable"))))
```

```
0 0      <- quoted
0 0      <- unquoted
```

Same result for `mariadb` with `CALL \`somefunction\`('a');`.

So the guard is rejecting a fix it did not need to reject, and RF06 silently under-fixes as a result.

## Scope

Round-tripped the dialect fixture corpus on `main` and counted where the guard fires. Every hit is RF06, and every hit is a procedure or function identifier context:

| dialect | fixtures | examples |
|---|---|---|
| mysql | 9 | `procedure_in_param`, `procedure_out_param`, `procedure_definer`, `function_return`, `function_comment`, `call_statement`, `delimiter_procedure` |
| mariadb | 11 | `call_statement`, `create_or_replace_procedure`, `create_or_replace_function`, `function_definer`, `delimiter_procedure` |

Twenty of the project's own fixtures, each printing a "please report this as a bug" warning to any user who runs `fix` over them.

## Relationship to #8462

Same rule, opposite direction, and I think that is the interesting part.

- **#8462** — RF06 unquotes `'user'@'host'` account specifications and the output genuinely does not parse. The guard **does not catch it**, so corruption is written to disk.
- **This issue** — the guard **fires when it should not**, so a safe fix is skipped.

The guard is currently wrong in both directions on the same rule, which suggests the check itself is the thing to look at rather than RF06's individual cases.

Happy to open a PR if you have a preference for which way to take it. My guess, from #8415, is that the reachable common cause is what the guard re-parses rather than how RF06 builds the edit — but that is a guess, and I would rather hear yours before writing code against it.

## Disclosure

Found with a scanner I wrote that runs every fixture in `test/fixtures/dialects` through `fix` and re-parses the output; an AI coding agent helped write that tooling and this description. What I verified myself, from source rather than from a model: the two `parse_string` results above on a clean `main` checkout, that `sqlfluff fix --rules RF06` leaves both files byte-identical, and that all twenty hits report `RF06` and no other rule.

issues.title: RF06 unquotes MySQL/MariaDB 'user'@'host' specifications, producing SQL that no longer parses
issues.body:
### Search before asking

- [X] I searched the [issues](https://github.com/sqlfluff/sqlfluff/issues) and found no similar issue. The open/closed RF06 issues are about case sensitivity, reserved keywords, TSQL special characters and RF04 conflicts — none about user specifications.

### What Happened

`sqlfluff fix` turns valid MySQL/MariaDB into SQL that sqlfluff itself cannot parse. RF06 unquotes both halves of a `'user'@'host'` specification, but that is not an identifier pair — the quoting is part of the syntax.

```sql
-- in
CREATE USER 'jeffrey'@'localhost' IDENTIFIED BY 'password';
-- after `sqlfluff fix --dialect mysql`
CREATE USER jeffrey@localhost IDENTIFIED BY 'password';   -- no longer parses
```

```
L:   1 | P:  23 | RF06 | Unnecessary quoted identifier 'localhost'.
```

Verified with parse status measured **before and after** the fix, so this is corruption rather than a pre-existing parse gap:

| statement | parses before | parses after |
|---|---|---|
| `CREATE USER 'jeffrey'@'localhost' IDENTIFIED BY 'password';` | yes | **no** |
| `GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON *.* TO 'prj_svc'@'localhost';` | yes | **no** |
| `DROP USER 'jeffrey'@'localhost';` | yes | **no** |

Same result on `--dialect mariadb`.

**Not part of this report:** `ALTER USER 'jeffrey'@'localhost' IDENTIFIED BY 'new';` does not parse *before* the fix either. That looks like a separate dialect gap, and I have deliberately kept it out of this issue rather than inflate it.

### Affected fixtures already in the repo

The repository's own corpus reproduces this — these four fixtures parse clean and stop parsing after `fix`:

- `test/fixtures/dialects/mysql/create_user.sql`
- `test/fixtures/dialects/mysql/grant.sql`
- `test/fixtures/dialects/mariadb/create_user.sql`
- `test/fixtures/dialects/mariadb/grant.sql`

### Expected Behaviour

`fix` should never produce SQL that does not parse. RF06 should not apply inside a user specification, in the same way it already declines other contexts where quoting is semantic.

### Observed Behaviour

RF06 treats `'jeffrey'` and `'localhost'` as quoted identifiers and strips both. In MySQL these are the account name and host parts of an account specification; unquoted they are not equivalent, and in general are not even valid.

### How to reproduce

```sh
echo "CREATE USER 'jeffrey'@'localhost' IDENTIFIED BY 'password';" > repro.sql
sqlfluff parse --dialect mysql repro.sql   # clean
sqlfluff fix   --dialect mysql -f repro.sql
sqlfluff parse --dialect mysql repro.sql   # unparsable
```

### Dialect

MySQL and MariaDB.

### Version

`4.3.0`, from a checkout of `main`.

### Configuration

Default. No `.sqlfluff` — RF06 is in the default rule set, so this is out-of-the-box behaviour.

### Are you willing to work on and submit a PR to address the issue?

Yes.

---

**How this was found.** I ran a round-trip check over the whole fixture corpus — for every fixture that parses cleanly, assert that `fix` output still parses. That surfaced 8 corruptions across 2,249 fixtures; these four are one root cause. The same method found #8415. If it is useful I am happy to write the remaining ones up separately rather than bundling unrelated bugs here.

**AI disclosure** (per [CONTRIBUTING](https://github.com/sqlfluff/sqlfluff/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md#ai-assisted-contributions)): I used an AI coding agent to run the corpus scan and draft this report. What I verified myself is the before/after parse status of every statement in the table above, through the CLI with default configuration, and the separation of the `ALTER USER` case as a distinct pre-existing gap rather than part of this bug.

### Observed Behaviour

LT01 reports `Expected single whitespace between 'SEMANTIC_VIEW' keyword and start bracket '('` for `SEMANTIC_VIEW(`. Running `sqlfluff fix` changes it to `SEMANTIC_VIEW (`. Conversely, LT01 accepts the spaced form.

On current `main` after #8447, save the SQL above as `semantic_view.sql`, then run:

issues.title: Databricks: PRIVATE streaming tables and CREATE FLOW append flows (INSERT [ONCE] INTO ... BY NAME) are unparsable
issues.body:
### Search before asking

- [x] I searched the [issues](https://github.com/sqlfluff/sqlfluff/issues) and found no similar issues.

### What Happened

Three pieces of Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines (LDP) DDL are unparsable under the `databricks` dialect on 4.3.0. All three are current, documented syntax, and each has a close relative that *does* parse.

**1. `PRIVATE` is not accepted on streaming tables (but is on materialized views)**

Per [CREATE STREAMING TABLE (pipelines)](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/ldp/developer/ldp-sql-ref-create-streaming-table), the grammar is:

```
CREATE [ OR REFRESH ] [ PRIVATE ] STREAMING TABLE table_name ...
```

`CreateMaterializedViewStatementSegment` already models the equivalent keyword — `dialect_databricks.py` has `Ref.keyword("PRIVATE", optional=True),  # DLT-specific` — but the streaming-table path goes through `TableDefinitionSegment` in `dialect_sparksql.py`, which has `EXTERNAL` / `STREAMING` / `LIVE` and no `PRIVATE`.

**2. `CREATE FLOW` only supports the `AUTO CDC` form, not append flows**

[CREATE FLOW (pipelines)](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/ldp/developer/ldp-sql-ref-create-flow) gives:

```
CREATE FLOW flow_name [ COMMENT comment ] AS
{ AUTO CDC [ ONCE ] INTO target_table create_auto_cdc_flow_spec |
  INSERT [ ONCE ] INTO target_table BY NAME [ replace_using_spec ] query }
```

`CreateFlowStatementSegment` (added in #7359 / #7360) hardcodes `Sequence("AS", "AUTO", "CDC", "INTO")`, so the `INSERT ... INTO ... BY NAME` branch is unparsable. Append flows are the most common flow type — they are how a pipeline points several sources at one streaming table.

**3. `ONCE` and `COMMENT` are missing from the `CREATE FLOW` grammar**

`AUTO CDC ONCE INTO` and `CREATE FLOW f COMMENT '...' AS ...` are both in the syntax block above and both fail, including on the CDC branch that is otherwise supported.

(Small documentation inconsistency worth knowing while implementing: the syntax block on the reference page says `INSERT [ONCE] INTO target_table BY NAME`, while the examples on [Use flows in Lakeflow pipelines](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/ldp/flow-examples) and [Backfilling historical data](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/ldp/flows-backfill) write `INSERT INTO ONCE target_table BY NAME`. Both spellings are in the docs; I have listed both below.)

### Expected Behaviour

All of the statements below parse cleanly under `--dialect databricks`, and a `.sql` file containing LDP flow definitions can be linted.

### Observed Behaviour

Each is reported as an unparsable section. Running the reproduction file below, one statement at a time:

```
UNPARSABLE : CREATE OR REFRESH PRIVATE STREAMING TABLE
UNPARSABLE : CREATE PRIVATE STREAMING TABLE
parses ok  : CREATE OR REFRESH STREAMING TABLE                    (control)
parses ok  : CREATE OR REFRESH PRIVATE MATERIALIZED VIEW          (control)
UNPARSABLE : CREATE FLOW ... AS INSERT INTO ... BY NAME
UNPARSABLE : CREATE FLOW ... AS INSERT ONCE INTO ... BY NAME
UNPARSABLE : CREATE FLOW ... AS INSERT INTO ONCE ... BY NAME
UNPARSABLE : CREATE FLOW ... COMMENT '...' AS INSERT INTO ...
parses ok  : CREATE FLOW ... AS AUTO CDC INTO ...                 (control)
UNPARSABLE : CREATE FLOW ... AS AUTO CDC ONCE INTO ...
```

The error in each case:

```
== [one.sql] FAIL
L:   1 | P:   1 |  PRS | Line 1, Position 1: Found unparsable section: 'CREATE OR
                       | REFRESH PRIVATE STREAMING TABL...'
WARNING: Parsing errors found and dialect is set to 'databricks'. Have you configured your dialect correctly?
```

and the parse tree shows the statement never entering a statement segment:

```
[L:  1, P:  1]      |file:
[L:  1, P:  1]      |    unparsable:      !! Expected: "<Sequence: [<AnyNumberOf: [<Ref: 'DelimiterGrammar'>..., <Delimited: [<Ref: 'StatementSegment'>]>, <AnyNumberOf:...]>"
[L:  1, P:  1]      |        word:        'CREATE'
[L:  1, P:  7]      |        whitespace:  ' '
[L:  1, P:  8]      |        word:        'OR'
[L:  1, P: 10]      |        whitespace:  ' '
[L:  1, P: 11]      |        word:        'REFRESH'
[L:  1, P: 18]      |        whitespace:  ' '
[L:  1, P: 19]      |        word:        'PRIVATE'
[L:  1, P: 26]      |        whitespace:  ' '
[L:  1, P: 27]      |        word:        'STREAMING'
```

### How to reproduce

`repro.sql`:

```sql
CREATE OR REFRESH PRIVATE STREAMING TABLE st_private (a BIGINT);

CREATE PRIVATE STREAMING TABLE st_private_2 (a BIGINT);

CREATE FLOW append_flow AS INSERT INTO st_target BY NAME
SELECT * FROM STREAM(src);

CREATE FLOW backfill_flow AS INSERT ONCE INTO st_target BY NAME
SELECT * FROM src;

CREATE FLOW backfill_flow_alt AS INSERT INTO ONCE st_target BY NAME
SELECT * FROM src;

CREATE FLOW commented_flow COMMENT 'a flow' AS INSERT INTO st_target BY NAME
SELECT * FROM STREAM(src);

CREATE FLOW cdc_once AS AUTO CDC ONCE INTO st_target
FROM STREAM(src)
KEYS (id)
SEQUENCE BY ts
STORED AS SCD TYPE 2;
```

```bash
sqlfluff parse --dialect databricks repro.sql
```

For comparison, these two parse cleanly:

```sql
CREATE OR REFRESH STREAMING TABLE st (a BIGINT);

CREATE OR REFRESH PRIVATE MATERIALIZED VIEW v AS SELECT 1 AS a;
```

### Dialect

`databricks`

### Version

```
sqlfluff, version 4.3.0
Python 3.12.8
```

### Configuration

Reproduced with no configuration file at all (defaults, dialect passed on the command line):

```bash
sqlfluff parse --dialect databricks repro.sql
```

### Are you willing to work on and submit a PR to address the issue?

- [ ] Yes I am willing to submit a PR!

issues.title: Snowflake: LT02 incorrectly indents EXCEPTION in a nested scripting block
issues.body:
### Search before asking

- [x] I searched the [issues](https://github.com/sqlfluff/sqlfluff/issues) and found no similar issues.


### What Happened


When linting a Snowflake Scripting procedure containing an exception handler in a nested `BEGIN ... END` block, rule LT02 incorrectly expects `EXCEPTION` to be indented as an executable statement inside the block.

`EXCEPTION` should align with the `BEGIN` that owns the exception handler.

This also affects formatting: `sqlfluff format` moves `EXCEPTION`, `END`, and subsequent statements progressively deeper instead of closing their respective blocks.


### Expected Behaviour


The following indentation should pass LT02 unchanged:

```sql
BEGIN
    IF (TRUE) THEN
        BEGIN
            LET x NUMBER := 1;
        EXCEPTION
            WHEN OTHER THEN
                RETURN 'handled';
        END;
    END IF;

    RETURN 'ok';
END;
```

`EXCEPTION` is a section of the nested Snowflake Scripting block and should align with its corresponding `BEGIN`. `WHEN` should be indented one level beneath `EXCEPTION`.

This structure is consistent with Snowflake’s excep 
 tion-handler syntax and documentation:

https://docs.snowflake.com/en/sql-reference/snowflake-scripting/exception

### Observed Behaviour


SQLFluff reports an LT02 violation on the `EXCEPTION` line:

```text
LT02 | Expected indent of 12 spaces. [layout.indent]
```

Depending on the version, it can also report cascading indentation violations on `WHEN`, `END`, `END IF`, and subsequent statements.

Running the formatter produces output resembling:

```sql
BEGIN
    IF (TRUE) THEN
        BEGIN
            LET x NUMBER := 1;
            EXCEPTION
                WHEN OTHER THEN
                RETURN 'handled';
            END;
        END IF;

        RETURN 'ok';
    END;
```

The formatter appears not to emit a dedent before `EXCEPTION`, and the incorrect indentation then propagates to the rest of the procedure.


### How to reproduce

Create "test.sql" file:
```sql
CREATE OR REPLACE PROCEDURE p()
RETURNS VARCHAR
LANGUAGE SQL
AS
BEGIN
    IF (TRUE) THEN
        BEGIN
            LET x NUMBER := 1;
        EXCEPTION
            WHEN OTHER THEN
                RETURN 'handled';
        END;
    END IF;

    RETURN 'ok';
END;
```

Run:

```bash
sqlfluff lint test.sql --dialect snowflake
```

```text
snowflake
```

```text
sqlfluff: 4.3.0
Python: 3.14.4
```

The problem can be reproduced without a configuration file by passing the dialect directly:

```bash
sqlfluff lint test.sql --dialect snowflake
```

```ini
[sqlfluff]
```

issues.title: Snowflake SEMANTIC_VIEW queries parse as generic functions and trigger RF01
issues.body:
### Search before asking

- [x] I searched the [issues](https://github.com/sqlfluff/sqlfluff/issues) and found no similar issues.


### What Happened

The Snowflake dialect does not have first-class grammar for the [`SEMANTIC_VIEW(...)`](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/sql-reference/constructs/semantic_view) query construct. A simple invocation is accepted through generic function grammar, so the semantic-view object name and logical-table-qualified fields are represented as ordinary references. RF01 then reports false positives. Adding the construct's internal `WHERE` clause produces an unparsable section.

I searched issues, pull requests, source, changelog, and git history and found no existing query-grammar implementation or report for `SEMANTIC_VIEW`.

### Expected Behaviour

Snowflake `SEMANTIC_VIEW(...)` relations should parse into intentional segments for the semantic-view object, metrics, facts, dimensions, aliases, and predicate. RF01 should ignore semantic identifiers inside the construct while continuing to check genuine relational references in the surrounding query.

### Observed Behaviour

Given:

```sql
SELECT
    order_date,
    revenue
FROM SEMANTIC_VIEW(
    analytics.semantic.sales_analysis
    DIMENSIONS orders.order_date
    METRICS orders.revenue
);
```

SQLFluff 4.3.0 parses `SEMANTIC_VIEW(...)` as a generic `function`. RF01 reports three false positives: the semantic-view object plus both semantic fields. Adding the documented internal predicate `WHERE orders.order_date >= DATE '2025-01-01'` causes a PRS violation for the parenthesized semantic-view body.

### How to reproduce

Save the SQL example above as `semantic_view.sql`, then run:

```console
sqlfluff parse semantic_view.sql --dialect snowflake
sqlfluff lint semantic_view.sql --dialect snowflake --rules RF01
```

To reproduce the PRS behavior, add this line after the `METRICS` clause:

```sql
WHERE orders.order_date >= DATE '2025-01-01'
```

### Dialect

Snowflake

### Version

SQLFluff 4.3.0; Python 3.10.13. The behavior is also present on current `main` at `dd429de04190d336090e5880f1b54dfd6730039d`.

### Configuration

No project configuration. The commands specify `--dialect snowflake` and, for reference analysis, `--rules RF01`.

issues.title: SELECT SELECT 1 parses without error - a second SELECT keyword is silently accepted as a nested statement
issues.body:
### Search before asking

- [x] I searched the [issues](https://github.com/sqlfluff/sqlfluff/issues) and found no similar issues.

### What Happened

`SELECT SELECT 1` parses with zero violations on `ansi` and `bigquery`: the second `SELECT` is read as a nested `select_statement` used as the outer select clause's expression, equivalent to `SELECT (SELECT 1)` but without requiring the parentheses. BigQuery and Snowflake both reject the unparenthesized form as a syntax error, so this is a grammar gap, not an intentional extension.

### Expected Behaviour

A `PRS` parsing violation, the same way three consecutive `WHERE` keywords (`WHERE WHERE WHERE (x = 1)`) already correctly produce one.

### Observed Behaviour

Zero violations; `sqlfluff lint` reports `All Finished!`. `sqlfluff parse` shows the second `SELECT` starting a nested `select_statement` segment inside the first one's `select_clause_element`, with no requirement for surrounding parentheses.

Confirmed this is a real syntax error, not a style preference: tested against a live BigQuery project via a dry-run query -

```
SELECT SELECT 1
→ Error 400: Syntax error: Unexpected keyword SELECT at [1:8]
```

while the parenthesized form runs cleanly (`SELECT (SELECT 1)` → succeeds). Also rejected by BigQuery Studio's UI and Snowflake's UI - not engine-specific, this is invalid SQL generally.

### How to reproduce

```sql
SELECT SELECT 1;
```

`sqlfluff lint --dialect bigquery example.sql` (also reproduces with `--dialect ansi`) reports no violations at all.

### Dialect

Reproduces on both `ansi` and `bigquery` - appears to be a core grammar issue (likely in how `select_statement` becomes reachable as a bare expression/`select_clause_element`), not a BigQuery-specific dialect extension.

### Version

`sqlfluff, version 4.3.0`, Python 3.13.9.

### Configuration

No `.sqlfluff` config file used for this repro - bare `sqlfluff lint --dialect bigquery example.sql` / `sqlfluff parse --dialect bigquery example.sql` with no other flags or config.

issues.title: Oracle positional substitution variables are not parsed
issues.body:
### Search before asking

- [x] I searched the [issues](https://github.com/sqlfluff/sqlfluff/issues) and found no similar issues.


### What Happened

SQLFluff's Oracle dialect does not successfully parse positional SQL*Plus substitution variables such as `&1` and `&&1`, despite the support added by commit [87242d4fc2add5e0de5a7f252c810139260c5ed6](https://github.com/sqlfluff/sqlfluff/commit/87242d4fc2add5e0de5a7f252c810139260c5ed6).

The introducing commit added lexer and grammar changes, plus fixture coverage, but the resulting positional tokens are still emitted as generic `raw` segments. The parser therefore cannot consume them as `substitution_variable` segments.

Affected syntax:

```sql
SELECT &1, &2
FROM employees
WHERE employee_id = &3;

SELECT *
FROM employees
WHERE employee_id = &&1;
```

Concatenated SQL*Plus forms are also relevant:

```sql
@LOGANALYZER_&&CLIENT_OS..SQL &&1. &&2.
```

Possible root cause (to be investigated further):

The introducing commit registers this lexer matcher:

```python
RegexLexer("substitution_variable", r"&&?\d+", CodeSegment)
```

Although the matcher name is `substitution_variable`, its `segment_class` is `CodeSegment`, whose segment type is `raw`. The lexer therefore does not produce a typed `substitution_variable` segment.

`SubstitutionVariableSegment` attempts to consume positional variables using:

```python
TypedParser("substitution_variable", CodeSegment)
```

Because the lexer output is not typed as `substitution_variable`, the positional grammar does not match in expression contexts.



### Expected Behaviour

The Oracle dialect should parse positional substitution variables without producing parse violations. The variables should be represented as `substitution_variable` segments, consistently with named variables such as `&MYTABLE` and `&&myv`.

### Observed Behaviour

The fixture fails with unparsable sections such as:

```text
Found unparsable section: '&1, &2'
Found unparsable section: '= &3'
Found unparsable section: '= &&1'
```

Direct lexer inspection shows that the positional text is emitted as generic raw text:

```text
&1   -> raw
&&1  -> raw
```

Named variables continue to use the existing ampersand-plus-identifier path.

Also note that using the following command to generate fixtures fails:

```python
%> python test/generate_parse_fixture_yml.py -d oracle
Match Pattern Received:
        filter=* dialect=oracle new-only=False
Found 101 file(s) to generate
'oracle' complete.              3 fails. ⚠️
  - 'sqlplus_commands.sql'
  - 'trailing_decimal_numeric.sql'
  - 'substitution_variable.sql'
[SQLParseError('Could not parse: test/fixtures/dialects/oracle/sqlplus_commands.sql'), SQLParseError('Could not parse: test/fixtures/dialects/oracle/trailing_decimal_numeric.sql'), SQLParseError('Could not parse: test/fixtures/dialects/oracle/substitution_variable.sql')]
FAILED TO GENERATE ALL CASES
```

### How to reproduce

Run the existing Oracle fixture test:

```bash
source .venv/bin/activate
pytest -q test/dialects/dialects_test.py -k 'oracle and substitution_variable'
```

Or parse a minimal example:

```bash
sqlfluff parse repro.sql --dialect oracle
```

where `repro.sql` contains:

```sql
SELECT &1, &2 FROM employees WHERE employee_id = &3;
```

Also try `python test/generate_parse_fixture_yml.py -d oracle` (see details on "observed behavior").

### Dialect

oracle

### Version

4.3.0

### Configuration

Default.

issues.body:

### What Happened

SQLFluff's Oracle dialect does not fully parse Oracle constraint state modifiers at table level or column level.

The affected modifiers include:

- `ENABLE` / `DISABLE`
- `VALIDATE` / `NOVALIDATE`
- `RELY` / `NORELY`
- `DEFERRABLE` / `NOT DEFERRABLE`
- `INITIALLY IMMEDIATE` / `INITIALLY DEFERRED`

These modifiers are part of Oracle constraint syntax and can follow primary-key, unique, check, and foreign-key constraints.

Parsing failures.

It should parse the examples.

issues.title: CV12 raises AssertionError on valid SQL when a clause follows the WHERE clause
issues.body:
### Search before asking

- [X] I searched the [issues](https://github.com/sqlfluff/sqlfluff/issues) and found no similar issues.

### What Happened

Rule CV12 raises `AssertionError` on valid ANSI SQL. The linter reports it as an internal error and asks the user to open an issue. The default rule set triggers it, so no `--rules` flag is needed.

The trigger is a join condition in a WHERE clause with any clause after it. `ORDER BY`, `GROUP BY` and `LIMIT` all reproduce it.

### Expected Behaviour

CV12 reports the join condition and, under `fix`, moves it to an `ON` clause. The clause after the WHERE clause stays where it is.

### Observed Behaviour

```
$ printf 'SELECT foo.a FROM foo INNER JOIN bar WHERE foo.x = bar.y ORDER BY foo.a;\n' \
  | sqlfluff lint --dialect ansi -
CRITICAL   [CV12] Applying rule CV12 to 'stdin' threw an Exception:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File ".../sqlfluff/core/rules/base.py", line 619, in crawl
    res = self._eval(context=context)
  File ".../sqlfluff/rules/convention/CV12.py", line 65, in _eval
    return [lint_result for lint_result in self._eval_gen(context)]
  File ".../sqlfluff/rules/convention/CV12.py", line 290, in _eval_gen
    assert select_statement.segments[-1].is_type("where_clause")
AssertionError
== [stdin] FAIL
L:   1 | P:   1 | CV12 | Unexpected exception: ;
```

`src/sqlfluff/rules/convention/CV12.py:289-297` reaches the WHERE clause by position:

```python
else:
    assert select_statement.segments[-1].is_type("where_clause")
    assert select_statement.segments[-2].is_type("whitespace", "newline")
    yield LintResult(
        anchor=where_clause,
        fixes=[
            LintFix.delete(select_statement.segments[-2]),
            LintFix.delete(select_statement.segments[-1]),
        ],
    )
```

This branch runs when the whole WHERE clause moves to the join, so the rule deletes it. The WHERE clause is the last child of the select statement only when nothing follows it. `ORDER BY`, `GROUP BY` and `LIMIT` each add a later child.

The other arm of the same `if/else` at `CV12.py:278-288` reaches its target by lookup (`where_clause.get_child("expression")`), not by position.

### How to reproduce

```
printf 'SELECT foo.a FROM foo INNER JOIN bar WHERE foo.x = bar.y ORDER BY foo.a;\n' | sqlfluff lint --dialect ansi -
printf 'SELECT foo.a FROM foo INNER JOIN bar WHERE foo.x = bar.y GROUP BY foo.a;\n' | sqlfluff lint --dialect ansi -
printf 'SELECT foo.a FROM foo INNER JOIN bar WHERE foo.x = bar.y LIMIT 1;\n'         | sqlfluff lint --dialect ansi -
```

Each of the three crashes. The same query without the trailing clause is the control and gives two normal CV12 violations:

```
$ printf 'SELECT foo.a FROM foo INNER JOIN bar WHERE foo.x = bar.y;\n' | sqlfluff lint --dialect ansi -
== [stdin] FAIL
L:   1 | P:  23 | CV12 | Use `JOIN ... ON ...` instead of `WHERE ...` for join
                       | conditions. [convention.join_condition]
```

### Dialect

ansi. The branch is dialect independent.

### Version

```
sqlfluff, version 4.3.0
Python 3.12.12
```

Reproduced on `ddd83f1d7`.

### Configuration

None. The command line above carries the whole configuration.

issues.title: A .sqlfluffignore in a subdirectory is ignored one level down when the path is relative
issues.body:
### Search before asking

- [X] I searched the [issues](https://github.com/sqlfluff/sqlfluff/issues) and found no similar issues.

### What Happened

A `.sqlfluffignore` file in a subdirectory stops applying one level below itself when the path on the command line is relative. `sqlfluff lint .` lints the ignored files, and `sqlfluff fix .` rewrites them.

The same tree behaves correctly when you pass an absolute path.

### Expected Behaviour

A `.sqlfluffignore` file applies to every file below its own directory, as `docs/source/configuration/ignoring_configuration.rst` describes. The result must not depend on whether the path argument is relative or absolute.

### Observed Behaviour

`sub/deeper/b.sql` is linted and fixed, although `sub/.sqlfluffignore` holds `*.sql`.

```
$ sqlfluff lint .
== [sub/deeper/b.sql] FAIL
L:   1 | P:   7 | LT01 | Expected only single space before numeric literal. Found
                       | '    '. [layout.spacing]
L:   1 | P:  12 | LT01 | Expected only single space before 'from' keyword. Found
                       | '   '. [layout.spacing]
L:   1 | P:  15 | CP01 | Keywords must be consistently upper case.
                       | [capitalisation.keywords]
All Finished!

$ sqlfluff lint /tmp/sfign/proj
All Finished!
```

`sqlfluff fix .` then writes the ignored file:

```
$ cat sub/deeper/b.sql
SELECT    3   from t
$ sqlfluff fix . --force
== [sub/deeper/b.sql] FIXED
3 fixable linting violations found
$ cat sub/deeper/b.sql
SELECT 3 FROM t
```

The cause is in `src/sqlfluff/core/linter/discovery.py:199-203`:

```python
if not (
    dirname == inner_dirname
    or dirname.startswith(os.path.abspath(inner_dirname) + os.sep)
):
    inner_ignore_specs.remove((inner_dirname, inner_file, inner_spec))
```

`dirname` and `inner_dirname` both come from the same `os.walk(path)`, so both are relative when `path` is relative. Only the right side is made absolute. The `startswith` test is then always false and the spec is dropped as soon as the walk descends one level. The `dirname == inner_dirname` branch still holds, so a file in the same directory as the ignore file is ignored correctly. Only the levels below it leak.

### How to reproduce

```
mkdir -p /tmp/sfign/proj/sub/deeper
cd /tmp/sfign/proj
printf '[sqlfluff]\ndialect = ansi\n' > .sqlfluff
printf '*.sql\n' > sub/.sqlfluffignore
printf 'SELECT 1\n' > top.sql
printf 'SELECT 2\n' > sub/a.sql
printf 'SELECT    3   from t\n' > sub/deeper/b.sql

sqlfluff lint .                 # lists sub/deeper/b.sql, wrong
sqlfluff lint /tmp/sfign/proj   # lists top.sql only, correct
```

Directly on the discovery function:

```python
>>> from sqlfluff.core.linter.discovery import paths_from_path
>>> sorted(paths_from_path("."))
['sub/deeper/b.sql', 'top.sql']
>>> sorted(paths_from_path("/tmp/sfign/proj"))
['/tmp/sfign/proj/top.sql']
```

`sub/a.sql` sits next to the ignore file and is ignored in both runs.

### Dialect

ansi. The defect is in path discovery, so every dialect is affected.

### Version

```
sqlfluff, version 4.3.0
Python 3.12.12
```

Introduced in 16006dd0f (#6080).

### Configuration

`/tmp/sfign/proj/.sqlfluff`:

```
[sqlfluff]
dialect = ansi
```

`/tmp/sfign/proj/sub/.sqlfluffignore`:

```
*.sql
```

issues.title: RF05 raises IndexError on an all-underscore identifier, and false-positives on other dialects
issues.body:
### Search before asking

I searched the open issues and found nothing covering this. #6733 is a different RF05 false positive, on TSQL table-valued method aliases.

### What Happened

`RF05` raises `IndexError` on an identifier made only of underscores, and reports it as an internal error.

The rule strips underscores before it inspects the identifier:

```python
# We always allow underscores so strip them out
identifier = identifier.replace("_", "")
```

An identifier such as `_` therefore becomes an empty string, and the redshift temporary table check then reads index 0 of it.

### Expected Behaviour

`SELECT _ FROM t` lints cleanly. `_` holds no special characters, and the rule's own comment says underscores are always allowed.

### Observed Behaviour

On redshift, the rule crashes:

```
CRITICAL [RF05] Applying rule RF05 to 'q.sql' threw an Exception: string index out of range
  File "src/sqlfluff/rules/references/RF05.py", line 204, in _eval
    and identifier[0] == "#"
IndexError: string index out of range
L:   1 | P:   8 | RF05 | Unexpected exception: string index out of range;
                       | Could you open an issue at ...
```

On other dialects the `#` check is skipped, so the empty string reaches the alphanumeric test at line 221 and `"".isalnum()` is `False`, producing a false positive:

```
L:   1 | P:   8 | RF05 | Do not use special characters in identifiers.
```

I reproduced the false positive on postgres, snowflake, tsql and bigquery. On ansi a bare `_` does not parse, so the rule is never reached there.

### How to reproduce

`q.sql`:

```sql
SELECT _ FROM t
```

```
sqlfluff lint --dialect redshift --rules RF05 q.sql    # IndexError
sqlfluff lint --dialect postgres --rules RF05 q.sql    # false positive
```

### Dialect

redshift for the crash; postgres, snowflake, tsql and bigquery for the false positive.

### Version

sqlfluff 4.3.0, reproduced on `main`.

issues.title: Redshift dialect does not support scoped GRANT statements
issues.body:
### Search before asking

- [x] I searched the [issues](https://github.com/sqlfluff/sqlfluff/issues) and found no similar issues.


### What Happened

SQLFluff can't parse Redshift SQL scripts containing scoped GRANT statements.

### Expected Behaviour

Redshift allows to grant some/all privileges for all objects on the DATABASE or SCHEMA level, as described in https://docs.aws.amazon.com/redshift/latest/dg/r_GRANT.html, under `Granting scoped permissions` section. I'd expect SQLFluff to be able to parse these statements, so scripts containing them can enjoy all the goodness `sqlfluff fix` provides.

### Observed Behaviour

Running `sqlfluff fix example.sql` on a script with scoped GRANT statements results in `templating/parsing errors found`, which prevents it from fixing rule violations. Seems that this feature is not supported yet by Redshift dialect. 

### How to reproduce

Let's create a small script with a violation of `layout.spacing`, which I'd like to have fixed by SQLFluff. The script grants a scoped permission:
```bash
echo "GRANT    SELECT FOR TABLES IN DATABASE analytics TO developer_user;" > example.sql
```

Now it's time to fix it:
```bash
uv run sqlfluff fix ./example.sql
```

Which yields:

issues.title: Analyzer crashes with AssertionError on a non-lambda `->` operator (duckdb/trino JSON arrow)
issues.body:
### Search before asking
Yes — no existing issue covers the `->` JSON/arrow operator crashing the analyzer (closed #6683 is a different Snowflake-lambda concern).

### What Happened

Linting valid SQL that uses the `->` operator as a **JSON/arrow operator** (not a lambda) crashes the analyzer with an `AssertionError`, surfaced as "Unexpected exception" violations on several rules.

Reproduced on sqlfluff 4.3.0:

```python
from sqlfluff.core import Linter, FluffConfig
lnt = Linter(config=FluffConfig(overrides={"dialect": "duckdb"}))
res = lnt.lint_string("select 1::json -> 'a' from t")
print(sorted({v.rule_code() for v in res.violations if "Unexpected exception" in str(v.description)}))
# ['AL04', 'AL05', 'AM04', 'RF01', 'RF02', 'RF03', 'ST05']
```

Each traceback ends at:
```
File ".../sqlfluff/utils/analysis/select.py", line 417, in _get_lambda_argument_columns
    assert len(argument_segments) == 1
AssertionError
```

Also reproduces on **trino** (identical 7-rule crash). The SQL parses with zero lex/parse errors — it's valid JSON extraction.

`_get_lambda_argument_columns` treats every `->` as a lambda arrow (`param -> body`) and asserts exactly one lambda-parameter segment precedes it. When `->` is instead a binary operator whose left operand isn't a single parameter — a cast (`1::json -> 'a'`), a function call (`map_from_entries(l) -> 'k'`), etc. — `argument_segments` is empty and the hard assert fires, taking down the whole analysis pass.

### Expected Behaviour

A `->` that isn't a lambda should contribute no lambda argument columns, not crash. Genuine lambdas (`x -> x + 1`, `(x, y) -> x + y`) should keep working.

### Are you willing to work on and submit a PR?
Yes — PR incoming (replace the hard assert with a guard; keeps lambda extraction intact).

### Version
sqlfluff 4.3.0 / main · dialects: duckdb, trino (confirmed)

issues.title: CV11 autofix corrupts a shorthand cast whose operand has multiple children (e.g. array subscript a[1]::INT)
issues.body:
### Search before asking
Yes — the existing CV11 issues (#8171 CONVERT arg-swap, #8177, #7927 try_cast) are about `CONVERT`/`try_cast`; this is a different shorthand-cast corruption.

### What Happened

`sqlfluff fix` with CV11 (`convention.casting_style`) silently corrupts a valid `::` shorthand cast whose left operand parses into more than one child — e.g. an array subscript `a[1]::INT`. The array subscript is destroyed and the produced SQL is wrong, presented as a safe fix.

Reproduced on sqlfluff 4.3.0:

```python
from sqlfluff.core import Linter, FluffConfig
cfg = FluffConfig.from_string('[sqlfluff]\ndialect = ansi\nrules = CV11\n')
sql = 'SELECT CAST(z AS INT) AS zz, a[1]::INT AS y FROM t'
print(Linter(config=cfg).lint_string(sql, fix=True).tree.raw)
```

Output:
```
SELECT CAST(z AS INT) AS zz, cast(cast(a as [1]) as INT) AS y FROM t
```

The `a[1]` subscript is gone — it's been turned into `cast(a as [1])`. The leading `CAST(z AS INT)` is only there so `consistent` mode picks the `cast` style and rewrites the shorthand.

### Expected Behaviour

`a[1]::INT` should become `cast(a[1] as INT)` — the full operand preserved. The `convert` styles similarly mangle it (`convert(INT, convert([1], a))`).

Root cause: in `Rule_CV11._eval`, the shorthand-handling sites take the SQL data type from the `cast_expression` child at a fixed positional index, so when the operand is `column_reference` + `array_accessor` they grab the wrong child. (The `preferred_type_casting_style = cast` path, which reconstructs differently, produces the correct result — so the operand and the type are separable.)

### Are you willing to work on and submit a PR to address the issue?
Yes — PR incoming (identify the `data_type` child by type rather than index, preserving the whole operand; covers the cast and convert shorthand sites, with rule test cases).

### Version
sqlfluff 4.3.0 / main

### dialect
ansi (also affects any dialect with array subscripts)

issues.title: Snowflake: no grammar for alert DDL — CREATE / ALTER / DROP ALERT are unparsable
issues.body:
### Search before asking

- [x] I searched the [issues](https://github.com/sqlfluff/sqlfluff/issues) and found no similar issues.

### Description

The `snowflake` dialect has no grammar for alert DDL. `CREATE [OR REPLACE] ALERT`, `ALTER ALERT` and
`DROP ALERT` are all unparsable. The only occurrence of `ALERT` in the dialect is the `EXECUTE ALERT`
*privilege* inside a `GRANT` clause:

https://github.com/sqlfluff/sqlfluff/blob/main/src/sqlfluff/dialects/dialect_snowflake.py#L3891

Documented syntax — [CREATE ALERT](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/sql-reference/sql/create-alert):

```
CREATE [ OR REPLACE ] ALERT [ IF NOT EXISTS ] <name>
  [ [ WITH ] TAG ( <tag_name> = '<tag_value>' [ , ... ] ) ]
  [ SCHEDULE = '{ <num> MINUTE | USING CRON <expr> <time_zone> }' ]
  [ WAREHOUSE = <warehouse_name> ]
  [ COMMENT = '<string_literal>' ]
  [ CONFIG = '<configuration_string>' ]
  [ RUNBOOK = '<string_literal>' ]
  [ SUSPEND_ALERT_AFTER_NUM_FAILURES = <number> ]
  IF( EXISTS(
    <condition>
  ))
  THEN
    <action>
```

`ALTER ALERT` (with `RESUME` / `SUSPEND` / `SET` / `UNSET` / `MODIFY CONDITION` /
`MODIFY ACTION`), `DROP ALERT`, `DESCRIBE ALERT`, `SHOW ALERTS` and `EXECUTE ALERT` are separate
documented commands.

Minimal repro:

```sql
CREATE OR REPLACE ALERT my_alert
    WAREHOUSE = my_wh
    SCHEDULE = '60 MINUTE'
    IF (EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM t))
    THEN CALL my_proc();
```

```
sqlfluff lint alert.sql --dialect snowflake
== [alert.sql] FAIL
L:   1 | P:   1 |  PRS | Line 1, Position 1: Found unparsable section: 'CREATE OR
                       | REPLACE ALERT my_alert ...'
```

Reproduced on 4.1.0, 4.3.0 and `main`.

### Use case

Alerts are how a Snowflake-only deployment gets notified about anything — we use them for load
failures, reconciliation aborts and row-count anomalies, with the alert bodies checked into version
control alongside the rest of the SQL.

There is a second-order cost worth mentioning, because it is what made us go looking. An unparsable
section swallows everything to EOF and no rule fires inside it, so a single `CREATE ALERT` turns off
**every style rule for the remainder of the file** — under `--ignore parsing` those files report zero
findings and look conformant. In our repo 11 files are unlinted purely because they contain alert
DDL, including four whose *entire* purpose is an alert definition.

Happy to be told this belongs behind a more general "unsupported statement" story instead; filing it
because the statement is stable, widely used and fully documented.

### Dialect

snowflake

### Are you willing to work on and submit a PR to address the issue?

- [x] Yes I am willing to submit a PR!

Willing, though I would appreciate a maintainer view first on scope — whether to land
`CREATE`/`ALTER`/`DROP` together or start with `CREATE ALERT` alone.

### Code of Conduct

- [x] I agree to follow this project's [Code of Conduct](https://github.com/sqlfluff/sqlfluff/blob/main/CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md)

issues.title: Snowflake: RAISE <exception_name> is unparsable; only the argument-less RAISE parses
issues.body:
### Search before asking

- [x] I searched the [issues](https://github.com/sqlfluff/sqlfluff/issues) and found no similar issues.

(Closest prior art: #6664 and #4855, both about `DECLARE` of `RESULTSET`/cursors — those now parse.
This is the `RAISE` statement itself.)

### What Happened

`RAISE <exception_name>;` is unparsable in the `snowflake` dialect. Only the argument-less form
`RAISE;` parses.

`ScriptingRaiseStatementSegment` matches the bare keyword, with no place for the exception name:

https://github.com/sqlfluff/sqlfluff/blob/main/src/sqlfluff/dialects/dialect_snowflake.py#L11085

```python
type = "scripting_raise_statement"
match_grammar = Ref.keyword("RAISE")
```

Per [the RAISE docs](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/sql-reference/snowflake-scripting/raise) the
syntax is `RAISE <exception_name> ;`, and the name is omitted **only** when re-raising the current
exception from inside a handler. So the grammar currently accepts only the exceptional case and
rejects the documented normal one.

Because an unparsable section swallows the remainder of the file, one `RAISE MY_EXCEPTION;` silently
disables **every style rule from that line to EOF** — which is how this went unnoticed in our repo
for a long time: the affected files reported zero findings under `--ignore parsing`.

### Expected Behaviour

The example from the Snowflake documentation parses.

### Observed Behaviour

The documentation's own example fails, on 4.1.0, 4.3.0 and `main`:

```
== [doc_example.sql] FAIL
L:   4 | P:   5 |  PRS | Line 4, Position 5: Found unparsable section: 'RAISE
                       | MY_EXCEPTION'
```

### How to reproduce

Verbatim from the RAISE documentation page:

```sql
DECLARE
    MY_EXCEPTION EXCEPTION (-20002, 'Raised MY_EXCEPTION.');
BEGIN
    RAISE MY_EXCEPTION;
END;
```

```
sqlfluff lint doc_example.sql --dialect snowflake
```

For contrast, all of these already parse cleanly, which narrows it to the name argument:

```sql
BEGIN RAISE; END;                                  -- ok
DECLARE e_bad EXCEPTION (-20980, 'nope');          -- ok
DECLARE res RESULTSET; BEGIN res := (SELECT 1 AS a); RETURN TABLE(res); END;   -- ok
```

### Dialect

snowflake

### Version

Reproduced on 4.1.0, 4.3.0 and `main` (commit installed from `git+https://github.com/sqlfluff/sqlfluff@main`, 2026-08-21).

```
sqlfluff, version 4.3.0
Python 3.12
```

### Configuration

```
[sqlfluff]
dialect = snowflake
templater = raw
```

Also reproduces with no config file at all, via `--dialect snowflake`.

### Are you willing to work on and submit a PR to address the issue?

- [x] Yes I am willing to submit a PR!

Making the exception name an optional trailing identifier fixes it. I have this working locally —
`RAISE;` keeps parsing, the documented form parses, and across a ~41k-line Snowflake repo it takes
the unparsable-file count from 70 to 22. PR to follow with dialect fixtures.

### Code of Conduct

- [x] I agree to follow this project's [Code of Conduct](https://github.com/sqlfluff/sqlfluff/blob/main/CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md)

### Search before asking

### What Happened

Running `sqlfluff lint --dialect mysql` on this MySQL query (simplified for reproduction)

```mysql
SELECT 1 FROM a LEFT JOIN ((b INNER JOIN c ON TRUE)) ON TRUE;
```

```sh
sqlfluff lint --dialect mysql sql/views/test.sql
== [sql/views/test.sql] FAIL

                       | JOIN ((b INNER JOIN c ON TRUE)) ON ...'
WARNING: Parsing errors found and dialect is set to 'mysql'. Have you configured your dialect correctly?
All Finished 📜 🎉!
```

But this query is valid MySQL and executes successfully on my MySQL 8.4.10 server when replacing a, b, and c with real table names.

If you remove the extra parentheses around the right-hand side of the join:

The mysql dialect parser should not fail to parse due to a set of redundant parentheses around a nested join.

### Observed Behaviour

Parsing error on valid MySQL.

```bash
printf 'SELECT 1 FROM a LEFT JOIN ((b INNER JOIN c ON TRUE)) ON TRUE;\n' | sqlfluff lint - --dialect mysql
```

issues.title: Databricks magic dialect linting LT01 issues
issues.body:
### Search before asking

- [x] I searched the [issues](https://github.com/sqlfluff/sqlfluff/issues) and found no similar issues.


### What Happened

I get a linting error when using the feature proposed in https://github.com/sqlfluff/sqlfluff/issues/7877 on even the most simple notebook.

> LT01 Expected single whitespace between magic start and magic line. [layout.spacing]

For example, we can try linting the included test fixture:

```bash
$ sqlfluff lint -d databricks test/fixtures/dialects/databricks/magic_line.sql
== [test/fixtures/dialects/databricks/magic_line.sql] FAIL                                                                                                                                                   
L:   3 | P:   1 | LT01 | Expected single whitespace between magic start and magic
                       | line. [layout.spacing]
L:  14 | P:   1 | LT01 | Expected single whitespace between magic start and magic
                       | line. [layout.spacing]
L:  24 | P:   1 | LT01 | Expected single whitespace between magic start and magic
                       | line. [layout.spacing]
```
The LT01 here makes no sense.

### Expected Behaviour

No linting error.

### Observed Behaviour

We get an LT01.

issues.title: oracle: bare "/" in CREATE VIEW ... AS SELECT misparsed as SQL*Plus slash-buffer-executor (regression in 4.3.0)
issues.body:
### Search before asking

- [x] I searched the [issues](https://github.com/sqlfluff/sqlfluff/issues) and found no similar issues.


### What Happened

While upgrading from 4.2.0 to 4.3.0, we found what looked like an [ST03](https://github.com/sqlfluff/sqlfluff/issues/8250) false positive, but tracing it back, the real defect is in the parser: a bare (unparenthesized) `/` division operator in the SELECT/WHERE of a CREATE VIEW ... AS SELECT ... statement (Oracle dialect) gets misparsed as the SQL*Plus slash-buffer-executor. Everything after it collapses into one opaque unparsable section, so any rule needing structure past that point, ST03 in our case; misbehaves as a downstream symptom. This is not every use of `/`: wrapping it in parens, or having it already sit inside a function call's parens, avoids it. Measured against our ~2,900 SQL files: 64 of 685 CREATE VIEW files containing a `/` are actually affected.

Examples:
`where sample_time > sysdate - 1/24` → **breaks** (bare, unparenthesized division)
`where sample_time > sysdate - (1/24)` → **parses fine** (wrapped in parens)
`round(write.value / 1024 / 1024) as write_mb` → **parses fine** (the whole division sits inside round(...)'s own parens)
`nvl(bytes, 0) / 1024 / 1024 as size_mb` → **breaks** (the nvl(...) call only wraps its own arguments, the / 1024 / 1024 trailing it is still bare/unparenthesized at the top level)


### Expected Behaviour

`/` inside `CREATE VIEW ... AS SELECT` ... should parse as division, same as `CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT` and same as it did in 4.2.0.

### Observed Behaviour

A bare `/` is consumed as `slash_buffer_executor`; the same division wrapped in parens parses fine.

### How to reproduce

Three conditions required, removing any one fixes it:

1) Statement is CREATE VIEW ... AS SELECT ... (CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT is fine).
2) SELECT/WHERE contains /.
3) That / is not already inside parens (its own or a function call's).

repro.sql as 
```
CREATE VIEW myview AS
select 1 / 100 as z from dual;
```

`sqlfluff parse --dialect oracle repro.sql`
Result: PRS | Found unparsable section: '100 as z from dual;'. Expected: clean parse.

Isolation notes: `CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT` unaffected; `+`/`-`/`*` unaffected; bare `WITH ... SELECT (no CREATE VIEW`) unaffected; literal vs. column operand doesn't matter.

### Dialect

oracle

### Version

Introduced in 4.3.0. Confirmed clean in 4.2.0

### Configuration

No project-specific configuration needed; a bare --dialect oracle on the CLI reproduces it:

pip install sqlfluff==4.3.0
sqlfluff lint --dialect oracle --rules ST03 repro.sql

issues.title: Bracketed matches an empty body even when its content grammar is required
issues.body:
### Search before asking

- [x] I searched the issues and found no similar issues.

### What Happened

`Bracketed(...)` successfully matches empty brackets `()` even when its content grammar contains required (non-optional) elements. In `Bracketed.match` (`src/sqlfluff/core/parser/grammar/sequence.py`), the content match result is never checked: when the content grammar fails, matching proceeds directly to the end-bracket check, so `()` (where the end bracket immediately follows the start bracket) always matches, in STRICT parse mode too. Non-empty invalid content is correctly rejected (the end-bracket match fails at the leftover content), so this only affects the empty-body case.

This makes it impossible for a dialect to express "these brackets must not be empty". Examples in the Snowflake dialect: `WORKLOAD_IDENTITY = ()` (docs require `TYPE`), `OIDC_AUDIENCE_LIST = ()` (requires at least one string), `IN ()` — all parse without an unparsable section today. Spotted while working on #8367 (see review discussion there).

### Expected Behaviour

When the content grammar of a `Bracketed` cannot match an empty sequence (i.e. it contains required elements), empty brackets should fail to match in STRICT mode (or produce an unparsable section in GREEDY mode).

### Observed Behaviour

Empty brackets always match regardless of the content grammar.

### How to reproduce

```python
from sqlfluff.core import Linter

linter = Linter(dialect="snowflake")
parsed = linter.parse_string("ALTER USER u SET WORKLOAD_IDENTITY = ();")
print([v for v in parsed.violations if v.rule_code() == "PRS"])  # [] — no parse error
```

### Dialect

snowflake (but the behaviour is dialect-independent — it's in the core `Bracketed` grammar)

### Version

main (f26ed33), also reproduces on 4.3.0

### Configuration

Default.

issues.title: LT02 forces a line break before `LATERAL` keyword of the first lateral join only when a second sibling join follows it
issues.body:
### Search before asking

- [x] I searched the [issues](https://github.com/sqlfluff/sqlfluff/issues) and found no similar issues.


### What Happened

When a `FROM` clause's bracketed subquery is followed by 2+ consecutive `CROSS JOIN LATERAL` clauses, `LT02` requires the *first* `LATERAL` to be pushed onto its own indented line, but has no complaint about the *second* one staying on the same line as `CROSS JOIN`. If only one `JOIN LATERAL` clause is present, it's allowed to stay on one line with no violation at all.

The content of the two join clauses doesn't matter -- swapping which one comes first just moves the forced break to whichever one is now first.

### Expected Behaviour

`CROSS JOIN LATERAL` stays on the same line regardless of how many such statements are present.

### Observed Behavior

Keyword `LATERAL` of the first join is pushed to the next line with subsequent clause contents indented.

### How to reproduce

Lint is passed with single join:
```sql
SELECT *
FROM (
    SELECT 1 AS id
) t
    CROSS JOIN LATERAL (
        SELECT 1 AS x
    ) a
```

```
$ sqlfluff lint --dialect postgres min_single.sql --rules LT02
All Finished!
```

List isn't passed with multiple joins:
```sql
SELECT *
FROM (
    SELECT 1 AS id
) t
    CROSS JOIN LATERAL (
        SELECT 1 AS x
    ) a
    CROSS JOIN LATERAL (
        SELECT 1 AS y
    ) b
```

```
$ sqlfluff lint --dialect postgres min.sql --rules LT02
L:   5 | P:  15 | LT02 | Expected line break and indent of 8 spaces before
                       | 'LATERAL'. [layout.indent]
L:   6 | P:   1 | LT02 | Expected indent of 12 spaces. [layout.indent]
L:   7 | P:   1 | LT02 | Expected indent of 8 spaces. [layout.indent]
```

### Dialect

`postgres`

### Version

sqlfluff: 4.2.2
Python: 3.12.10

### Configuration

```ini
[sqlfluff]
dialect = postgres

[sqlfluff:indentation]
indented_joins = True
```

issues.title: ClickHouse: a couple of issues with the ```CREATE DICTIONARY``` statement
issues.body:
### Search before asking

- [x] I searched the [issues](https://github.com/sqlfluff/sqlfluff/issues) and found no similar issues.


### What Happened

The create dictionary statement is not parsed correctly in the clickhouse dialect in the following cases:
1. Primary key values are bracketed, e. g. ```PRIMARY KEY (id)```.
2. Source [Null](https://clickhouse.com/docs/reference/statements/create/dictionary/sources/null) is used.
3. [RANGE](https://clickhouse.com/docs/reference/statements/create/dictionary/layouts/range-hashed) clause is used (if range_hashed dictionary layout types are used).
4. The order of SOURCE, LAYOUT, LIFETIME, SETTINGS, RANGE clauses is not strictly defined, e.g SOURCE -> LAYOUT -> LIFETIME -> SETTINGS -> RANGE is valid, LAYOUT -> LIFETIME -> RANGE -> SETTINGS -> SOURCE is also valid, i.e. the order does not matter as long as the clauses come after PRIMARY KEY and before COMMENT. Right now only  SOURCE -> LAYOUT -> LIFETIME -> SETTINGS order is parsed.

CREATE DICTIONARY is parsed correctly

### Observed Behaviour

issues.title: Support quiet output consistently across lint, fix, and format
issues.body:
AI written, human reviewed.

### Search before asking

- [x] I searched the [issues](https://github.com/sqlfluff/sqlfluff/issues) and found no similar issues.

### Description

Make `-q`/`--quiet` available consistently for `sqlfluff lint`, `sqlfluff fix`, and `sqlfluff format`.

Currently, `fix` supports `--quiet`, while successful `lint` and `format` runs always print the `All Finished 📜 🎉!` completion message. Tools which invoke SQLFluff as a linter or formatter must therefore filter an exact human-readable banner to remain silent. That filtering is brittle if the message changes.

Quiet mode should suppress routine success output, including the completion message, while preserving diagnostics, machine-readable output, exit codes, formatted stdin output, and interactive prompts.

### Use case

Editor integrations, build systems, and formatter wrappers should be able to run SQLFluff without printing routine success messages. They should only need to inspect SQLFluff's output when there is a diagnostic or other actionable result, without maintaining output-text filters around the CLI.

### Dialect

Not dialect-specific.

issues.title: [tsql] Align aliases with leading commas and '=' syntax adds spurious space before column name
issues.body:
### Search before asking

- [x] I searched the [issues](https://github.com/sqlfluff/sqlfluff/issues) and found no similar issues.


### What Happened

When using the '=' alias syntax in TSQL query and leading commas, fixing sometimes adds extra spaces after the leading comma and before the alias designation. This does not appear to happen when using the more standard '<field> AS <alias_name>' syntax:

For example, refer to this starting query:

```
SELECT
    FirstCol = 'Some Value'
    , SecondCol = 'Some other value'
    , ThirdCol = 'yet another val'
    , t.NonaliasedCol
FROM TestTable AS t
;

SELECT
    'Some Value' AS FirstCol
    , 'Some other value' AS SecondCol
    , 'yet another val' AS ThirdCol 
    , t.NonaliasedCol
FROM TestTable AS t
;
```

### Expected Behaviour

This is the expected outcome:

```
SELECT
    FirstCol    = 'Some Value'
    , SecondCol = 'Some other value'
    , ThirdCol  = 'yet another val'
    , t.NonaliasedCol
FROM TestTable AS t
;

SELECT
    'Some Value'         AS FirstCol
    , 'Some other value' AS SecondCol
    , 'yet another val'  AS ThirdCol
    , t.NonaliasedCol
FROM TestTable AS t
;
```

### Observed Behaviour

When formatting/fixing this is the output (notice the extra spaces before 'SecondCol' and 'ThirdCol' alaises with the '=' alias syntax statement):

```
SELECT
    FirstCol     = 'Some Value'
    ,  SecondCol = 'Some other value'
    ,  ThirdCol  = 'yet another val'
    , t.NonaliasedCol
FROM TestTable AS t
;

SELECT
    'Some Value'         AS FirstCol
    , 'Some other value' AS SecondCol
    , 'yet another val'  AS ThirdCol
    , t.NonaliasedCol
FROM TestTable AS t
;

```

```
FROM TestTable AS t
;
```
